## About ISACA

For more than 50 years, ISACA® (www. isaca.org) has advanced the best talent, expertise and learning in technology. ISACA equips individuals with knowledge, credentials, education and community to progress their careers and transform their organizations, and enables enterprises to train and build quality teams. Among those credentials, ISACA advances and validates business-critical skills and knowledge through the globally respected Certified Information Systems Auditor® (CISA®), Certified in Risk and Information Systems Control® (CRISC®), Certified Information Security Manager® (CISM®), Certified in the Governance of Enterprise IT® (CGEIT®) and Cera  rd       (     and learning organization that leverages the expertise of its 145,000 members who work in information security, governance, assurance, risk and privacy to drive innovation through technology. It has a presence in 188 countries, including more than 220 chapters worldwide.

## Disclaimer

ISACA has designed and created the CISM® Review Manual 16th Edition primarily as an educational resource to assist individuals preparing to take the CISM certification exam. It was produced independently from the CISM exam and the CISM Certification Working Group, which has no responsibility for its content. Copies of past exams are not released to the public and were not made available to ISACA for preparation of this publication. ISACA makes no representations or warranties whatsoever with regard to these or other ISACA publications assuring candidates' passage of the CISM exam.

## CISMReviewManual16thEdition

ISACA is pleased to offer the sixteenth edition of the CISM® Review Manual. The purpose of the manual is to provide CISM candidates with information and references to assist in the preparation and study for the Certified Information Security Manager® (CISM) exam.

The CISM® Review Manual is updated regularly to keep pace with rapid changes in the management of information security. As with previous manuals, the sixteenth edition is the result of contributions from many qualified authorities who have generously volunteered their time and expertise. We respect and appreciate their contributions and hope their efforts provide extensive educational value to CISM manual readers.

The sample questions contained in this manual are designed to depict the types of questions typically found on the CISM exam and to give further clarity to the content presented in this manual. The CISM exam is a practice-based exam. Simply reading the reference material in this manual will not properly prepare candidates for the exam. The self-assessment questions are included for guidance only. Scoring results do not indicate future individual exam success.

Certification has resulted in a positive impact on many careers, including worldwide recognition for professional experience and enhanced knowledge and skills. The CISM certification is designed for IT and business professionals who have hands-on experience with information security management. ISACA wishes you success with the CISM exam.

## New-CISM Job Practice

Beginning in 2022, the Certified Information Security Manager® exam will test the new CISM job practice.

An international job practice analysis is conducted periodically to maintain the validity of the CISM certification program. A new job practice forms the basis of the CISM exam beginning in 2022.

The primary focus areas of the job practice are the current tasks performed and the knowledge used by CISMs. By gathering evidence of the current work practice of CISMs, ISACA ensures that the CISM program continues to meet the high standards set for the certification of professionals throughout the world.

The findings of the CISM job practice analysis are carefully considered and directly influence the development of new test specifications to ensure that the CISM exam reflects the most current best practices.

The new job practice reflects the areas of study to be tested. The complete CISM job practice can be found at www.isaca.org/credentialing/CISM.

| Old CISM Job Practice                                         | New CISM Job Practice                      |
|---------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Information Security Governance (24%)                         | Information Security Governance (17%)      |
| Information Risk Management (30%)                             | Information Security Risk Management (20%) |
| Information Security Program Development and Management (27%) | Information Security Program (33%)         |
| Information Security Incident Management (19%)                | Incident Management (30%)                  |

## About This Manual

## Overview

The CISM® Review Manual 16th Edition is a reference guide designed to assist candidates in preparing for the CISM examination. The manual is one source of preparation for the exam but should not be thought of as the only source or viewed as a comprehensive collection of all the information and experience required to pass the exam. No single publication offers such coverage and detail.

As candidates read the manual and encounter topics that are new to them or ones in which they feel their knowledge and experience are limited, additional references should be sought. The examination will be composed of questions testing the candidate's technical and practical knowledge, and ability to apply the knowledge (based on experience) in given situations.

## Organization of This Manual

The CISM Review Manual 16th Edition is divided into four chapters covering the CISM domains tested on the exam in the percentages listed below:

| Domain 1   | Information Security Governance      | 17 percent   |
|------------|--------------------------------------|--------------|
| Domain 2   | Information Security Risk Management | 20 percent   |
| Domain 3   | Information Security Program         | 33 percent   |
| Domain 4   | Incident Management                  | 30 percent   |

The manual has been developed and organized to assist in the study of these areas. Exam candidates should evaluate their strengths, based on knowledge and experience, in each of these areas.

Note: Each chapter defines the tasks that CISM candidates are expected to understand and includes a series of knowledge statements required to perform those tasks. These constitute the current practices for the IT risk practitioner. The detailed CISM job practice can be viewed at www.isaca.org/credentialing/CISM/CISM-jobpractice-areas.

## Format of This Manual

Each chapter of the CISM Review Manual follows the same format:

- The Overview section provides a summary of the focus of the chapter, along with:
- The domain exam content outline
- Related task statements
- Suggested resources for further study
- Self-assessment questions
- The Content section includes:
- Content to support the different areas of the job practice
- Definitions of terms commonly found on the exam

Please note that the manual is written in standard American English, except for material imported from publications written in International English.

Submit suggestions to enhance the review manual or suggested reference materials to studymaterials@isaca.org.

## Preparing for the CISM Exam

The CISM exam evaluates a candidate's practical knowledge based on experiences and application of the job practice domains as described in this review manual. We recommend that the candidate look to multiple resources to prepare for the exam, including this review manual and external publications. This section includes some tips for studying for the exam.

Read to understand which areas need more attention. See reference sources to expand knowledge and gain experience in those areas.

Actual exam questions test the candidate's practical application of relevant knowledge. At the end of each chapter, a sample self-assessment, consisting of questions, answers and explanations, introduces the question structure and general content. Remember that the sample questions may not be similar to questions appearing on the actual exam. Use reference material to find other publications that offer more detailed information on the topics addressed in this manual.

<!-- page: 20 -->

## Getting Started

Having adequate time to prepare for the CISM exam is critical. Most candidates spend between three and six months studying prior to taking the exam. Set aside a designated time each week to study, and perhaps increase study time as the exam date approaches. It helps to develop a study plan for preparing for the exam.

## Using the CISMReview Manual

The CISM Review Manual is divided into four chapters, each corresponding to a domain in the CISM job

| Review Manual Feature                 | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|---------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

The suggested references for each chapter are resources to help enhance study efforts.                                                     |

## Types of Questions on the CISM Exam

CISM exam questions are developed with the intent of measuring and testing practical knowledge and the application of information security management principles. All questions are presented in a multiplechoice format and are designed to elicit one best answer.

The candidate is cautioned to read each question carefully. Knowing that these types of questions are asked will go a long way toward answering them correctly. The best answer is one of the choices provided. There can be many potential solutions to the problems posed in the scenarios, depending on industry, geographical location, etc. It is advisable to consider the information provided in the question and to determine the best answer among the options provided.

Each CISM question has a stem (question) and four options (answer choices). The candidate is asked to choose the correct or best answer from the options. The stem may be in the form of a question or incomplete statement. In some instances, a scenario or description may be included. These questions normally describe a situation and require the candidate to answer two or more questions based on the information provided.

<!-- image -->

practice. While the review manual does not include every concept that could be tested on the CISM exam, it does cover a breadth of topics to provide a solid base for the exam candidate. The manual is one source of preparation for the exam and should not be thought of as the only source or viewed as a comprehensive collection of all the information and experience required to pass the exam.

## Features in the Review Manual

The CISM Review Manual includes several features to help candidates navigate the job practice and enhance learning and retention of the material.

<!-- page: 21 -->

<!-- image -->

A helpful approach to these questions includes the following:

- Read the entire stem and determine what the question is asking. Look for key words such as "best,""most," "first," etc., and key terms that may indicate which domain or concept is being tested.
- Read all the options, and then read the stem again to attempt to eliminate options based on initial understanding of the question.

Reread the remaining options and bring in any personal experience that may illuminate the best answer to the question.

## Preparing for the Exam

When preparing for the exam, the candidate should recognize that information security is a global profession, and the candidate's perceptions and experiences may not reflect the global position. Because the exam and CISM manuals are written for the international information security management community, the candidate must be flexible when reading about a condition that may contradict the candidate's experience.

- CISM Online Review Course
- CISM review courses (provided by local ISACA chapters and accredited training organizations)

## About the CISM Review Questions, Answers &amp; Explanations Manual

Candidates may also wish to enhance their study and preparation for the exam by using the CISM® Review Questions, Answers &amp; Explanations Manual 10'h Edition.

The CISM Review Questions, Answers &amp; Explanations Manual 10th Edition consists of 1,000 multiple-choice study questions, answers and explanations arranged in the domains of the current CISM job practice.

Questions in this publication are representative of the types of questions that could appear on the exam and include explanations of the correct and incorrect answers. Questions are sorted by the CISM domains and as a sample test. These publications are ideal for use in conjunction with the CISM Review Manual 16th Edition. These manuals can be used as study sources throughout the study process or as part of a final review to determine where candidates may need additional study. It should be noted that these questions and suggested answers are provided as examples; they are not actual questions from the examination and may differ in content from those that actually appear on the exam.

## 1 About the CISM Review Questions, Answers &amp; Explanations Database

Note that the CISM exam questions are written by experienced information security professionals from around the world. Each question on the exam is reviewed by ISACA's CISM Exam Item Development Working Group, which consists of international members. This geographic representation ensures that all exam questions are understood equally well in every country and language.

## Using ISACA Exam Preparation Resources

The CISM Review Manual can be used in conjunction with other CISM exam preparation activities. The following products are based on the CISM job practice, and referenced job practice areas can be used to find related content within the CISM Review Manual. These resources include:

The online database consists of the 1,000 questions, answers and explanations included in the CISM Review Questions, Answers &amp; Explanations Manual 10th Edition. With this product, CISM candidates can quickly identify their strengths and weaknesses by taking random sample exams of varying length and breaking the results down by domain. Sample exams can be chosen by domain, allowing for concentrated study, one domain at a time. Other sorting features, such as the omission of questions previously answered correctly, are available.

## Chapter 1:

## Information Security Governance

<!-- page: 24 -->

## Overview

This chapter reviews the body of knowledge and associated tasks necessary to develop an information security governance structure aligned with organizational objectives.

It provides an overview of what an information security manager needs to do in order to establish and maintain an information security governance framework and supporting processes to ensure that the information security strategy is aligned with organizational goals and objectives.

This domain represents 17 percent of the CISM examination (approximately 26 questions).

## Domain 1 Exam Content Outline

## A. Enterprise Governance

1. Organizational Culture
2. Legal, Regulatory and Contractual Requirements
3. Organizational Structures, Roles and Responsibilities

## B. Information Security Strategy

1. Information Security Strategy Development
2. Information Governance Frameworks and Standards
3. Strategic Planning

## Learning Objectives/Task Statements

Upon completion of this chapter, the information security manager should be able to:

- Identify internal and external influences to the organization that impact the information security strategy.
- Establish and/or maintain an information security strategy in alignment with organizational goals and objectives.
- Establish and/or maintain an information security governance framework.
- Integrate information security governance into corporate governance.
- Establish and maintain information security policies to guide the development of standards, procedures and guidelines.
- Develop business cases to support investments in information security.
- Gain ongoing commitment from senior leadership and other stakeholders to support the successful implementation of the information security strategy.
- Define, communicate and monitor information security responsibilities throughout the organization and lines of authority.
- Align the information security program with the operational objectives of other business functions.
- Integrate information security requirements into contracts and activities of external parties.
- Monitor external parties' adherence to established security requirements.
- Establish and/or maintain a process for information asset identification and classification.
- Identify legal, regulatory, organizational and other applicable compliance requirements.
- Establish and maintain processes to investigate and document information security incidents in accordance with legal and regulatory requirements.

## SELF-ASSESSMENT QUESTIONS

CISM exam questions are developed with the intent of measuring and testing practical knowledge in information security management. All questions are multiple choice and are designed for one best answer. Every CISM question has a stem (question) and four options (answer choices). The candidate is asked to choose the correct or best answer from the options. The stem may be in the form of a question or incomplete statement. Many times, a CISM examination question will require the candidate to choose the most likely or best answer.

In every case, the candidate is required to read the question carefully, eliminate known incorrect answers and then make the best choice possible. Knowing the format in which questions are asked, and how to study to gain knowledge of what will be tested, will go a long way toward answering them correctly.

1. A security strategy is important for an enterprise PRIMARILY because it:
- A. provides a basis for determining the best logical security architecture.
- B. provides the approach to achieving the outcomes management wants.
- C. provides users guidance on how to operate securely in everyday tasks.
- D. helps IT auditors ensure compliance with rules and regulations.
2. Which of the following is the MOT important reason to provide effective communication about information security?
- A. It makes information security more palatable to resistant employees.
- B. It mitigates the weakest link in the information security landscape.
- C. It informs business units about the information security strategy.
- D. It helps the enterprise conform to regulatory information security requirements.
3. Which of the following approaches BEST helps the information security manager achieve compliance with various regulatory requirements?
- A. Rely on corporate counsel to advise which regulations are the most relevant.
- B. Stay current with all relevant regulations and request legal interpretation.
- C. Involve all impacted departments and treat regulations as just another risk.
- D. Ignore many of the regulations that have no penalties.
4. The MOST important consideration in developing security policies is that:
- A. they are based on a threat profile.
- B. they are complete and no detail is left out.
- C. management signs off on them.
- D. all employees read and understand them.

<!-- page: 26 -->

5. The PRIMARY security objective in creating good procedures is:
- A. to make sure they work as intended.
- B. that they are unambiguous and meet the standards.
- C. that they are written in plain language and are widely distributed.
- D. that compliance can be monitored.
6. Which of the following MOST helps ensure that assignment of roles and responsibilities is effective?
- A. Senior management is in support of the assignments.
- B. The assignments are consistent with existing proficiencies.
- C. The assignments are mapped to required skills.
- D. The assignments are given on a voluntary basis.
7. Which of the following benefits is the MOST important to an enterprise with effective information security governance?
- A. Maintaining appropriate regulatory compliance
- B. Ensuring disruptions are within acceptable levels
- C. Prioritizing allocation of remedial resources
- D. Maximizing return on security investments
8. From an information security manager's perspective, the MOST important factors regarding data retention are:
- A. business and regulatory requirements.
- B. document integrity and destruction.
- C. media availability and storage.
- D. data confidentiality and encryption.
9. Which role is in the BEST position to review and confirm the appropriateness of a list of approved users?
- A. Data owner
- B. Information security manager
- C. Domain administrator
- D. Business manager
10. In implementing information security governance, the information security manager is PRIMARILY responsible for:
- A. developing the security strategy.
- B. reviewing the security strategy.
- C. communicating the security strategy.
- D. approving the security strategy.

## Chapter 1 ANSWER KEY

## Self-Assessment Questions

1. A. Policies have to be developed to support the security strategy, and an architecture can only be developed after policies are completed (i.e., the security strategy is not the basis for architecture— policies are).
- B. A security strategy will define the approach to achieving the security program outcomes management wants. It should also be a statement of how security aligns with and supports business objectives. It provides the basis for good security governance.
- C. A security strategy may include requirements for users to operate securely, but it does not address how that is to be accomplished.
- D. IT auditors do not determine compliance based on strategy but, rather, on elements such as standards and control objectives.
2. A. Effective communication may assist in making information security more palatable, but that is not the most important aspect.

B. Security failures are, in the majority of instances, directly attributable to lack of awareness or failure of employees to follow policies or procedures. Communication is important to ensure continued awareness of security policies and procedures among staff and business partners.

- C. Effective communication will allow business units to be informed about various aspects of information security, including the strategy, but it is not the most important aspect.
- D. Effective communication will assist in achieving compliance because it is unlikely that employees will be compliant with regulations unless they are informed about them. However, it is not the most important consideration.
3. A. Corporate counsel is generally involved primarily with stock issues and the associated filings required by regulators and with contract matters. It is unlikely that legal staff will be current on information security regulations and legal requirements.
- B. While it can be useful to stay abreast of all current and emerging regulations, it is, as a practical matter, nearly impossible—especially for a multinational company.
- C. Because departments such as human resources, finance and legal are most often subject to new regulations and must be involved in determining how best to meet the existing and emerging requirements, they typically would be most aware of these regulations. Treating regulations as another risk puts them in the proper perspective, and the mechanisms to deal with them should already exist. The fact that there are so many regulations makes it unlikely that they can all be specifically addressed efficiently. Many do not currently have significant consequences and may be addressed by compliance with other regulations. The most relevant response to regulatory requirements is to determine potential impact to the enterprise, just as with any other risk.
- D. Even if certain regulations have few or no penalties, ignoring them without consideration for other potential impacts (e.g., reputational damage) and whether they might be relevant to the enterprise is not a prudent approach.
4. A. The basis for developing relevant security policies is addressing viable threats to the enterprise, prioritized by the likelihood of occurrence and their potential impact on the business. The strictest policies apply to the areas of greatest business value. This ensures that protection proportionality is maintained.
- B. Policies are a statement of management's intent and direction at a high level and provide little, if any, detail.
- C. Management would not be asked to sign policies under development prior to their completion.
- D. Employees would not be reading and understanding the policies during development.
5. A. While it is important to make sure that procedures work as intended, their failure may not be a security issue.

<!-- page: 28 -->

- B. All the answers are important, but the first criterion must be to ensure that there is no ambiguity in the procedures and that, from a security perspective, they meet the applicable standards and comply with policy.
- C. Having clearly written procedures that are provided to all staff as needed is important, but it is not as important as ensuring that procedures comply with policy.
- D. Compliance is important, but it is essential that compliance is achieved with a correct procedure.
6. A. Senior management support is always important, but it is not crucial to the effectiveness of employee activities.
- B. The level of effectiveness of employees will be determined by their existing knowledge and capabilities—in other words, their proficiencies.
- C. Mapping roles to the tasks that are required can be useful, but it is no guarantee that people can perform the required tasks.
- D. While employees are more likely to be enthusiastic about a job they have volunteered for, it is not a requirement for them to be effective.
7. A. Maintaining appropriate regulatory compliance is a useful, but secondary, outcome. B. The bottom line of security efforts is to ensure that business can continue to operate with an acceptable level of disruption that does not unduly constrain revenue-producing 7. A. - B. The information security strategy is the responsibility of a steering committee and/or senior management.
- C. The information security manager is not necessarily responsible for communicating the security strategy.
- D. Final approval of the information security strategy must be made by senior management.

## Part A: Enterprise Governance

Information can be defined as "data endowed with meaning and purpose." Information plays a critical role in all aspects of our lives. Information has become an indispensable component of conducting business for virtually all enterprises. In a growing number of companies, information is the business. Similarly, a broad array of technology continues to make it possible to access information. Together, IT constitutes key elements in every enterprise.

Enterprise IT is increasingly important. Because a majority of national critical infrastructures in the developed world are controlled by the private sector, much of the task of protecting critical information ręsources falls squarely on private corporations. In many enterprises, reponsibility for that resource protection resides within two important and distinct components— governance and management. COBIT describes them as follows:

- Governance ensures that the needs of various stakeholders are evaluated to determine balanced, agreed-on enterprise objectives. Those objectives are then used to set direction (through prioritization and decision making) and to monitor performance and compliance.
- Management plans, builds, runs and monitors activities, in alignment with the direction set by the governance body, to achieve enterprise objectives.

Given the criticality of IT, one would expect those factors to be key considerations for the governing body. However, studies show a large percentage of enterprises do not adequately address either existing or emerging security issues. Some enterprise leaders continue to believe that existing information security programs are insufficient to meet the needs of the enterprise and often feel that the security budget is inadequate to address current risk effectively.

Information security failures can be seen predominantly as a failure of governance and cannot be solved by technology alone. The need for adequate protection of information resources needs to be raised at the board level, like other critical governance functions, to lead to action. The complexity, relevance and criticality of information security and its governance mandate that it be addressed and supported at the highest organizational levels. Similarly, governance objectives increasingly include the need to determine the internal and external requirements for the enterprise's privacy programs and practices. While these objectives are distinct from information security considerations and are the jurisdiction of a data privacy engineer,' the governance body should ensure that both security and privacy are adequately addressed throughout the enterprise.

Ultimately, to achieve significant improvement in information security, senior management and the board of directors must be held accountable for information security governance and must provide the necessary leadership, organizational structures, oversight, resources and processes to ensure that information security governance is an integral and transparent part of enterprise governance. Because information security risk is a business risk and has direct line of sight to business objectives in most enterprises, accountability among security practitioners and business leaders regarding enterprise risk decisions needs to be balanced.

Increasingly, those who understand the scope and depth of risk to information take the position that information, as a critical resource, must be treated with the same care, caution and prudence as any other asset essential to the survival of the enterprise.

Often, the focus of protection has been on the IT systems that process and store the vast majority of information rather than on the information itself. However, this approach is too narrow to accomplish the level of integration, process assurance and overall security that are required. Information security takes the larger view that content and information, and knowledge based on it, must be adequately protected, regardless of how it is handled, processed, transported or stored. Increasingly, this protection includes the need to consider cloud-based technology and other virtual technology platforms.

Enterprises exist to create value for their stakeholders. Consequently, any enterprise—commercial or not—has value creation as a governance objective. Value creation means realizing benefits at an optimal resource cost while optimizing risk (figure 1.1). Benefits can take many forms, such as financial for commercial enterprises and high-quality public service for government entities.

1 See the CDPSE job practice at www.isaca.org/credentialing/certified-data-privacy-solutions-engineer for more context.

<!-- page: 30 -->

<!-- image -->

Enterprises have many stakeholders, and "creating value" means different——and sometimes conflicting— things to each of them. Governance is about negotiating and deciding among different stakeholders'value interests. Consequently, the governance system should consider all stakeholders when making benefit, risk and resource assessment decisions. Stakeholder needs must be transformed into the enterprise's actionable strategy (for example, through the COBIT goals cascade).

Senior management is increasingly confronted by the need to stay competitive in the global economy and heed the promise of ever greater gains from the deployment of more information resources. Even as enterprises reap those gains, the increasing dependence on information and the systems that support it, and the advancing risk from an increasing host of threats, are forcing management to make difficult and often costly decisions about how to effectively address information security. In addition, scores of new and existing laws and regulations are increasingly demanding compliance and higher levels of accountability due to government efforts to address increasingly sophisticated attacks and growing losses that pose mounting threats to their national critical infrastructures.

COBIT provides some helpful principles for enterprise governance, including core requirements of a governance system for enterprise information and technology, and a governance framework that can be used to build a governance system.

<!-- image -->

It states that a governance system for enterprise IT:

- Is built from numerous components that can be of different types and that work together holistically.
- Is dynamic and adjusts to changes in the environment and the impact of those changes.
- Clearly distinguishes between governance and management activities and structures.
- Is tailored to the needs of the enterprise, using a set of design factors as parameters to customize and prioritize governance system components.
- Covers the enterprise end to end, focusing not only ● on the IT function but also on all the other technology and information processing the enterprise puts in place to achieve its goals, regardless of where the processing is located in the enterprise.

## 1.1 Importance of Information Security Governance

From an enterprise's perspective, information security governance is increasingly critical. For many, information has become essential to survival.

Information and the knowledge based on it are among the most important enterprise assets because conducting business without them would not be possible. The systems and processes that handle information are pervasive throughout enterprises globally. Reliance on information and related systems has made information security governance a critical facet of overall enterprise governance. In addition to addressing legal and regulatory requirements, effective information security governance supports good business practices. Prudent management provides a series of significant benefits, including:

- Addressing the increasing potential for civil or legal liability inuring to the enterprise and senior management as a result of information inaccuracy, insufficient information protection or inadequate regulatory compliance
- Providing assurance of policy compliance
- Increasing predictability and reducing uncertainty of business operations by lowering risk to definable and acceptable levels
- Providing the structure and framework to optimize allocations of limited security resources

<!-- page: 31 -->

<!-- image -->

- Providing a level of assurance that critical decisions are not based on faulty information
- Providing a firm foundation for efficient and effective risk management, process improvement, rapid incident response and continuity management
- Providing greater confidence in interactions with trading partners
- Improving trust in customer relationships
- Protecting the enterprise's reputation
- Enabling new and better ways to process electronic transactions
- Providing accountability for safeguarding information during critical business activities, such as mergers and acquisitions, business process recovery and regulatory response
- Effective management of information security resources

## 1.1.1 Outcomes of Information Security Governance

Information security governance includes the elements required to provide senior management assurance that its direction and intent are reflected in the security posture of the enterprise. This is achieved by using a structured approach to implementing a security program. Once the elements are in place, senior management can be confident that adequate and effective information security will protect the enterprise's vital information assets.

The objective of information security governance is to develop, implement and manage a security program that achieves the following six basic outcomes:

1. Strategic alignment—Aligning information security with business strategy to support organizational objectives, such as:
2. Security requirements that are driven by enterprise requirements and provide guidance on what must be done along with a means of measuring achievement
3. Security solutions that are compatible with enterprise processes and take into account the culture, governance style, technology and structure of the enterprise
4. Information security investments that are aligned with enterprise strategy and operations
5. and enable development of a well-defined threat, vulnerability and risk profile
2. Risk management—Mitigating risk and reducing potential impacts on information resources to an acceptable level through execution of appropriate measures, such as:
7. Collective understanding of the enterprise's threat, vulnerability and risk profile
8. Understanding of risk exposure and potential consequences of compromise
9. Awareness of risk management priorities based on potential consequences
10. Risk mitigation sufficient to achieve acceptable consequences of residual risk
11. Risk acceptance/deference based on an understanding of the potential consequences of residual risk
3. Value delivery—Optimizing security investments in support of business objectives, such as:
13. A standard set of security practices (i.e., E baseline security requirements following adequate and sufficient practices proportionate to risk and potential impact)
14. Maintaining information security overheads at a minimum level while maintaining a security program that enables the enterprise to achieve its objectives
15. Prioritization and distribution of effort to areas with the greatest risk probability and highest business impact and benefit
16. Institutionalized and commoditized standardsbased solutions that provide the greatest cost-effectiveness
17. Complete solutions covering enterprise processes and technology based on an understanding of the end-to-end business of the enterprise
18. A continuous improvement culture based on the understanding that security is an ongoing process, not an event
4. Resource optimization—Using information security knowledge and infrastructure efficiently and effectively to:
20. Ensure that knowledge is captured and available
21. Ensure that complete processes are added to the organizational IT manual as policies and procedures

<!-- page: 32 -->

- Document security processes and practices
- Develop security architectures to define and utilize infrastructure resources efficiently
5. Performance measurement—Monitoring and reporting on information security processes to ensure that objectives are achieved, including:
- A well-defined, agreed-upon and meaningful set of metrics that are properly aligned with strategic objectives and provide the information needed for effective decisions at the strategic, management and operational levels
- A measurement process that helps identify shortcomings and provides feedback on progress made toward resolving issues
- Independent assurance provided by external assessments and audits
- Criteria for identifying the most useful metrics among the variety of things that can be measured
6. Assurance process integration—Integrating all relevant assurance factors to ensure that processes operate as intended from end to end by:
- Determining all organizational assurance functions
- Developing formal relationships with other assurance functions
- Coordinating all assurance functions for more cost-effective security
- Ensuring that roles and responsibilities between assurance functions overlap and leave no gaps in protection
- Employing a systems approach to information security planning, deployment, metrics and management

As these elements are developed and updated, the process by which the entity will perform governance of information and technology should be instantiated as policy and shared with applicable stakeholders.

## 1.1.2 Scope and Charter of Information Security Governance

Information security deals with all aspects of information in any medium (e.g., written, spoken, electronic), regardless of whether it is being created, viewed, transported, stored or destroyed. It differs from IT security, which is concerned with security of information within the boundaries of the technology domain, usually in a custodial capacity. It is important to note this distinction. IT usually is not the owner of most of the information in its systems; rather, it owns the machinery that processes it. The information is in IT's care, control and custody, and IT functions as a custodian for the data owners.

<!-- image -->

Many enterprises have a corporate security function in addition to an IT security operation. Ensuring the security of the IT systems is an essential function that must be governed by the information security policies and standards. However, confidential information disclosed in an elevator conversation or sent via the postal mail would be outside the scope of IT security and would fall squarely in the purview of information security.

Cybersecurity is an area of concern and importance to information security governance and management. It includes both information and IT security. Although definitions vary widely, a common view is that cybersecurity is a subdiscipline of information security. Specific areas of concern for cybersecurity include advanced persistent threats (APTs), malware, ransomware, phishing in all its forms and the host of other threats related to cyberspace. Figure 1.2 shows the relationship of cybersecurity to information security. Figure 1.3 shows how these two areas differ and overlap within an enterprise. Note that in many areas there has been a convergence of cybersecurity and information security in recent years.

<!-- image -->

<!-- page: 33 -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

In the context of information security governance, it is important that the scope and responsibilities of information security are clearly set forth in the information security strategy and reflected in the policies. It is also essential that information security is fully supported by senior management and the various organizational units. Without clearly defined information security responsibilities, it is impossible to determine accountability.

## 1.2 Organizational Culture

Information security is primarily influenced through transparency and accountability throughout the enterprise culture. Culture is represented by organizational behavior, methods for navigating and influencing the enterprise's formal and informal structures to get work done, attitudes, norms, level of teamwork, existence or lack of turf issues, and geographic dispersion. Culture is impacted by individual backgrounds, work ethics, values, experiences, filters or blind spots, and the perceptions of life that individuals bring to the workplace. Every enterprise has a culture, whether it was purposely designed or simply emerged over time as a reflection of the leadership, and it must be considered in determining roles and responsibilities.

Information security primarily involves logical and analytical activities. However, building relationships, fostering teamwork and influencing organizational attitudes toward a positive security culture rely more on good interpersonal skills. The astute information security program manager will recognize the importance of developing both types of skills as essential to being an effective manager.

Building a security-aware culture depends on individuals in their respective roles performing their jobs in a way that protects information assets. All individuals, no matter what their level or role within the enterprise, should be able to articulate how information security relates to their role. For this to happen, the security manager must plan communications, participate in committees and projects, and provide individual attention to end users' and managers' needs. The security department should be able to answer the questions "What is in it for me?" and "Why should I care?" for every person in the enterprise. Once these questions have been answered, effective communications can be tailored to support the appropriate messages.

Some indicators of a successful security culture are the information security department being brought into projects at appropriate times, end users knowing how to identify and report incidents, the enterprise's ability to identify the security manager, and people knowing their role in protecting the information assets of the enterprise and integrating information security into their daily practices.

## 1.2.1 General Rules of Use/Acceptable Use Policy

To support a risk-aware and secure enterprise culture, all participants need to understand what behavior is acceptable, what activities are required and what actions are explicitly prohibited. An acceptable use policy provides a user-friendly summary of what personnel should do and avoid doing. This policy can detail—in everyday terms and in a straightforward, concise manner—the obligations and responsibilities of all users. It is necessary to effectively communicate the acceptable use policy to all users and ensure it is read and understood. The use policy should be provided to all new personnel who will have access to information assets, regardless of employment status.

Typically, the rules of use for all personnel include the policy and standards for access control, classification, marking and handling of documents and information, reporting requirements disclosure constraints, mobile computing, unlawful uses and enforcement. They may also include rules on email and Internet usage. The rules of use provide a general security baseline for the entire enterprise. It is often necessary to provide supplemental or additional information to specific groups in the enterprise, consistent with their responsibilities.

<!-- page: 34 -->

The information security manager should work with human resources (HR) and/or the compliance department to obtain acknowledgment from new hires that they understand and agree to fully comply with the acceptable use policy.

## 1.2.2 Ethics

Many enterprises have implemented ethics training to provide guidance on what the enterprise considers legal and appropriate behavior. This approach is most common when individuals are required to engage in activities of a particularly sensitive nature such as monitoring user activities, penetration testing, and accessing sensitive personal data. Information security personnel must be sensitive to potential conflicts of interest or activities that may be perceived as detrimental to the enterprise. Objectives and activities for ethical behavior should be coordinated with objectives and activities for privacy and data protection to ensure consistent and comprehensive consideration. These activities might include integration of data ethics frameworks² that can help define processes for appropriate and responsible data use in the enterprise.

Information security managers can set an example by sharing and adhering to their own ethical standards. The ISACA Code of Professional Ethics³ is one example that guides the professional and personal conduct of members of the association and its certification holders. All information security personnel should refer to and acknowledge the enterprise's code of conduct or similar organizational policy for guidance on how to identify and report potential conflicts of interest. Examples of conflicts of interest include but are not limited to selfdealing, accepting gifts, improper influence, dual/multiple employment and use of corporate assets for private advantage. The signed acceptance of the code should be kept as a part of employee records.

2

3 ISACA, "Code of Professional Ethics,"www.isaca.org/credentialing/code-of-professional-ethics

## 1.3 Legal, Regulatory and Contractual Requirements

Each enterprise faces a broad array of requirements derived from local and international laws, other regulatory oversight mandates and contract-specific provisions related to information security. In preparation for creating strategy, the information security manager must gather as much information as possible about these overarching requirements. Information security is inevitably intertwined with questions of privacy; intellectual property; and contractual, civil and criminal law. Any effort to design and implement an effective information security strategy must be built on a solid understanding of the pertinent legal requirements and restrictions.

Different regions in a global enterprise may be governed by conflicting laws. For example, the level of legislative focus on privacy differs in different parts of the world, resulting in stricter privacy laws and regulations in some jurisdictions. In some countries, thorough background checks may be performed on new employees—checks that are illegal in other countries. To address these situations, the global enterprise may need to establish different security strategies for each regional division, or it can base policy on the most restrictive requirements to be consistent across the enterprise.

A number of legal and regulatory issues are associated with Internet business, global transmissions and transborder data flows (e.g., privacy, tax laws and tariffs, data import/export restrictions, warrants or subpoenas, restrictions on cryptography, warranties, patents, copyrights, trade secrets and national security). These vary depending upon the enterprise's location and may impose constraints and boundaries on security strategies. Research into these areas must be undertaken in conjunction with legal and regulatory departments and any areas of the business that may be affected.

From the perspective of the information security manager, regulatory compliance should be treated as any other risk and the extent of compliance is ultimately a business decision that must be made by senior management with input as to risk and potential impact.

See the following for examples of a data ethics framework: GOV.UK, "Guidance overview: Data Ethics Framework," 13 June 2018, www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-ethics-framework Floridi, L.; M. Taddeo; "What is data ethics?", Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences, 2016,www.turing.ac.uk/research/publications/what-data-ethics

<!-- page: 35 -->

<!-- image -->

Corporate legal departments are often primarily focused on contracts and securities or company stock-related matters. The result is that they are, in many cases, not directly tracking regulatory requirements, and the information security manager should not rely on the legal department to identify them. Typically, the impacted department will be the most knowledgeable about legal and regulatory issues. It is, however, prudent for the information security manager to request legal review and interpretation of legal requirements that have security implications to ensure clarity on the enterprise's official position on the matter. Governance, risk and compliance (GRC) automated capabilities may assist with maintaining a comprehensive catalog of legal and regulatory requirements.

In addition, the information security manager may be required to support legal standards related to privacy of information and transactions, the collection and handling of audit records, email retention policies, incident investigation procedures and cooperation with legal authorities. Legal issues must be taken into careful consideration whenever an employee of the enterprise is investigated or monitored, or when disciplinary action is taken for inappropriate behavior. Because legal and regulatory requirements differ considerably in different regions and jurisdictions, it is prudent to engage the HR and legal departments prior to taking such actions.

## 1.3.1 Requirements for Content and Retention of Business Records

Business records constitute a large subset of the information to be protected by the security strategy that will be developed, so it is important for the information security manager to understand the underlying requirements regarding those records. As one who provides input for creating the strategy, the information security manager must understand the business requirements regarding all types of enterprise records. Often, representatives from the enterprise legal department can help determine what types of records must be protected to ensure their confidentiality, integrity and availability. The legal affairs representatives can also provide information regarding legal and regulatory requirements for enterprise documents (including electronic messages and files).

Business requirements may exceed the legal and regulatory requirements imposed by applicable legislating bodies due to the nature of the enterprise's business. Some enterprises have business needs requiring access to data that are 10 to 20 years old, or more. This type of data can include, for example, customer records, patient records and engineering information. As a rule, the retention strategy and subsequent policy must, at a minimum, meet the legal requirements in the applicable jurisdiction and industry.

Depending upon location and industry, regulatory bodies have requirements that an enterprise must comply with, including those applicable to legal, medical and tax records.

Regulations such as Sarbanes-Oxley4 have imposed various mandatory retention requirements for various types and categories of information, regardless of the storage medium. The enterprise's retention strategy will require the information security manager to stay current with these requirements and ensure compliance. There may also be requirements stemming from any lawful preservation order that would require an enterprise or individual to retain specific data at the behest of law enforcement or other authorities. It is also generally the case that archived information must be indexed sufficiently to be located and retrieved.

Increasingly, civil and criminal actions rely on evidence obtained from email and other electronic communications in response to a production request or subpoena. If information has been archived without being classified and cataloged, retrieving the required material can be an arduous and expensive task, as a number of high-profile cases have shown. The increasing prevalence of this type of discovery contributes to the need for careful consideration of a retention policy that limits the length of time—within the bounds of legal requirements—that certain information, such as email, is retained. Generally, the best option is to have a policy that requires destruction of any data not required to be retained by law or for specific business reasons.

The information security manager should, in conjunction with all applicable departments, enforce and maintain a data retention policy that includes a retention schedule. Additionally, certificates of destruction should be maintained as proof of compliance with secure disposal requirements when an authorized third party eradicates any media.

4 Corporate Finance Institute, "Sarbanes-Oxley Act," https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/knowledge/other/sarbanes-oxley-act/

## 1.4 Organizational Structures, Roles and Responsibilities

Enterprise governance requires responsibility and accountability from all participants. Due to their interdependencies, the organizational operating structures, the various roles defined within those structures and the responsibilities of participants in each role will constitute key inputs into an information security strategy.

COBIT points out some attributes of a successful organizational structure that should be understood by information security managers in preparation for strategy development. If these attributes are not in place, strategy activities might include working with enterprise stakeholders to incorporate them. Key considerations for an effective organizational structure:

- The organizational structure is formally established.
- The organizational structure has a clear, documented and well-understood mandate.
- Operating principles are documented and followed.
- Levels of authority and responsibilities for decisionmaking are defined and documented, including clear organizational charts or organigrams where possible.
- Provisions for delegation of authority are understood and implemented.
- Escalation procedures are defined and applied.
- Objectives for the performance of the organizational structures are identified, monitored and adjusted, as needed.
- Interfaces between the organizational structure and other stakeholders are managed to ensure both effective communication and clear assignment of responsibility.
- Regular evaluations result in the required continuous improvement of the organizational structure—in its composition, mandate and other parameters.

An examination of the organizational hierarchy and structure within the enterprise will enable the information security manager to understand the various stakeholders involved in the coordination, creation and management of the information security strategy. Notably, that hierarchy may not always be intuitive. The tendency to segment security into separate but related functions has created the need to integrate a variety of assurance processes found in a typical enterprise. These activities are often fragmented and segmented in silos with different reporting structures. The terminology associated with these activities generally reflects different understandings of processes and outcomes, at times with little in common. These assurance silos can include risk management, change management, internal and external audit, privacy offices, insurance offices, HR, legal and others. Evaluating business processes from start to finish (along with their controls), regardless of which particular assurance process is involved, can mitigate the tendency for security gaps to exist in various assurance functions.

<!-- image -->

Convergence is another structural consideration. Security-related activities are sometimes divided into separate divisions, such as physical security, IT security, risk management, privacy, compliance and information security. This approach has not been conducive to achieving optimal results, leading professionals and managers to reconsider this separation. The chief information security officer (CISO) may be elevated to chief security officer (CSO), with responsibility for a broad range of risk types, which can help to better integrate security elements. Integration of both the roles and infrastructure for physical security and information security is becoming commonplace. Because it is not possible to effectively deliver information security without a number of physical considerations, the evolution is natural. It is reasonable to expect that integration of many security activities will center around information security in the coming decade. As a result, integration of physical security and other assurance functions will be an increasingly relevant consideration for management.

Convergence is a holistic and encompassing approach

that looks beyond assets and considers such factors as culture, organizational structure and processes. Delivering on convergence requires more than organizational integration. It is about integrating the security disciplines with the business's mission to deliver shareholder value through consistent, predictable operations while optimizing the allocation of security resources.

As new technologies emerge and threats become increasingly complex and unpredictable, senior security executives recognize the need to merge security functions throughout the entire enterprise. An incident at the Sumitomo Mitsui Bank in London, England, in which hackers attempted to steal £229 million from the bank, underlies this principle.5 Even though the bank had strong IT security measures in place, a physical security lapse occurred. Adversaries posing as janitors installed devices on computer keyboards (i.e., keyloggers) that allowed them to obtain valuable login information. This incident highlights and reinforces the need to converge all components of an enterprise's security through an integrated and deliberate approach. To be effective, a converged approach should reach across people, processes and technology, and enable enterprises to prevent, detect, respond to and recover from any type of security incident.

<!-- page: 37 -->

<!-- image -->

In addition to the costs that companies face to deal with their immediate consequences, security incidents can cause long-term harm, such as damage to reputation and brand. Beyond the impact on market capitalization, there is the possibility that regulators may intervene if the issue threatens the public good, enacting stricter requirements for future business practices.

## 1.4.1 Roles and Responsibilities

Clear definitions, both of organizational roles and of the responsibilities of those who hold them, are key to effective information security governance. Because everyone in the enterprise has some information security responsibilities, it is essential to clearly define them and communicate those responsibilities throughout the enterprise on a recurring basis.

A role is a designation assigned to an individual by virtue of a job function or other label. A responsibility is a description of some procedure or function related to the role that someone is accountable to perform. Roles are important to information security because they enable responsibilities and access rights to be assigned based on the function an individual performs rather than to specific individuals. There are typically many job functions in the enterprise that support security functions, and the ability to assign access authorizations based on roles simplifies administration.

An important tool for documenting and coordinating responsibility is the RACI chart (or RACI matrix).

The name of this chart is derived from the names of the activities it describes for each role. This matrix depicts a set of roles on one axis and a set of responsibilities on another. At the intersection of each, an indication of one or more relevant role assignments is included, as follows:

- Responsible (R) roles take the main operational stake in fulfilling the practice and create the intended outcome. Who is getting the task done? Who drives the task?
- Accountable (A) roles carry overall accountability. As a principle, accountability cannot be shared. Who accounts for the success and achievement of the task?
- Consulted (C) roles provide input for the practice. Who is providing input?
- Informed (I) roles are informed of the achievements and deliverables of the practice. Who is receiving information?

Note that while the party in the accountable (A) role may delegate some or all responsibility to other participants, that party retains accountability for ensuring that a task or activity is fulfilled in an acceptable manner. Thus, while several parties may have R indications included in the matrix, there will generally be only one role with an A in each row.

RACI charts can be used effectively in defining the various roles associated with an information security program. Clear designation of roles and responsibilities is necessary to ensure effective implementation. Figure 1.4 shows a number of typical organizational roles and related governance activities.

## Skills

Skills must be considered when developing RACI charts. Skills are the training, expertise and experience held by the personnel in a given job function. It is important to understand the proficiencies of available personnel to ensure they map to competencies required for program implementation. Specific skills needed for program implementation can be acquired through training or from external resources. External resources, such as consultants, are often a more cost-effective choice for skills required for only a short time for specific projects.

Upon agreement that certain personnel will have specific information security responsibilities, formal employment agreements should be established that reference those responsibilities. Those agreements must be considered when screening applicants for employment.

## Board of Directors

Board members need to be aware of the enterprise's information assets, risk to those assets and their criticality to ongoing business operations. The board should periodically be provided with the high-level results of comprehensive risk assessments and business impact analyses (BIAs). This information should inform board members in validating/ratifying the key assets they want protected and ensuring that protection levels and priorities are appropriate to a standard of due care.

Security expectations should be met at all levels of the enterprise. Penalties for noncompliance must be defined, communicated and enforced from the board level down.

Beyond these requirements, the board has an ongoing obligation to provide a level of oversight with respect to information security activities. Given the legal and ethical responsibility of directors to exercise due care in protecting the enterprise's key assets, which include its confidential and other critical information, an ongoing level of information security involvement and oversight is required.

There are specific reasons that mandate the board of directors involvement with and oversight of information security activities. A common concern is liability. Most enterprises, to protect themselves from shareholder lawsuits, provide specific insurance to create a level of protection for the board in exercising its governance responsibilities. However, a typical requirement of this insurance is that directors make a good faith effort to exercise due care in the discharge of their duties. Neglecting to address information security risk may constitute a failure to exercise due care and may void the protection provided by insurance.

The US Sarbanes-Oxley Act mandates that every company listed on a US stock exchange maintain an audit committee with a required level of experience and demonstrable competence. This committee is often comprised of members of the company's board of directors. One of the committee's key responsibilities is the ongoing monitoring of the enterprise's internal controls that directly affect the reliability of financial statements. Most financial controls are technical and procedural, with the technical portion generally under the scope of the information security manager. It is important for the security manager to maintain an open channel of communication with this committee.

Institutional investors and others have come to understand that the long-term prospects for an enterprise are heavily impacted by the overall state of governance. Corporate rating enterprises provide a governance rating or metric based on a number of factors. Failure to provide an adequate level of governance and support for activities that protect the major assets of the enterprise is likely to be reflected in those scores. The weight and relevance of the scores will be driven by the consequences for enterprises that suffer the loss of significant critical and sensitive information. The bottom line is that a board of directors should provide direction, oversight and requirements for appropriate metrics. A 2019 meeting of the National Association of Corporate Directors Risk Oversight Advisory Council affirmed that cyber-risk reporting to the board should evolve to keep pace with the changing needs of the enterprise and of the board itself.⁶

## Senior Management

As with any other major initiative, information security must have leadership and ongoing support from senior management to succeed. An enterprise's senior management team is responsible for ensuring that needed organizational functions, resources and supporting infrastructure are available and properly used to fulfill the information security-related directives of the board, achieve regulatory compliance and meet other demands.

National Association of Corporate Directors, "NACD Risk Oversite Advisory Council: Current and Emerging Practices in Cyber-Risk Oversight,"4 June 2019, www.nacdonline.org/insights/publications.cfm?ItemNumber=65591

<!-- page: 40 -->

In addition, IT is often faced with performance pressures, while security must deal with risk and regulatory issues. These imperatives all too often fall at opposite ends of the spectrum. The result can be tension between IT and security, and it is important that senior management promote cooperation, arbitrate differences in perspective and be clear about priorities, so that performance, cost and security can be balanced appropriately.

## Business Process Owners

Development of an effective information security strategy requires the involvement and cooperation of business process owners. A successful outcome is the alignment of information security activities in support of business objectives. The extent to which this outcome is realized determines the cost-effectiveness of the information security program in achieving the desired objectives of a predictable, defined level of assurance for business processes and an acceptable level of impact from adverse events.

## Steering Committee

Security affects all aspects of an enterprise to some extent and must be pervasive throughout the enterprise to be effective. To ensure that all stakeholders impacted by security considerations are involved, many enterprises form a steering committee comprised of senior representatives of affected groups. The steering committee helps to achieve consensus on priorities and trade-offs. It serves as an effective communications channel and ensures the security program is aligned with business objectives. It can also be instrumental in achieving modification of behavior toward a culture more conducive to good security.

Common topics, agendas and decisions for a security steering committee include:

- Security strategy and integration efforts, especially efforts to integrate security with business unit activities
- Specific actions and progress relative to business ● unit support of information security program functions and vice versa
- Emerging risk, business unit security practices and C compliance issues

<!-- image -->

e The information security manager should make sure that the roles, responsibilities, scope and activities of the information security steering committee are clearly defined. This should include articulating clear objectives and agenda topics to avoid poor productivity or distractions from committee priorities.

It is important that materials be distributed, reviews encouraged and solution discussions held in advance of full committee meetings so that meeting participants can focus on resolving issues and making decisions. The use of subcommittees and individual action assignments is appropriate for this type of management strategy.

## Chief Information Security Officer

All enterprises have a CISO, regardless of whether anyone officially holds that title. It may be the chief information officer (CIO), chief security officer (CSO), chief financial officer (CFO) or chief executive officer (CEO). For many enterprises, the CISO also works closely with the chief privacy officer (CPO) or data privacy officer (DPO) who has overall responsibility for the enterprise privacy management program.

The scope and breadth of information security is such that the authority required to make decisions and the responsibility to act will inevitably be held by a C-level officer or senior manager. Legal responsibility will extend up the command structure by default and ultimately reside with senior management and the board of directors. Failure to implement appropriate governance structures can result in senior management being unaware of this responsibility and exposed to the attendant liability. It usually results in a lack of effective alignment of security activities with organizational objectives.

While the elevation of the information security manager to an executive role is a global trend, it is not consistent across sectors and the responsibilities and authority of information security managers vary dramatically among enterprises. These responsibilities currently range from the CISO or vice president for security reporting to the CEO or board of directors, to system administrators who have part-time responsibility for security management reporting to the IT manager or CIO.

<!-- page: 41 -->

<!-- image -->

A main concern, according to PricewaterhouseCoopers, is a CISO having an inadequate budget to successfully execute the security program and provide adequate attention to end users'or managers' needs.' It is essential that the information security manager be able to demonstrate why an adequate budget is a necessary component to ensuring that information security programs are able to address current and emerging risk. As shown in Chapter 2, identification and quantification of risk helps the manager to build and support an effective business case.8 Through this process, the information security manager is not simply asking for more resources, but also working with stakeholders to align objectives, resource optimization and risk management.

## Risk Management Roles and Responsibilities

Managing risk effectively at an acceptable cost is the basis for the objectives and drivers of information security governance and programs to implement, develop and manage it. While risk management is ultimately a responsibility of senior management and the board of directors, everyone in an enterprise has a role to play. It is important that all risk management activities be integrated and operate under a consistent set of rules and clear objectives. This will help prevent gaps in protection, provide a more consistent level of protection, reduce needless redundant efforts and help keep different parts of the enterprise from operating at cross purposes.

The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication 800-30 Revision 1: Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments describes the key roles of personnel who must support and participate in the risk management process. While the specifics in different enterprises and different countries may vary, this highlevel view generally maps to most enterprises. In many enterprises, the information security manager is the CISO with executive-level status, reporting directly to senior management.
