## 2.2.1 Security Control Baselines

Controls are designed as part of the information security risk management framework, which incorporates policies, standards, procedures, practices and organizational structures. It is designed to provide reasonable assurance that business objectives are achieved and the potential impacts of undesired events are sufficiently addressed. The framework must consider people, processes and technology and encompass the physical, technical, contractual and procedural aspects of the enterprise. It must take into account the strategic, programmatic, operational and tactical components of the enterprise to be effective.

Safeguards include any practice, procedure, process or other instrumentation that serves to reduce risk through the application of a precautionary measure to protect a business asset. Safeguards are considered proactive controls in that they are applied and used in an attempt to prevent an event from occurring. Some examples of proactive controls or safeguards inclúde employee background checks, intrusion prevention systems (IPSs) and turnstile gates.

Countermeasures include practices, procedures, processes or other instrumentation used to respond to an event that has occurred. Countermeasures typically respond to a threat or vulnerability once it has been identified. The implementation and integration of countermeasures can take a variety of forms and can range from modifying architecture or reengineering processes, to reducing or eliminating internal threats to technical vulnerabilities, to creating an employee awareness program to target social engineering and promote early recognition and reporting of security incidents.

There is a wealth of information available from NIST, COBIT, ISO and security vendors regarding standards for information security controls. However, the information security manager must keep in mind that every enterprise has its own needs and priorities. While NIST, ISO, COBIT and vendors can provide starting points of support for developing controls, specific analysis should always be performed.

<!-- image -->

Controls suitable for the enterprise must be developed based on a variety of factors—such as culture, ethics, organizational structure, staffing, skills and available supporting infrastructure—in the context of the enterprise's defined risk appetite and tolerance. When defining the risk analysis program, it is important to consider people and processes in addition to technology. The information security manager needs to develop procedural and physical security baselines. This will often present a challenge due to some areas typically being outside the control of the information security department. Appropriate standards approved by the steering committee, as described in Chapter 1, can be the most effective approach to address this issue. Internal audit and regular security reviews can help provide assurance of conformance required by the governing authority.

Implementing baselines for security processes sets the minimum security requirements throughout the enterprise so they are consistent with acceptable risk levels. Different baselines must be established for different security classifications, with more stringent security controls required for the higher classification levels of the more critical or sensitive assets. If the enterprise has not implemented a classification scheme, it will be difficult for the information security manager to develop a rational basis for setting baselines without the risk of overprotecting some resources and underprotecting others.

In order to formulate a baseline of security controls, some measurement of the effectiveness and efficiency of controls is necessary. A baseline is not established on a single test of controls, but on the overall capacity of controls to collectively mitigate risk to acceptable levels.

To set control baselines, security managers can refer to many of the published standards that may be implemented within the enterprise. Based on these standards, a test of the control can be performed multiple times to establish an evaluation of the effectiveness and efficiency of the control required by the standard.

Setting security baselines for an enterprise has a number of benefits. It standardizes the minimum number of security measures that must be employed throughout the enterprise; this not only results in positive benefits for risk management but also allows operational management according to classification level instead of a Selecting relevant metrics among the numerous available per system or per asset basis. It provides a convenient point of reference to measure changes to security and identify corresponding effects on risk.

<!-- page: 97 -->

<!-- image -->

Working in conjunction with the enterprise architecture group, an information security technology baseline of controls can be developed that is appropriate for the enterprise's operating environment.

There is a consensus among many vendors, security organizations, information security professionals and systems auditors about security configuration specifications that represent a prudent level of due care. These cooperative efforts continue to define consensusbased, good practice security configurations for various systems and platforms. The information security manager should examine these specifications and, if appropriate, should tailor them for incorporation into organizational security baselines.

While it is important for information security managers to be aware of industry standard baselines, they must assess the level of security that should be employed in various areas of the enterprise. The commingling of different technologies, data and users/consumers can often introduce new risk and change a secure system or platform into one that has new vulnerabilities. A tailored risk assessment that recognizes these interactions and dependencies will enable the information security manager to determine whether security processes and procedures above the defined baselines are necessary to provide adequate security commensurate with the enterprise's defined levels of acceptable risk. Some enterprises and industries may require higher baselines, such as highly regulated industries. That may also be the case for an enterprise that handles information that is classified as highly critical or sensitive. In both of these cases, the enterprise must have control mechanisms that provide a high level of security commensurate with these requirements.

Standards must be developed or modified to set the appropriate boundaries of protection for each security domain. Standards provide the basis for measurement and testing approaches for evaluating whether security baselines are being met by existing controls. The objective is for residual risk across the security domain to be at a consistent acceptable level. This should be validated by periodic risk assessments to address the ever-changing nature of threats, vulnerabilities and technologies.

choices can be achieved by using a set of criteria. Effective metrics for risk management, including controls for evaluation, can be selected based on the best ranking of the following characteristics:

- Specific—Based on a clearly understood goal; clear and concise
- Measurable—Able to be measured; quantifiable ● (objective), not subjective
- Attainable—Realistic; based on important goals and values
- Relevant—Directly related to a specific activity or goal
- Timely—Grounded in a specific time frame
- MeaningfulUnderstood by the recipients
- Accurate—Reasonably accurate
- Cost-effective—Not too expensive to acquire or maintain
- Repeatable—Able to be acquired reliably over time
- Predictive—Indicative of outcomes
- Actionable—Clear to the recipient regarding what action to take

Example: To establish a baseline for antivirus processes, the information security manager requires periodic (weekly, monthly) reports of infected systems, virus alerts, virus incidents reported to the help desk, definition file updates and other pertinent information. Based on this information, it is possible to evaluate the effectiveness of the control and based on additional information—such as staff resource hours required, software costs, remediation/response expenses, and residual risk—to evaluate the efficiency of the antivirus process as an IT control. This demonstrates how metries can be used to monitor the effectiveness of established baselines and provide a basis for adjusting them as necessary to manage risk.

## 2.2.2 Events Affecting Security Baselines

A number of factors may change the risk, probability or impact equation, necessitating that baseline security be changed. Baseline security is determined by the collective ability of controls to protect the enterprise's information assets. Baseline security is essentially controlled by the least restrictive aspect of collective standards and is the minimum level of security across the enterprise. Baseline security levels should also be reflected in control objectives.

<!-- page: 98 -->

Any incident can be attributed to either a control failure or the lack of a control. Any significant incident will require a risk reassessment and performing a root cause analysis of the failure, which may require increasing or modifying baseline security by changing the relevant policies, processes, procedures, standards or controls.

Information security managers need to monitor and assess events that affect security baselines and, thus, might affect the enterprise's security posture. Based on this assessment, the information security manager must determine if the enterprise's security strategy, roadmap and test plans require modification to address changing risk.

Security baselines may be modified for various reasons. For example, a vendor may identify a parameter in its software or hardware that must be changed to achieve or maintain the desired protection levels. Another reason for modification could be an outside event that necessitated an increase in the established baselines. For example, a protest or other civil unrest near an enterprise facility might warrant an increase in the baseline for physical security for a period until the threat passed. Other drivers include new or changing laws or regulations, identification of unacceptable risk levels because of new or changing threats, degradation of controls over time, and system changes creating new vulnerabilities.

## 2.3 Risk Analysis, Evaluation and Assessment

Risk management consists of a series of processes that take into account the end-to-end requirements of identifying, analyzing, evaluating and maintaining risk at acceptable levels. These include weighing policy alternatives in consultation with interested parties, considering risk assessment and other factors, and selecting appropriate prevention and control options that have acceptable costs and impacts on the enterprise's ability to operate efficiently.

Risk management functions usually include performance of a number of the following processes:

- Establish scope and boundaries—A process for the establishment of global parameters for the
- performance of risk management within an enterprise. Both internal and external factors have to be taken into account to provide context.
- Identify assets and valuation—A complete asset inventory and valuation process to determine assets at risk and potential impacts from incidents
- Perform risk assessment—A process consisting of risk identification, analysis and evaluation, including:
- Identifying viable threats, vulnerabilities and exposures
- Analyzing the level of risk, in the context of probability and potential outcomes
- Evaluating whether the risk meets the criteria for acceptance
- Recommend risk treatment or response—A ● process of selecting strategies to deal with identified risk that exceeds the acceptable level. Risk treatment strategies are avoiding, by cessation of risky activities; mitigating, by developing and implementing controls; transferring risk to a third party, either inside or outside the enterprise; and accepting. Risk is usually accepted if the risk is below the defined risk appetite and tolerance criteria.
- Accept residual risk—The decision and approval by management to accept the remaining risk after any required treatment process is concluded (i.e., the risk may be accepted after evaluation shows it is within acceptable limits or if no effective treatment option is available)
- Communicate about and monitor risk—A process ● to exchange and share information related to risk and review the effectiveness of the whole risk management process. Communication of risk is usually performed among decision makers and other stakeholders inside and outside the enterprise. Through communication and monitoring, the scope, boundaries, evaluated risk and action plans remain relevant and updated.

<!-- image -->

Developing a systematic, analytical and continuous risk management process, as shown in figure 2.6, is critical to any successful security program and must be implemented as a formal process. Determining the correct or appropriate level of security is dependent on the potential risk that an enterprise faces, the potential impact, and the enterprise's ability to accept or otherwise mitigate risk. Risk is unique to each enterprise.

<!-- page: 99 -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The information security manager should set up a regular, formal process in which risk assessments are performed at the organizational, system and application levels, including business processes both logical and physical. Ensuring that there are appropriate measurements (metrics) in place to assess the risk and the effectiveness of security measures is part of the information security manager's ongoing responsibility. The effectiveness of security measures or controls should be assessed against control objectives and security baselines. 'The information security manager should explore continuous manual and automated techniques to monitor risk and make recommendations to risk and control owners. This risk assessment process is important because it focuses the enterprise's security activities on issues that have the greatest likelihood, impact and significance.

Overgeneralization by applying risk factors across industries or regions should be avoided. Furthermore, the effectiveness of an information security program is frequently challenged by organizational, technological and business/operational change. These changes can be monitored, to a large extent, through links to all change management processes in the enterprise. Risk management should be a continuous and dynamic process to ensure that changing threats and vulnerabilities are addressed in a timely manner.

Processes must be developed to monitor the status of security controls and countermeasures to determine their ongoing effectiveness. Controls usually degrade over time and are subject to failure, mandating ongoing control monitoring and periodic testing.

There are three distinct phases within risk assessment:

- Risk identification
- Risk analysis
- Risk evaluation

The output of these three phases is the overarching risk assessment, which then can be used to inform risk treatment.

In risk identification, a set of threat scenarios is developed based on a thorough assessment of the threat landscape. It combines appropriate threat modeling and supporting vulnerability assessments (both logical and physical, including consideration of exposures) to understand and determine credible threats to the enterprise. See Section 2.1 Emerging Risk and Threat Landscape for more information.

Among the variety of available methodologies for assessing risk, some are more complex than others. Whichever approach is used, the outcome should be similar. The choice of methodologies, unless mandated by management or a regulatory body, should be based on the best fit for the enterprise.

The COBIT approach to performing a risk assessment, which aligns with ISO/IEC 27005:2018, includes identification, analysis and evaluation (figure 2.7).

<!-- page: 100 -->

<!-- image -->

There is no single best approach to risk assessment. The enterprise should define an approach that best aligns with its goals and objectives in determining the relative risk rating of assets and processes critical to the business. It is essential to identify as much significant risk as possible. An approach to achieving this is to develop risk scenarios.

## 2.3.1 Determining the Risk Management Context

In business terms, the process of managing risk must provide a balance between benefits and costs. The context defines the scope of risk management activities and the environment in which risk management operates, including the organizational structure, principles, culture, people, skills and infrastructure.

Determining the risk management context involves defining the:

- Range of the enterprise and the processes or activities to be assessed
- Full scope of the risk management activities
- Roles and responsibilities, not only pertaining to the various parts of the enterprise participating in the

<!-- image -->

risk management process, but also with regard to risk and control ownership

- Organizational culture in terms of risk-averseness or -aggressiveness

The criteria for evaluating risk must be determined and agreed upon. Deciding whether risk treatment is required is usually based on operational, technical, financial, regulatory, legal, social or environmental criteria or combinations thereof. The criteria should be in line with the scope and analysis of the enterprise's internal policies and procedures and must support its goals and objectives.

Important criteria to be considered are:

- Impact—The kinds of consequences that will be considered
- Likelihood—The probability of a negatively impacting event occurring
- Cost-benefits analysis—To determine the best approach for mitigation versus transferring impact of a risk event
- Risk appetite/risk tolerance—The rules that determine whether the risk level is such that further treatment activities are required

These criteria may need to change during later phases of the risk management process due to changing circumstances or as a consequence of the risk assessment and evaluation process itself.

## 2.3.2 Operational Risk Management

Operational risk is defined as the risk of loss resulting from ineffective, inefficient, inadequate or failed processes, people and systems, or from external events. Interruption to business operations is a major concern, and preventing it should be a primary focus of risk management. In most cases, incident management is adequate to managing materialized risk, minimizing significant disruption to operations and potential impacts. In some cases, incidents will escalate to disasters and fall under the purview of business continuity and disaster recovery. In either circumstance, the backstop to limit risk and ensure it is managed is the understanding and capability to address relevant issues sufficiently to ensure the survival of the enterprise. The following section covers the main elements that must be addressed by the information security manager and other

organizational units to manage risk effectively under most foreseeable circumstances.

## 2.3.3 Risk Management Integration with IT Life Cycle Management Processes

Ensuring that risk identification, analysis, evaluation, assessment and response activities are integrated into life cycle processes is an important task for information security management.

The need to minimize the negative impact on an enterprise and to establish a sound basis for decision making are the fundamental reasons enterprises implement a risk management process for their IT systems. Effective risk management must be fully integrated into the system development life cycle (SDLC). An IT system's SDLC has five phases: initiation, development or acquisition, implementation, operation or maintenance, and disposal. In some cases, an IT system may occupy several of these phases at the same time. However, the risk management methodology is the same, regardless of the SDLC phase for which the assessment is being conducted. Risk management is an iterative process that can be performed during each major phase of the SDLC. See Section 3.6.3 Life Cycle Principles Supporting the Road Map for more information.

Enterprises typically have change management procedures that can provide the information security manager with an approach to implementing risk management processes on an ongoing basis. Because changes to any information resource are likely to introduce new vulnerabilities and change the overall risk equation, it is important that the information security manager be aware of proposed modifications within the environment. With distributed computing having become the norm, changes are made more easily in a dispersed environment by people with limited knowiedge. Enterprises often experience a lack of standardization in their hardware and software environments. Management in many enterprises has therefore instituted more robust change management procedures and, as a consequence, has begun to achieve better control over enterprise information resources. This is a moving target, and enterprises with remote operations are, in some cases, still finding effective change management an elusive goal.

Change management processes may already be established for other business areas and activities. One benefit is that many enterprises now have change management procedures that span the entire enterprise. The information security manager must be aware of these change management activities and ensure that security is properly integrated with business operations so changes are not made without considering the implications to the overall security of the enterprise's information assets. One method of helping to ensure this is for information security management to participate as a member of the change management committee and ensure that all changes are subject to review and approval by security, and that proposed changes meet policy and standards requirements. Any proposed deviations should be identified and documented for further analysis.

While the normal change management focus is on hardware and software changes (testing, sign-offs, etc.) and security impact, the change management process should extend well beyond the system owners and IT population. The change management process must include facilities management with respect to data center infrastructure and any other area that may impact overall information security (e.g., physical access control of sensitive or critical areas).

The impact of change management on system and facilities maintenance windows must be addressed with facilities personnel (often outsourced) and business continuity management. Often, changes are not documented on a timely basis within these areas. Facilities may not have current single-line drawings and blueprints. Correspondingly, computer infrastructure/configuration management may not have the changes properly documented or updated on a timely basis. Business continuity may lag when relevant updates occur in cycles. Emergency response and business continuity may suffer communications lapses when current and changing processes are not reviewed within facility infrastructure areas.

Facilities personnel often have access to environmental monitoring and control systems (building management system [BMS]/supervisory control and data acquisition [SCADA] systems) for heating, ventilating and air conditioning (HVAC), water and electricity, or even physical access control systems (PACS). These are often programmed for remote computer access, an area that often escapes information security oversight. Physical security and control systems have been designed within the context of their deployment within a closed/controlled environment.

<!-- page: 102 -->

Closed-circuit camera systems once configured to transmit data over the backbone network are often integrated with the IT infrastructure, introducing the risk of compromise to these systems from IT facilities and the network.

IT systems can also be compromised due to vulnerabilities in the physical security system. Physical security and control systems, because of their importance in the protection of facilities and people, may be part of the enterprise's critical infrastructure. The means of protecting these systems, their system codes and data need to be integrated into the enterprise security classification schemes. Facility service contracts in support of physical and control systems often have emergency response clauses. Those contracts should be reviewed, because they may lack adequate service level agreements or fail to provide sufficient details and accountability for an adequate emergency response. A high-availability application may suffer unforeseen business impacts as a result of facilities failures.

Internal or external parties managing the facilities are sometimes overlooked from a risk management perspective, even though human beings pose the greatest threat to information security. Human beings may be negligent in complying with established processes, ignorant of known threats, willing to engage in collusion or subject to emotional behavior. It is important to include the human factor in assessing the risk associated with critical information assets. Internal parties include operators whose job roles grant them direct physical access to the systems and facilities. External parties include servicing agents (e.g., cleaning or maintenance crew). Possible controls are background screening, employment terms, annual confirmation (via signature) of compliance to code of conducts, or contractual terms in the case of external parties.

It is not uncommon for enterprises to leverage or rely on third-party services in a number of different areas, not just IT services. Facility management may be outsourced to a third party, as may certain business activities and processes. The enterprise must ensure that risk acceptance and tolerance levels are not exceeded in areas outsourced to a third party. Risk management needs to be integrated in all phases of third-party management, including identification of requirements, evaluation and selection of suppliers, contracting, and regular review, in addition to onboarding and offboarding.

<!-- image -->

By integrating risk identification, analysis, assessment and response activities into change management (life cycle processes), the information security manager can ensure that critical information resources are adequately protected. This is a proactive approach, enabling the information security manager to better plan and implement security policies and procedures in alignment with the business goals and objectives of the enterprise. It permits the interjection of information security controls into an activity that holds the greatest potential for degrading existing controls.

Because risk management is a continuous process, the information security manager should view risk management itself as having a continuous life cycle. This life cycle includes assessment, treatment and monitoring phases, as illustrated in figure 2.8. Employing a life cycle-based risk management approach that is integrated with change management limits costs in that a full risk assessment does not have to be performed periodically. Instead, updates may be made to the risk assessment and risk management processes on an incremental basis.

<!-- image -->

<!-- page: 103 -->

<!-- image -->

## 2.3.4 Risk Scenarios

Risk analysis consists of the thorough analysis of credible risk scenarios using various techniques (i.e., FAIR™ or HARMT methodologies) to decompose the respective elements of the scenario and understand their relationships. Determination of the potential frequency and outcome of a specific risk event occurring is determined during this phase.

The main areas to focus on for developing risk scenarios are shown in figure 2.9.

<!-- page: 105 -->

<!-- image -->

Technical methods, including software, can be used for identifying and tracking risk and providing reporting tools to record the analysis of risk. As with any process, the best tool to use is the one that is best suited to meet the unique needs of the enterprise. In applying risk identification and analysis methods, the information security manager should define resource requirements and establish a budget and timetable for carrying out the most important tasks.

Once an inventory of information assets is completed, a comprehensive list of sources of threats, vulnerabilities, exposures and risk can be generated as a list of events that might have an impact on the ability of the enterprise to achieve its identified objectives, defined by scope and framework. These threats might prevent, degrade, delay or enhance achievement of the enterprise objectives.

In general, a risk can be related to or characterized by:

- Actor (origin)——Threat actors exist internally (e.g., hostile employees, employees who have not been properly trained) or externally (e.g., competitors, governments, business partners) and as acts of nature.
- Type of threat (driver, intent and motivation) The type of threat experienced by an enterprise, i.e., was there malicious intent or was the cause accidental? Did hardware fail or was it the result of some act of nature?
- Resulting event (specific reason for its occurrence)—System design error, human intervention, prediction ofor failure to predict competitor activity
- Asset/resource (what we need to protect) Encompassing both the tangible and intangible, assets and resources are the things the enterprise has determined to be of value and worth protecting. Assets and resources can vary from the classic confidentiality, integrity and availability of systems, to public confidence and trust, to the ability to meet strategic goals and objectives.
- Consequences, results or impact (what happens should this occur)The range of outcomes should the event occur. The outcomes can be either negative or positive. Examples include service unavailability, a loss or increase of market share/profits, increase in
- regulation, increase or decrease in competitiveness, fines and penalties, and enterprise efficiency gains.
- Frequency (how likely it is this will happen in the next...)Forecasting the chances of when an event may occur. When considering all the known and unknown factors, making an estimated projection of when the event will be realized, given a defined period of time. For example: estimating the rate of occurrence during a year on a weekly (52 times), monthly (12 times), semi-annually (six times), annually (one time) or biennially (.5 times) basis.

Additionally, the following elements should be considered:

- Protective mechanisms and controls (estimated ● effectiveness)—Consisting of all applicable controls, based upon both their effectiveness and integration into the environment; examples of controls range from physical access control systems to network intrusion detection systems, policies, two-person integrity, logging and monitoring, security training, market research and surveillance of market.
- Exposure (where)—Defining where the asset or resource is most susceptible to an adverse event occurring. Is the asset located internally within the enterprise network behind multiple firewalls and security zones, or is it publicly available on the Internet with minimal controls in place? What is the business value of the resource, and are the applied controls commensurate with its value?

The development of risk scenarios is based on describing a potential risk event and documenting the factors and areas that may be affected by the risk event. Risk events may include system failure, loss of key personnel, theft, network outages, power failures, natural disasters or any other situations that could affect business operations and mission. Each risk scenario should be related to a business objective or impact experienced by the enterprise. The key to developing effective scenarios is to focus on real and relevant potential risk events. Examples are developing a risk scenario based on a radical change in the market for an enterprise's products, a change in government or leadership, or a supply chain failure. Figure 2.10 shows an example of the many inputs that are required to develop risk scenarios.

## 2.3.5 Risk Assessment Process

Risk assessment—coupled with either a business impact analysis or information asset classification process to determine criticality or sensitivity and subsequent analysis—is used as a basis for identifying appropriate and cost-effective controls or countermeasures to mitigate identified risk. Sensitivity or criticality is often stated as business value.

Most risk assessment approaches have four discrete phases. These include:

- Risk identification—the process for determining and documenting the risk an enterprise faces.
- Risk analysis—a process by which frequency and magnitude of IT risk scenarios are estimated. It also includes analyzing the value of assets to the business, identifying threats to those assets and evaluating how vulnerable each asset is to those

threats. Risk analysis can include an evaluation of the probable frequency of a particular event and the probable impact of that event. Analysis may include statistical computations to gain greater insight into risk distribution (i.e., the maximum risk and probable risk and potential consequences [impact]).

- Risk evaluation—the process of comparing the results of the risk analysis in the context of the defined risk appetite and tolerance criteria. Deciding the appropriate risk response is usually based on operational, technical, financial, regulatory, legal, social or environmental criteria, or combinations of criteria. The criteria should be in line with the scope and analysis of the enterprise's internal policies and procedures and must support its goals and objectives.
- Risk assessment—the process of determining the recommended course of action based upon the results of the risk analysis in the context of the risk evaluation process. This forms the basis for the

<!-- page: 107 -->

<!-- image -->

recommended course of action the enterprise should take to address the specific risk scenario.

Figure 2.11 shows the practical application of the IT risk assessment process, taking a risk-driven business approach for selecting an appropriate risk response. In this example, the asset to be protected is identified as sensitive/regulated data.

Assuming an asset is of significant value, the next step is to determine what vulnerabilities to loss or damage exist.

If vulnerabilities exist, an assessment of viable threats must be performed. If the asset has value and vulnerabilities susceptible to viable threats, then there is a risk. To clarify, it is obvious that vulnerabilities for which no threats exist pose no risk (although threats are dynamic and may arise at any time). Another way to look at it is that the greater the value, and the greater the number and degree of vulnerabilities coupled with a greater number of viable threats, the greater the risk of loss.

<!-- image -->

<!-- page: 108 -->

## 2.3.6 Risk Assessment and Analysis Methodologies

Numerous risk management models and assessment approaches are available to the information security manager. The approach selected should be determined by the best form, fit and function. The approaches include COBIT, OCTAVE®, NIST 800-39, HB 158-2010, ISO 27005:20018, ISO/IEC 31000, ITIL® and CRAMM. Other approaches—such as Factor Analysis of Information Risk (FAIR), Holistic Approach to Risk Management (HARM), risk factor analysis and value at risk (VAR)—may be more suitable, depending on the enterprise and the specific requirements.

In the COBIT approach, risk scenarios involve the process of identifying risk, followed by analysis. Risk evaluation is the next step to determine whether risk exceeds acceptable levels. These three steps allow the risk assessment to generate a recommendation of the appropriate risk response, or risk treatment. Response (treatment) priorities are based on a cost-benefit and risk-level analysis, with high cost-benefit and high likelihood/high impact taking the highest priority.

<!-- image -->

Note: Information security managers should have broad knowledge of the existence of various methodologies to determine the most suitable approach or combination of approaches for their enterprise. Specific approaches will not be tested in the CISM examination.

## NIST Risk Assessment Methodology

The NIST risk assessment methodology encompasses nine primary steps:

- Step 1—System (or general domain) characterization
- Step 2——Threat identification
- Step 3—Vulnerability identification
- Step 4Control analysis
- Step 5—Likelihood determination
- Step 6—Impact analysis
- Step 7—Risk determination
- Step 8—Control recommendations
- Step 9—Results documentation

Steps 2, 3, 4 and 6 can be conducted in parallel after step 1 has been completed.

Figure 2.12 depicts these steps and the inputs to and outputs from each step.

## Cascading Risk

Cascading risk can manifest unacceptable impacts as a result of one failure leading to a chain reaction of failures. An example of this occurred on the East Coast of the United States when a failure at a small power utility in the Midwest caused a cascade of failures across the power grid, ultimately encompassing most of the northeastern quarter of the United States. Similarly, to the extent that portions of the enterprise's IT and other operations have closely coupled dependencies, the information security manager must consider how any particular failures or combinations of failures will affect dependent systems.

This is often realized when numerous minor vulnerabilities that individually are acceptable and may not by themselves result in an event are combined and chained together, resulting in a significant impact to the enterprise.

Vulnerabilities can exist outside the technical realm and will often be chained together to allow threat actors to pursue their objectives. For example, a vulnerability was discovered in large food distributor's accounts payable process. The process allowed an invoice submitted under FAIR provides a reasoned and logical framework for the a certain dollar amount to be paid 1) without a following: corresponding purchase order assigned to it, and 2) A taxonomy of the factors that make up information without being reconciled with the department being ● risk. ## 2.3.7 Other Risk Assessment Approaches

Developments over the past few decades have resulted in notable improvements in defining the bounds of probable risk. However, few directly address information risk effectively. Some of these developments are being adopted in the information security field and it is likely that the use of more sophisticated techniques and methods will continue to be developed. Some of these methods are described in the following sections.

## Factor Analysis of Information Risk (FAIR)

FAIR is a recognized industry approach for decomposing risk and understanding its components. The approach offers a reasoned, detailed analysis process that is designed primarily as a complement to other assessment approaches with the objective of increasing accuracy (figure 2.14).

- A computational engine that derives risk by mathematically simulating the relationships among the measured factors.
- A simulation model that allows one to apply the taxonomy, measurement method and computational engine to build and analyze risk scenarios of virtually any size or complexity.

The four primary components of risk taxonomy that identify threat agent characteristics affect:

- The frequency with which threat agents come into ● contact with an enterprise or assets
- The probability that threat agents will act against an enterprise or assets
- The probability of threat agent actions being successful in overcoming protective controls
- The probable nature (type and severity) of impact to assets

<!-- page: 113 -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Holistic Approach to Risk Management (HARM)

A methodology designed and developed to support and normalize an enterprise's approach relating to performing risk analysis. Designed to leverage the FAIRTM risk analysis model, HARM's focus is to:

1. Refine the estimation process
2. Remove subjectivity from analysis
3. Provide an appropriate level of assurance
4. Define a repeatable method to ensure consistent results
5. Provide a defensible method for risk analysis efforts

Benefits of using the HARM methodology include:

- Consistency in results through use of repeatable, well-defined processes
- Confident estimations
- Ability to demonstrate due care
- Reasonable assurance
- Ability to make better-informed decisions
- Higher confidence in results
- Defensible results

HARM is not meant to be a replacement for FAIR; rather, it provides the information security manager the ability to mature risk analysis efforts, providing confidence in analysis results in addition to the ability to provide the appropriate level of assurance desired by many enterprises.

<!-- page: 114 -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Probabilistic Risk Assessment

Probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) has emerged as an increasingly popular analysis tool, especially during the last decade. PRA is a systematic and comprehensive methodology to evaluate risk associated with every life cycle aspect of a complex engineered technological entity, from concept definition through design, construction and operation, and up to removal from service. Developed for use by the US National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and the nuclear power industry, the approach is complex and time-consuming, but it may see increasing application in cases that require high network security.

The approach aims to answer three questions:

- What can go wrong?
- How likely is it?
- What are the consequences?

The answers are based on a thorough deconstruction of all the elements at risk in a particular set of circumstances, followed by systematically identifying, modeling and quantifying scenarios that can lead to adverse consequences based on probability and statistical theory, reliability engineering, decision theory and other information. Elements that go into assessing a possible chain of events include hardware and software failure, human actions, control failures and other possible interactions that can lead to serious consequences.

## 2.3.8 Risk Analysis

Risk analysis is the phase in which potential probability and resulting outcomes are calculated and determined. This phase includes determining threat actor capabilities and motivations, the effectiveness of existing controls, and the extent to which they may influence a particular identified risk.

Risk analysis involves:

- Thorough examination of the risk sources (threats and vulnerabilities) determined in the risk identification phase
- The extent to which information assets have exposure to potential threats and the effect on likelihood
- The potential negative consequences (impact) if the assets are successfully attacked
- The likelihood that those consequences may occur and the factors that affect them
- Inclusion of applicable existing controls or processes that tend to minimize negative risk or enhance positive outcomes (these controls may derive from a wider set of standards, controls or good practices selected according to an applicability statement [i.e., the application of controls identified in the risk register] and may also come from previous risk treatment activities)

The level of risk can be estimated in various ways, including using statistical analysis and calculations combining impact and likelihood. Impact may not be clear unless BIAs have been performed to provide an understanding of the cost to the enterprise as the result of the loss of a particular function or asset.

<!-- page: 115 -->

<!-- image -->

Any formulas and methods for combining impact and likelihood must be consistent with the criteria defined when establishing the risk management context, because an event may have multiple outcomes and affect different objectives. Therefore, consequences and likelihood need to be combined to calculate the level of risk. If no historical or statistically reliable data are available (e.g., incident data kept for an incident database), other estimates based on impacts affecting other enterprises may be made, but they must be appropriately communicated to and approved by the decision makers.

Information used to estimate impact and likelihood usually comes from:

- Experience or data and records (e.g., incident ● reporting)
- Reliable practices, international standards or guidelines
- Market research on other enterprises and analysis
- Experiments and prototypes
- Economic, engineering or other models
- Specialist and expert advice

Risk analysis techniques vary and may include:

- Interviews with experts in the area of interest and questionnaires
- Use of existing models and simulations
- Statistical and other analysis

Risk analysis may vary in detail according to the risk, the purpose of the analysis, and the required protection level of the relevant information, data and resources. Analysis may be qualitative, semi-quantitative (hybrid), or quantitative. In any case, the type of analysis performed should be consistent with the criteria developed as part of the definition of the risk management context, and consensus should be gained on the approach used.

## Gap Analysis

Gap analysis in the context of risk management refers to determining the gap between existing controls and control objectives. Control objectives based on acceptable risk should have been defined as an outcome of developing an information security governance and management strategy as discussed in Chapter 1.

Control objectives should lead to controls that result in residual risk falling into acceptable levels, ensuring that the established information security baseline is maintained.

Control objectives may change as a part of risk management activities as exposures, business objectives, operations, contractual obligations or regulations change, potentially creating a gap between the existing control and its revised objectives. Periodically analyzing the gap between controls and their objectives should be a standard practice. This is normally accomplished as a part of the process of controls testing for effectiveness. To the extent that effectiveness of controls fails to meet the control objective and achieve acceptable risk, the controls may need to be modified, redesigned or supplemented with additional control activities. For more information on the relationship between controls and control objectives, see Chapter 3.

## Qualitative Analysis

In qualitative analysis, the magnitude and likelihood of potential consequences are presented and described in detail. The scales used can be formed or adjusted to suit the circumstances, and different descriptions may be used for different risk. Qualitative analysis may be used:

- As an initial assessment to identify risk that will be the subject of further, detailed analysis
- If nontangible aspects of risk are to be considered (e.g., reputation, culture, image)
- If there is a lack of adequate information and numerical data or resources necessary for a statistically acceptable quantitative approach

A common approach to qualitative analysis can be accomplished by using a risk map, as shown in figure 2.16.

<!-- page: 116 -->

<!-- image -->

## Semi-quantitative (Hybrid) Analysis

In semi-quantitative analysis, the objective is to define a set of agreed-upon ranged values that are wide enough to allow risk to be estimated consistently. The goal is to provide sufficient accuracy to allow for the understanding, comparison and prioritization of risk. Qualitative terms are usually subjective; the ability to define and map them to quantitative values normalizes basic definitions used to forecast potential outcomes.

For this approach to be useful, the values selected should be generally indicative and sufficient for the prioritization of one risk above another risk. For any process to operate successfully there should be a common understanding of the values and the terms employed. Definitions already in use within the enterprise can be substituted for those that follow. It may be possible to use a subset from the ERM framework if one exists.

Example values for impact are:

- Insignificant (value = 1): No meaningful impact or of limited consequence
- Minor (value = 2): Impact on a small part of the business only or less than US $1 million impact
- Major (value = 3): Impact on the enterprise's brand or more than US $1 million impact
- Material (value = 4): Impact of more than US $200 million and requiring external reporting
- Catastrophic (value = 5): Failure or significant downsizing of the enterprise

Example values for likelihood are:

- Rare (value = 1)
- Unlikely (value = 2): Not seen within the last five years
- Moderate (value = 3): Seen within the last five years but not within the last year
- Likely (value = 4): Seen within the last year
- Frequent (value = 5): Occurs on a regular basis

These values should be sufficient to allow risk prioritization according to a semi-quantitative approach.

Typically, the risk probability and consequences are calculated as:

- Risk = impact × likelihood

An example is Risk = 4 (material) × 3 (moderate) = 12.

## Quantitative Analysis

In quantitative analysis, numerical values are assigned to both impact and likelihood. These values are derived from a variety of sources. The quality of the entire analysis depends on the accuracy of the assigned values and the validity of the statistical models used. Impact can be determined by evaluating and processing the various results of an event or by extrapolation from experimental studies or past data.

Consequences may be expressed in various terms of:

- Monetary
- Technical
- Operational
- Human impact criteria

The specification of the risk level is not unique. Impact and likelihood may be expressed or combined differently, according to the type of risk and the scope and objective of the risk management process.

## Annual Loss Expectancy

Quantitative risk assessments attempt to arrive at a numerical value, usually expressed in financial terms. The most common form is either single loss expectancy (SLE) or annual loss expectancy (ALE). SLE is the product of the asset value (AV) multiplied by the exposure factor (EF): SLE = AV × EF.

<!-- image -->

<!-- page: 117 -->

<!-- image -->

EF represents the percentage of loss that a realized threat could have on a specific asset when the specific threat matches up with a specific vulnerability. Said another way, EF is the proportion of an asset's value that is likely to be destroyed by a particular risk, expressed as a percentage.

ALE is the annual expected financial loss to an asset, resulting from one specific threat. ALE adds the annualized rate of occurrence (ARO) to the equation with the result that multiple occurrences will result in greater potential losses. ALE is usually expressed as: ALE = SLE × ARO. The result is that the greater the asset value, coupled with a greater probability and greater magnitude of impact, the greater the potential risk of loss.

ARO is the number of times a threat on a single asset is estimated to occur. The higher the risk associated with the threat, the higher the ARO. For example, if insurance data suggest that a serious fire is likely to occur once in 25 years, then the annualized rate of occurrence is 1/25 = 0.04.

## Value at Risk

Another approach required in certain financial sectors is value at risk (VAR), which can also have general risk management utility and benefit. This approach has been studied by various researchers, suggesting its suitability for information security management.

VAR is a computation based on historical data of the probability distribution of loss for a given period of time at a certainty factor, typically of 95 percent or 99 percent. The probability distribution is arrived at using Monte Carlo simulations, typically run through thousands of iterations with random variables based on historical information.

## Other Risk Analysis Methods

A number of other analysis options may prove useful, although they are typically more sophisticated than most enterprises employ. Some of the more common approaches include:

- Bayesian analysis——A Bayesian analysis is a method of statistical inference that uses prior
- distribution data to determine the probability of a result. This technique's effectiveness and accuracy rely on the accuracy of the prior distribution data.
- Bow tie analysis—A bow tie analysis provides a diagram to communicate risk assessment results by displaying links among possible causes, controls and consequences. The cause of the event is depicted in the middle of the diagram (the knot of the bow tie). Triggers, controls, mitigation strategies and consequences branch off the knot.
- Delphi methodThe Delphi method uses expert ● opinion, which is often received using two or more rounds of questionnaires. After each round of questioning, the results are summarized and communicated to the experts by a facilitator. This collaborative technique is often used to build a consensus among the experts.
- Event tree analysis—An event tree analysis is a forward-looking, bottom-up model that uses inductive reasoning to assess the probability of different events resulting in possible outcomes.
- Fault tree analysis——A fault tree analysis uses deductive reasoning and starts with an event and examines possible means for the event to occur (top down) and displays these results in a logical tree diagram. This diagram can be used to generate ways to reduce or eliminate potential causes of the event.
- Markov analysis—A Markov analysis is used to analyze systems that can exist in multiple states. The Markov model assumes that future events are independent of past events.
- Monte-Carlo analysis—According to IEC 31010:2019:17

Monte Carlo simulation is used to establish the aggregate variation in a system resulting from variations in the system, for a number of inputs, where each input has a defined distribution and the inputs are related to the output via defined relationships. The analysis can be used for a specific model where the interactions of the various inputs can be mathematically defined. The inputs can be based upon a variety of distribution types according to the nature of the uncertainty they are intended to represent. For risk assessment, triangular distributions or beta distributions are commonly used.

17 ISO, International Electrotechnical Commission, IEC 31010:2019 "Risk Management—Risk Assessment Techniques,"2019, www.iso.org/standard/72140.html

<!-- page: 118 -->

## 2.3.9 Risk Evaluation

During the risk evaluation phase, decisions are made concerning how the enterprise responds to and prioritizes risk, based on the foregoing analysis, with allowances made for the likely margin of error, which may be considerable if reliable data are not available. This is done in the context of the enterprise's defined risk appetite, tolerance criteria and capacity—establishing a method to advise a reasonable and appropriate risk response.

If the risk meets the acceptable risk criteria, the treatment option is likely to be acceptance. If the risk exceeds the acceptable level and is not within the tolerance variance, then treatment will most likely be some form of mitigation. The mitigation options include modification or addition of controls or business process reengineering that would render a process less risky. A system redesign can serve to reduce technical risk (e.g., eliminating a single point of system failure), or risk transfer (or sharing) might be the most cost-effective option. If there are no cost-effective options for mitigating excessive risk, management may decide that the activity is not worth the risk, or it may decide to accept the risk if the benefits are sufficiently high.

Typically, risk transfer is selected for risk that has low likelihood and high impact. If risk is mitigated through the use of controls, control risk must also be considered (i.e., control risk is the probability the control will fail or be inadequate).

The risk evaluation may lead to a decision to undertake further analysis if the results are ambiguous or are considered inaccurate or misleading.

The criteria used by the risk management team must also take into account the organizational objectives, the stakeholder views, and the scope and objective of the risk management process itself and its probable margins of error. The decisions made are usually based on the level of risk but may be related to thresholds specified in terms of:

- Consequences (e.g., impacts) ●
- The likelihood of events
- The cumulative (aggregated) impact of a series of events that could occur simultaneously
- The effect of cascading risk (domino effect) in closely coupled systems
- The cost of treatment
- The ability of the enterprise to absorb losses ●

## 2.3.10 Risk Ranking

The risk practitioner uses the results of risk assessment to place risk in an order that can be used to help the risk owner direct the risk response efforts. Risk ranking is derived from a combination of all the components of risk, including the recognition of the threats and the characteristics and capabilities of a threat source, the severity of a vulnerability, the likelihood of occurrence when considering effectiveness of controls, control risk, and the impact to the enterprise should the risk be realized. Taken together, these indicate the level of risk associated with a threat.

<!-- image -->

<!-- page: 119 -->

<!-- image -->

## Part B: Information Risk Response

Once risk is identified, analyzed and evaluated, the risk assessment is concluded, and a reasonable recommendation can be made on how to suitably respond to a specific risk.

Figure 2.17 provides an example of a risk response workflow.

<!-- image -->

A key to understanding the appropriate risk response is to understand the enterprise's desired state of security, as discussed in Chapter 1. A major input into defining the desired state is the enterprise's defined risk appetite, tolerance criteria and capacity—that is, what management considers acceptable risk, tolerable deviations from acceptable risk levels, and total amount of risk that does not jeopardize the enterprise's viability to operate. This is another critical step, since defined acceptable risk translates into the control objectives or other risk mitigation measures employed and the criteria by which risk can be evaluated for acceptability. The defining of control objectives is instrumental in determining the type, nature and extent of controls and countermeasures the enterprise employs to manage risk. Figure 2.18 presents the relationship between risk, control measures and the cost of controls.

<!-- image -->

Without a reasonably clear definition of acceptable risk, it is difficult to determine whether information security is meeting its objectives and if the appropriate resources have been applied.

<!-- page: 120 -->

The definition of some risk—and ultimately what the enterprise defines as being acceptable—can be quantified by using the business continuity approach of developing recovery time objectives (RTOs). Using a summary approach to determining RTOs may provide adequate input for strategy development. This can be an informal determination by business process owners of the amount of time critical systems can be inoperative without serious business consequences. This provides the basis for approximating costs of achieving recovery. If costs are considered too high, iteration of the process will arrive at an acceptable recovery time at an acceptable cost. This may be considered the acceptable risk.

Acceptable risk can also be approximated by examining the amount of business interruption insurance the enterprise carries, the amount of the deductible and its cost (i.e., annual premiums). For example, if the enterprise has US $1 million of insurance with a $10,000 deductible at an annual cost of $50,000, the argument can be made that it is reasonable to spend up to $50,000 in control activities to reduce a $1 million risk to an acceptable risk level of $10,000 (i.e., the residual risk).

Developing the appropriate strategy objectives usually needs to be an iterative approach based on analysis of costs to achieve the desired state and achieve acceptable risk levels. It is likely that lowering the level of acceptable risk will be more costly. However, the approach to achieving the desired state will have a significant bearing on costs as well.

For example, risk may exist because of certain practices that are not necessary or useful to the enterprise or are detrimental to its operation. This could include practices that might be considered discriminatory or contrary to law, posing the risk of a lawsuit. Such practices, when examined, may have resulted from outmoded attitudes or approaches that can be efficiently changed at a lower cost, resulting in elimination or mitigation of the risk. In other cases, it may be possible to reengineer certain processes or provide better architectures to reduce inherent risk. In other words, the approach to addressing or treating specific risk has a significant impact on costs.

<!-- image -->

The information security manager must understand that technical controls (e.g., firewalls, intrusion detection systems [IDSs]) are merely one dimension to be considered. Physical, process and procedural controls may be more effective and less costly. In most enterprises, process risk poses the greatest hazard and technical controls are unlikely to adequately compensate for poor management or faulty processes.

Once objectives have been clearly defined, there will be several ways to architect solutions that will vary significantly in costs and complexity. Whichever process is used, the objective is to define, in meaningful, concrete terms, the desired overall state of security at some future point.

## 2.4 Risk Treatment/Risk Response Options

Selecting the appropriate response must be done in the context of the enterprise's defined risk appetite and tolerance criteria. Risk can then be quickly categorized and prioritized.

There are often multiple risk appetites within an enterprise. The enterprise's risk appetite is the total amount of risk the enterprise is willing to take on, which should encompass the risk appetites of subordinate business units. A simple example to illustrate this is provided in figure 2.19.

<!-- page: 121 -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

As illustrated, the enterprise's risk appetite is US $5 million. This is disbursed across the business units, with IT having a risk appetite of US $1 million, which is distributed across the various functional areas within that department. In this example, for a manager from the network group, a risk below US $75,000 could be accepted; however, approval would be required from an authority in the Infrastructure unit for acceptance of any risk exceeding that amount.

Regardless of the action taken on the risk, it should be documented in the risk register, and the enterprise should continue to monitor it for any changes in the environment that might cause that risk to become unacceptable. Accepted risk is another form of debt the enterprise carries and is responsible for, a debt that can be called upon for payment at any time.

When selecting a risk response, the information security manager may recommend an appropriate risk response, acting in the role of an internal advisor or consultant. Ultimately the risk owner is accountable for the risk and will make the final decision as to the desired action.

When concluding the risk assessment and making recommendations as to the appropriate risk response, the information security manager must clearly communicate to the risk owner how and why the response option was provided, with sufficient detail to allow an informed decision to be made.

## 2.4.1 Determining Risk Capacity and Acceptable Risk (Risk Appetite)

Every enterprise has a particular risk capacity, defined as the objective amount of loss an enterprise can tolerate without its continued existence being threatened. Subject to the absolute maximum imposed by this risk capacity, the owners or board of directors of an enterprise set the risk appetite for the enterprise. Risk appetite is defined as the amount of risk, on a broad basis, that an entity is willing to accept in pursuit of its mission. In some cases, the board of directors may delegate setting the risk appetite to senior management as part of strategic planning.

Acceptable risk determination or risk appetite and the criteria for assessment are essential to virtually all aspects of information security and most other aspects of organizational activities. Risk appetite will determine many aspects of strategy including control objectives, control implementation, baseline security, cost-benefit calculations, risk management options, severity criteria determinations, required incident response capabilities, insurance requirements and feasibility assessments, among others.

Risk appetite is translated into a number of standards and policies to contain the risk level within the boundaries set by the risk appetite, which need to be regularly adjusted or confirmed. Within the boundaries, risk may be accepted, a formal and explicit process that affirms that the risk requires and warrants no additional response by the enterprise as long as the specific risk and the risk environment stay substantially the same and accountability for the risk is assigned to a specific owner.

<!-- page: 122 -->

Risk acceptance generally should not exceed the risk appetite of the enterprise, but it must not exceed the risk capacity (which would threaten the continued existence of the enterprise). Risk tolerance levels are risk appetite deviations that are not desirable but are known to be sufficiently below the risk capacity that acceptance of risk is still possible when there is compelling business need and other options are too costly. Risk tolerance may be defined using IT process metrics or adherence to defined IT procedures and policies, which are a translation of the IT goals that need to be achieved. Like risk appetite, risk tolerance is defined at the enterprise level and reflected in the policies created by senior management. Exceptions can be tolerated at lower levels of the enterprise as long as the overall exposure does not exceed the risk appetite at the enterprise level.

## 2.4.2 Risk Response Options

Faced with risk, information security managers can advise enterprises as to four strategic options:

- Avoid the risk by terminating the activity that gives rise to it.
- Transfer risk to another party (note that risk transfer usually results from a transfer of impact).
- Mitigate risk with appropriate control measures or mechanisms.
- Accept the risk.

One thing to keep in mind is that while the information security manager is bound to recommend one of the four risk responses listed above, the enterprise may choose to ignore the risk, which can be dangerous. The distinction between ignoring and accepting risk is that acceptance means understanding the likelihood, probability and consequences and making an informed decision to accept the risk under the circumstances. Ignoring a risk may lead to a serious underestimation of both the likelihood and possible magnitude of the impact, with severe or disastrous consequences. Accordingly, this is an inadvisable course of action. The only time it may be prudent to ignore an identified risk is when the impact is so great and rare that there is no possibility of addressing it (e.g., a comet strike).

## Terminate the Activity

There are often ways activities might be modified or processes reengineered that can serve to mitigate or manage risk to acceptable levels. Analysis of the activity could also lead to the conclusion that it is not worth the risk. In this circumstance, even though the enterprise has decided to terminate the product or service, the liability remains as long as the product or service is being used.

## Transfer the Risk

An example of risk transference is purchasing insurance to address areas of risk. When an enterprise buys insurance, some risk is transferred to the insurance coxnt pt  n n   ecet the insurance company's assessment of the degree of risk it is assuming. However, the risk is actually not transferred; rather, the impact to the enterprise is reduced to the extent that insurance covers some or all of the costs associated with a compromise.

Risk can be transferred by outsourcing IT functionality to a third party, provided indemnification clauses are in the contracts. However, in transferring operational risk, third-party agreements and contracts must specifically address the liability and responsibilities of both parties in specific indemnification clauses.

Indemnity agreements that can be part of an outsourced service agreement provide a level of protection against harmful incidents. While some possible financial impacts associated with the risk can be transferred, the legal responsibility for the consequences of compromise generally cannot be transferred.

Risk is typically transferred to insurance companies when the probability of an incident is low, but the impact is high.

An example would be earthquake or flood insurance. For the information security manager, this means that a wellmanaged risk program must interface with other organizational assurance providers, such as the insurance department, to establish what risk is covered and to what extent. If some identified risk is adequately managed by other entities, duplication of effort is generally not warranted.
