## Part A: Information Security Program Development

An information security program encompasses all the activities and resources that collectively provide information security services to an enterprise. The program is the project plan to implement and establish ongoing management of the information security strategy as mentioned in Chapter 1. Primary program activities include design, development and integration of enterprise-wide controls related to information security, along with the ongoing administration and management of these controls. Controls can range from simple policies and processes to highly complex technology solutions. Depending on the size and nature of the enterprise, these activities can be executed by a single individual or a chief information security officer (CISO) managing a large staff with diverse skills. While information security program development has clear goals and provides a road map for large enterprises, it is not as easy and smooth for small and medium scale enterprises (SMEs) because the business needs vary in the short and near term. Hence, the security program needs to be more flexible concerning business needs for SMEs.

In some instances, the information security manager may be required to initiate an information security program from its inception or to restart a program after a corporate merger or other significant change. Often, the information security manager modifies and improves an existing program. In either case, it is important for the information security manager to have a solid understanding of the many aspects and requirements of effective program design, implementation and management.

## 3.1 Information Security Program Overview

Successful security program management is not significantly different from management of any other organizational activity. The primary difference is that, despite increased visibility, information security remains a somewhat ill-defined and frequently misunderstood discipline.

Often, information security managers have a technical background. Many did not embark on a management career; rather, they were technologists who found themselves increasingly faced with management functions and responsibilities. In many cases, the shift of information security toward a broader management role is driven by the increased desire of a business to understand why specific security controls are required, and how the business will benefit specifically from them. In short, senior management wants to understand the specific risk the information security program is addressing and why the controls it mandates are a sound investment and actually benefit the business. As a result, many information security professionals have had to expand their view beyond technology and develop a greater understanding of the business activities they are seeking to protect.

The dual trends of growing security organizations and increased pressure from the business to ensure that the security program is aligned with the business objectives have combined to broaden the body of knowledge security managers must master. An extensive range of business knowledge and understanding must now be added to the base of information security knowledge that all security professionals should possess. This presents an opportunity for the information security manager to establish an effective bridge between the organizational business needs and the needs of the information technology and security teams. Implementing and executing a program that manages information risk in a cost-effective manner—at the same time enabling business initiatives while protecting organizational interests—supports enterprise awareness and improvement.

## 3.1.1 Information Security Management Trends

In an increasing number of enterprises, the information security manager is a member of senior leadership, designated as vice president of security, CISO or chief security officer (CSO), as detailed in Section 1.4.1 Roles and Responsibilities. Also, a number of security functions may report to an independent corporate-level security organization. These functions include physical and information security, IT security, compliance, privacy, business continuity planning/disaster recovery and security architecture. In some large multinational enterprises, many or all these functions are currently included under a senior corporate risk manager or chief risk officer (CRO). Irrespective of the reporting structure of the CISO or information security manager, the critical requirement is to ensure the board of directors or the top decision-making board of the enterprise gets periodic updates from the security organization. Without such updates, business leadership of the enterprise has insufficient visibility of the information security posture.

<!-- page: 144 -->

The benefits of this trend are apparent. All these functions serve the basic need of ensuring the safety and preservation of the enterprise and are interdependent. Aggregating these assurance activities under a single corporate function is likely to gain favor as it becomes incs  a tt  pidpe approach to security is inefficient, costly and ineffective.

In addition, many enterprises have recognized the value of including IT risk along with other enterprise risk that must be evaluated, treated and monitored. As various risk response results from across the enterprise are integrated and combined with results from other risk management categories, senior leaders are able to gain a comprehensive risk awareness.

However, in other companies, information security continues to be a fragmented, low-level IT effort. In many sectors, such as manufacturing, the food industry and retail, information security is seen as primarily a technical activity largely dealing with compliance issues as opposed to a vital strategic business activity.

Regardless of trends and optimal considerations for security, the reality in the majority of enterprises is something less than optimal, but security must still be managed on an ongoing basis.

IT functions, including security elements, are increasingly performed by external partners or vendors. Where critical functions such as software development, IT operations and security monitoring are provided by third parties, the information security manager must also consider the additional supply chain risk inherent in those circumstances.

In addition to understanding security concepts and technologies, information security managers will increasingly need to gain expertise in a range of management functions such as budgeting, planning, business case development, recruiting and other personnel-related functions.

<!-- image -->

## 3.1.2 Essential Elements of an Information Security Program

'I'hree elements are essential to ensure successful security program design, implementation and ongoing management:

1. The program must demonstrate execution of a welldeveloped information security strategy that is closely aligned with and supports organizational objectives.
2. The program must be well-designed with cooperation and support from management and stakeholders.
3. Effective metrics must be developed for program design and implementation phases and the subsequent ongoing security program management phases to provide the feedback necessary to guide program execution to achieve the defined outcomes.

Many frameworks recommend that the risk assessment serve as the starting point for developing an information security strategy. While this may be adequate in some cases, it is not optimal and does not address the balance of important outcomes for information security, including strategic alignment, resource management, value delivery, assurance process integration and performance measurement. See Chapters 1 and 2 for more information.

A comprehensive approach to security strategy development, as presented in Chapter 1, goes beyond just addressing risk by defining overall objectives for information security. These objectives should be explicitly linked to organizational objectives. The outlined approach also describes methodologies for defining the desired state of security and provides the basis for developing a comprehensive and effective strategy to achieve those objectives. Beyond focusing solely on managing risk, this approach considers how information security should link to and actively support the enterprise's strategic objectives, ensure its preservation, and optimize security resources and activities.

Many enterprises are not ready to undertake the costs and efforts to implement information security governance. In these circumstances, the information security manager may need to tailor objective development. Use of a standard framework—such as COBIT or ISO/IEC 27001:2013—in conjunction with Capability Maturity Model Integration (CMMI®) or a process assessment model (PAM) will allow the information security manager to assess the current state of the information security program, set specific goals and determine a strategy to achieve them.

<!-- page: 145 -->

<!-- image -->

Achieving acceptable levels of information security at a reasonable cost requires good planning, an effective strategy and capable management. Properly designed, implemented and managed, the information security program provides critical support for many business functions that simply would not be feasible without it.

The information security manager must define objectives for the information security program, thus supporting management and stakeholder consensus. Without defined objectives for information security, it will be impossible to devise effective information security management metrics because there may be misalignment. Without a link to stakeholder objectives, it becomes difficult to demonstrate progress toward organizational goals, thereby hampering progress and resulting in ad hoc and haphazard results.

To be of any use, a strategy must be implemented and made operational through processes that achieve the strategic objectives. The security program is the process by which the enterprise's security systems are designed, engineered, built, deployed, modified, managed, monitored and maintained until they are removed from service. This critical aspect of the information security manager's responsibilities covers a broad area and requires substantial expertise and technical and managerial skills.

Regardless of how the objectives and strategy of information security are devised, the goals of an information security program are to implement the strategy and achieve the defined objectives. Once developed, the information security program should clearly represent the elements of the strategy.

Information security program development entails a variety of activities, projects and initiatives involving people, processes and technology over a protracted period of time. The information security manager should keep in mind that the objectives and expected benefits of the information security program are most useful when they are defined in business terms to help nontechnical stakeholders understand and endorse the program goals. This is also more likely to promote feedback and participation from business owners that will make it more likely that the security program will be aligned with overall organizational objectives. The information security manager should also consider that programs and initiatives that do not have specific identifiable business or organizational benefits should be carefully examined to determine whether they are justified or if resources can produce greater benefits elsewhere.

## 3.1.3 Importance of the Information Security Program

Information security program management is an ongoing requirement that serves to protect information assets, satisfy regulatory obligations, lead appropriate response to incidents, and minimize potential legal and liability exposures.

A well-executed security program is one that is effectively designed, implemented, managed and monitored, transforming strategy into actuality. While providing the capabilities to meet security objectives, the program also accommodates the inevitable changes in security requirements and risk landscape. The program takes advantage of security expertise, tools and techniques that are available in the infrastructure and draws upon partnerships (such as with external vendors and service providers) to support ongoing requirements. The well-designed security program increases the likelihood that the efforts are well integrated, decreasing costs of maintenance and administration while providing a consistent level of security across the enterprise.

It should be clear that an effective security program requires a great deal of planning along with expertise and resources. Effective planning can be significantly aided through application of an enterprise security architecture at the conceptual, logical, functional and physical levels. Well-defined models and frameworks that can assist in this process are detailed in Section 3.6 Defining an Information Security Program Road Map.

## 3.1.4 Applying the Security Program Business Case

Development of major information security program initiatives and projects is based upon the business case described in Chapter 1. That business case should provide a clear statement of the value proposition (or cost benefit) based on the identified needs of the enterprise.

<!-- page: 146 -->

## CHAPTER 3—INFORMATION SECURITY PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT CHAPTER 3-INFORMATIONSECURITY PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT

The need from an information security perspective is to identify the risk that must be addressed and to consider both the potential impacts if the project is not undertaken and the potential reduction in risk and resulting impacts if the project is carried out. To be effective, the business case must make it evident that there is a significant potential return on the proposed investment, that the project is feasible and practical, and that the impact on productivity is acceptable.

As Chapter 1 shows, budgeting is an essential part of information security program management and can have a significant impact on the program's success. Effective preparation and defense of a budget can mean the difference between having or not having sufficient staff and other resources to accomplish the objectives of the information security program.

As with many business activities, self-education and advance preparation are key factors in successfully navigating this frequently challenging process. Well before the budget cycle begins, the information security manager should become familiar with the budgeting process and methods used by the enterprise, including the timing of the various stages of the enterprise's budget cycle.

Another key consideration before beginning the budgeting process is the information security strategy. All budget expenditures for information security should be derived from and supported by the information security strategy. Ideally, detailed elements of the security strategy are laid out in a security road map, as discussed previously in this section. The strategy and security road map are informed by an assessment of the risk posture of the enterprise in the context of the business objectives. This risk quantification supports the effective balance among IT benefits, resource optimization and risk management.

Having consensus on the strategy objectives and the strategy communicated and approved by management before entering into the budgeting process is key to creating a successful budget proposal.

Many costs associated with an information security program are straightforward. Expenses such as personnel (salaries, training, etc.), basic hardware and software, and subscription services fall into this category. In addition to the typical program startup and yearly operational costs, short- and long-term projects represent various objectives on the security road map. These projects consume resources over the course of months (or years) and must be accounted for in the budget as accurately as possible. The information security manager should collaborate with the enterprise's project management office (PMO) and the appropriate subject matter experts to help estimate costs for projects that will start within the fiscal year. Elements of each project that should be considered include:

<!-- image -->

- Employee time
- Contractor and consultant fees
- Equipment (hardware, software) costs
- Space requirements (data center rack space, etc.)
- Testing resources (personnel, system time, etc.)
- Training costs (staff, users, etc.)
- Travel
- Creation of supporting documentation
- Ongoing maintenance
- Contingencies for unexpected costs
- License/subscription costs
- Cyberinsurance

While it will be impossible to be completely accurate, engaging the appropriate SMEs and skilled project managers can be invaluable in arriving at a fairly accurate estimate.

Some aspects of an information security program are not entirely predictable and can incur unanticipated costs particularly in the area of incident response. These costs often result from the need for external resources to assist with a security event that exceeds the skills or bandwidth of the enterprise's staff. One approach to budget for these situations is to use historical data from incidents and remediation costs of previous security events that required unbudgeted external resources.

Even if the enterprise has recently initiated its security program, prior events may have necessitated external resources. If the planned program does not anticipate having those skills on staff, it is likely that external resources will be needed again in the future. For example, if during the past three years the enterprise has engaged external forensic consultants to assist with security events because the required skill sets were not on staff, the security manager should consider adding a line item in the budget to account for this situation. Costs can be estimated based on the average costs over the previous years as a starting point. If this information is

<!-- page: 147 -->

一

一

<!-- image -->

not available, industry statistics from peer enterprises may be useful as an indicator of risk and remediation costs.

## 3.1.5 Outcomes of Information Security Program Management

Effective information security program management should achieve the objectives defined in the security strategy discussed in Chapter 1. As with other management activities, the goals must be defined in specific, objective and measurable terms. Appropriate metrics must then be established to determine whether the goals have been achieved and, if not, by how much they were missed and how performance might be improved.

Regardless of whether formal information security governance has been implemented, the objectives of an effective information security program should be based upon acceptable achievement of the following six outcomes:

- Strategic alignment
- Risk management
- Value delivery C
- Resource management
- Performance measurement
- Assurance process integration

Strategy development and the definition of the information security program attributes are primarily conceptual and logical exercises. Development of the security program will require transforming these concepts and logical relationships into technologies and processes. From an architectural perspective, that transformation will require development of the physical, functional and operational components necessary to achieve the defined objectives.

For a major initiative, a full security architecture should be developed to ensure that the goals and desired outcomes are realized. If an enterprise architecture already exists, then a security architecture should be incorporated into it. As with any complex structure with numerous moving parts, architecture can serve to define logical, physical and operational component and process relationships. It can also clarify potential issues and provide traceability from concept to implementation and operation.

## Strategic Alignment

Effective alignment of information security with business or mission objectives requires regular interaction with business owners and an understanding of their plans and objectives. This synergy often depends on garnering input from the major operating units within the enterprise and building consensus. In the realm of the information security manager, achieving consensus requires an understanding of:

- Organizational information risk
- Selection of appropriate control objectives and ● standards
- Gaining agreement on acceptable risk and risk tolerance
- Definitions of financial, operational and other constraints

Strategic alignment can be accomplished through a security steering committee, if business owners or their delegates are members and active participants. The security program can support the alignment of business objectives and information security by implementing processes that ensure that defined business objectives provide the ongoing input to guide security activities.

Both old and new issues requiring attention should be tracked and communicated regularly. Action items related to issue investigation, resolution and disposition should be monitored and reported as organizational security performance metrics. A regular information security strategy report should be delivered to executive management to provide visibility into successes and setbacks around strategic alignment. This information can range from progress on projects of interest to new risk or capabilities that may affect a particular line of business.

Day-to-day operational interactions provide powerful opportunities for building rapport and cooperation throughout the enterprise and clarifying accountability lines. In addition to facilitating timely action on information security issues, active relationships fostered by the information security manager can increase awareness and a sense of responsibility around information security.

If the enterprise has a strategic business planning unit, active participation in its activities may also provide insight into future business directions and ensure that security considerations are included in the planning process. This interaction may provide opportunities to orient security activities to support business objectives and identify potential risk.

<!-- page: 148 -->

Efforts to align information security with business objectives must include consideration of security solutions that are a good fit for current and planned business initiatives. Alignment must also consider enterprise processes, cost, culture, governance, existing technology and structure of the enterprise.

## Risk Management

Managing the risk to information assets is a primary responsibility of the information security manager and provides the foundation and rationale for virtually all information security activities. Risk analysis must be based on business requirements and an understanding of the enterprise's processes, culture and technology. To effectively manage risk, the information security manager must develop a comprehensive understanding of threats the enterprise faces, its vulnerabilities, its risk profile and the level of risk that management determines is acceptable. The potential impacts of threats that can materialize must be evaluated and used to establish treatment priorities. Risk must be managed to a level that is acceptable to the enterprise. However, the risk landscape is always changing, and new risk will inevitably arise during program development and administration. It is important that a continuous process of risk management be maintained during program development, implementation and evolution.

See Chapter 2 for more information.

## Value Delivery

Value delivery as an objective requires information security to deliver the required level of security effectively and efficiently. The execution of the security program can have a considerable effect on achieving this goal. Good planning and project management skills are needed to implement the strategy efficiently.

Security investments should be managed to optimize support of business objectives and deliver clear value to the enterprise. The information security manager should direct efforts toward achievement of a standard set of security practices and establishment of security baselines proportionate to risk. Protection efforts must be prioritized to allocate limited resources to areas of greatest need and benefit.

<!-- image -->

Continued delivery of value requires that security solutions be institutionalized as normal and expected practices based on standards. Solutions must comprehensively address logical, technical, operational and physical concerns based on an understanding of the end-to-end operating processes of the enterprise. Security management cannot remain static; it must embody a culture of continuous improvement.

## Resource Management

Developing and managing a security program require people, technology and processes. The information security manager must endeavor to use human, financial, technical and knowledge resources efficiently and effectively. An important aspect of resource management is to ensure that knowledge is captured and made available to those who need it.

Security processes and practices must be documented, and they must be consistent with standards and policies. Project planning, technology selection and skill acquisition or development significantly factor into the effectiveness of resource management. These considerations include the acquisition and maintenance of external resources. Security architectures should be developed to define and use infrastructures to achieve security objectives efficiently. These efforts help promote recognition of resource needs and shortfalls and provide the basis for good resource management.

## Performance Measurement

If an information security strategy has been developed, it should identify a variety of important monitoring and metrics requirements. It is likely that during the evolution and management of a security program, additional opportunities to develop meaningful metrics or points of useful monitoring will become apparent. There may be opportunities to roll up groups of metrics to provide a more holistic picture for managing security. This topic is covered in greater detail in Section 3.7 Information Security Program Metrics.

The development and implementation of the security program itself will require a means of measuring progress and monitoring activities. An effective information security program results in processes designed to achieve governance objectives and provide measurable artifacts that demonstrate whether the objectives are met. Security processes should be designed with measurable control points that allow independent auditors to attest that the program is in place and effectively managed.

<!-- page: 149 -->

<!-- image -->

The information security manager must develop monitoring processes and associated metrics to provide continuous reporting on the effectiveness of information security processes and controls. Good metrics design and implementation require an understanding of the information needed by various constituencies for effective management. Metrics must be developed at multiple levels, including strategic, tactical and operational levels. The metrics used should be defined, agreed on by management and aligned with strategic objectives. Care must be taken to ensure that metrics provide úseful information relevant to managing security activities to achieve defined objectives. These measurement processes help identify shortcomings and failures of security activities and provide feedback on progress made in resolving issues.

## Assurance Process Integration

It is important for the information security manager to be aware of and understand all organizational assurance functions because they invariably have significance for information security. The information security manager should develop formal relationships with other assurance providers and endeavor to integrate relevant activities with information security activities. In the typical enterprise, these providers might include physical security, risk management, privacy office, quality assurance, audit, change management, insurance, human resources (HR), business continuity and disaster recovery. Other groups may also have a role to play.

As dictated by the governance objectives discussed in Chapter 1, an information security manager should seek to increase information assurance and the predictability of business operations through mitigation measures that reduce information-related risk to defined and agreedupon levels of acceptability. The information security manager can use results from business and privacy impact assessments to identify enterprise assets that are most critical to strategic objectives and provide key performance indicators (KPIs) that will demonstrate adequate and effective protection.

In other cases, acceptable risk may be determined in terms of reliability, integrity, performance levels, confidentiality, acceptable downtimes and financial impacts.

## 3.2 Information Security Program Resources

To support continued alignment and consistent management of the information security program, the information security manager typically has access to numerous organizational resources. Application of these resources further supports the governance framework principles (such as those described in COBIT) by helping to ensure that the program:

- Is based upon a conceptual model with identified key components and relationships.
- Applies an open and flexible approach that can be adjusted based upon priorities and adjustments from key stakeholders while maintaining integrity and consistency.
- Supports ongoing alignment with relevant standards, frameworks and regulations.

Use of program resources also supports alignment with the architectural elements previously described, supporting a consistent organizational and communication approach to managing and reporting IT risk.

## 3.2.1 Information Security Program Objectives

The objective of the information security program is to implement the strategy in the most cost-effective manner possible, while maximizing support of business functions and minimizing operational disruptions. Chapters 1 and 2 explain how governance and risk management objectives for a security program are defined and incorporated into an overall strategy. The success of these initial steps will determine the degree of clarity in understanding the information security program development objectives.

For a well-developed security strategy, the primary task will be turning high-level strategy into logical and physical reality through a series of projects and initiatives. Even with a well-developed security strategy, elements will need to be modified or reconsidered during

<!-- page: 150 -->

## CHAPTER 3—INFORMATION SECURITY PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT CHAPTER 3—INFORMATION SECURITY PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT

program design, development and ongoing administration. Adjustments may be required for a variety of reasons, such as changes in business requirements, underlying infrastructure, topology, technologies or risk level. Another possibility is that better solutions may become available during the course of program development or subsequently. Unanticipated resistance from those affected by the new or modified security program can drive significant alterations in its design, implementation or operation.

Whether a strategy has been developed in significant detail or only to the conceptual level, a great deal of planning and design will be required to achieve working project plans. It is likely that standard system development life cycle (SDLC) approaches will be useful, including feasibility, requirements and design phases. Collaboration during development of plans is important to gain consensus and cooperation from various stakeholders and to minimize subsequent implementation and operational problems.

## Defining Objectives

An information security manager is rarely faced with a situation in which no information security activity is present in an enterprise. Therefore, only rarely will the information security program need to be built from scratch. More often, developing the information security program will be a process of comparing the existing program to what is required to reach the desired information security state of the enterprise. This is achieved by performing a gap analysis. As noted in Chapter 1, the IT organization should have identified this at a high level, but it may be necessary to further define these objectives at a more concrete and practical level. This may require a substantial amount of effort, but it is a critical component in developing the security program.

It is essential to determine the forces that drive the business need for the information security program. Primary drivers for an information security program include:

- The ever-increasing requirements for regulatory compliance
- Higher frequency and cost related to security incidents
- Concerns over reputational damage
- Adoption of industry best practices and standards
- Business processes or objectives that may increase organizational risk

<!-- image -->

Determining the drivers will help clarify objectives of the program and provide the basis for development of relevant metrics.

Once the security program objectives have been clearly defined, security program development activities are used to develop processes and projects that close gaps between the current state and desired state. Typically, much of the basic work is to identify necessary controls, implement them, develop suitable metrics, and then monitor control points in support of control objectives.

An example implementation of this process is provided by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity, commonly referred to as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. This program, developed through a series of collaborative community workshops, supports a comparison of the current program state with a defined target (or desired) state that will achieve acceptable levels of risk. Comparing these two states results in a gap assessment that can inform security program objectives. Users may be further assisted by ISACA's implementation guidance that combines application of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework with COBIT's governance and management objectives.

Whether there is an existing information security program or not, there are some basic building blocks that need to be in place to support control activity and ensure that it is effective. The first step is to determine management objectives for information security, develop key goal indicators (KGIs) that reflect those objectives, and then develop ways to measure whether the program is heading in the right direction to meet those objectives.

## 3.2.2 Information Security Program Concepts

As an information security program is created, the developers must keep in mind the fundamental purpose of the security program (i.e., to implement the security strategy and achieve the defined outcomes, as detailed in Chapter 1).

If security governance has not been implemented and/or a strategy has not been developed, it will still be

<!-- page: 151 -->

<!-- image -->

## CHAPTER 3-INFORMATION SECURITY PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT CHAPTER 3-INFORMATION SECURITY PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT

necessary to define overall objectives for security activities. Off-the-shelf, ready-made objectives can include conforming to a particular set of standards or achieving a defined maturity level based on the CMMI model.

A security program implementation effort should include a series of specific control objectives, such as those defined in COBIT or the ISO 27000 family of standards. It is likely that any security program will consist largely of designing, developing and implementing controls, whether technical, procedural or physical. As these controls are developed, monitoring and metrics must also be considered. Processes to measure control effectiveness and determine control failure will be essential. Some metrics development approaches and processes are detailed in Section 3.7 Information Security Program Metrics.

Implementation will typically consist of a series of projects and initiatives. It generally involves project management skills, including resource utilization, budgeting, scheduling and time management skills (i.e., meeting timelines and milestones), quality assurance and user acceptance testing (UAT).

Many projects involve unusual or complex technical elements and may require detailed specification, design and engineering efforts. Because they often requires skills outside the information security manager's capabilities, it is generally prudent to consider engaging the services of consultants or contractors with subject matter expertise.

## Management and Process Concepts

Implementing and managing a security program will require the information security manager to'understand and have a working knowledge of a number of management and process concepts including:

- Architectures
- Budgeting, costing and financial issues
- Business case development
- Business process reengineering
- Communications
- Compliance monitoring and enforcement
- Contingency planning
- Control design and development
- Control implementation and testing
- Control monitoring and metrics
- Control objectives
- Critical thinking
- Deployment and integration strategies
- Documentation
- Personnel issues
- Problem resolution
- Project management
- Quality assurance
- Requirements development
- Risk management
- Software development life cycles
- Specification development
- Supply chain management
- Threat intelligence
- Training needs assessments and approaches
- Variance and noncompliance resolution

## Technology Resources

An information security program involves a variety of technologies in addition to processes, policies and people. The information security manager must be qualified to make decisions with respect to technology, including the viability and applicability of available solutions in terms of the program's goals and objectives. It is essential that the information security manager understand where a given technology fits into the basic prevention, detection, containment, reaction and recovery framework, and how it will serve to implement strategic elements.

Some technologies related directly to information security that the information security manager should be familiar with include:

- Antivirus/antimalware systems
- Application security methodologies (including secure software development and application testing)
- Authentication and authorization mechanisms (onetime passwords [OTPs], challenge-response, public key infrastructure [PKI] certificates, multifactor authentication, biometrics)

<!-- page: 152 -->

## CHAPTER 3—INFORMATION SECURITY PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT

- Backup and archiving approaches such as redundant array of inexpensive disks (RAID)
- Cloud-based resource provisioning and management techniques
- Cryptographic techniques (e.g., PKI, Advanced Encryption Standard [AES], Transport Layer Security/Secure Sockets Layer [TLS/SSL])
- Cyberthreat information sharing methodologies and techniques
- Data integrity controls (e.g., backups, data snapshots, data replication, RAID), storage area network [SAN] real-time replication)
- Data leak prevention methodologies (e.g., removable media security, content filtering) and associated technologies
- Digital signatures ●
- Identity and access management systems
- Firewalls
- Intrusion monitoring and detection, including hostbased and network-based intrusion detection systems (IDSs) and intrusion prevention systems (IPSs)
- Log collection, analysis and correlation tools (i.e., security information and event management [SIEM])
- Mobile device operations, security, and management
- Remote access methodologies (virtual private networks [VPNs], etc.)
- Secure cloud access techniques (secure access service edge [SASE], cloud access request broker [CASB])
- Security features inherent in networking devices (e.g., routers, switches)
- Vulnerability scanning and penetration testing tools
- Web security techniques
- Wireless security methodologies

While many of these technologies are specifically related to security (and most function as controls), the information security manager must recognize that virtually all deployed technologies will have security implications.

In addition to technologies that are security-related, the information security manager must be familiar with the broader aspects of IT including, but not limited to:

- Application servers
- Bring your own device (BYOD)
- Cloud computing
- Containerization ●
- Cryptocurrency
- Cyber-physical systems
- Databases
- DevOps/DevSecOps
- Enterprise architectures (two- and three-tier client servers, messaging, etc.)
- Internet and network protocols (e.g., TCP/IP, BGP)
- Internet of things (IoT)
- Local area networks (LANs)
- Machine learning
- Middleware
- Network routing concepts and protocols
- Operating systems
- Red team/blue team
- Servers
- Storage area networks (SANs)
- Virtualization (system and network level)
- Web-related technologies and architectures
- Wide area networks (WANs)

Note: These lists are not meant to be comprehensive; instead, they are representative of the areas and types of technologies the information security manager should be familiar with to successfully manage an information security program. Any CISM candidate who is unfamiliar with any of the terms listed should review the glossary at the end of this manual. CISM candidates can also refer to the Resources section of the ISACA website for additional information on trends and topics in information security.

## 3.2.3 Scope and Charter of an Information Security Program

Whether forming a new information security program or coming into an existing one, the information security manager will need to determine the scope, responsibilities and charter of the program. These elements are often less clearly defined than technical elements (e.g., firewalls, IDSs and virus detection). The

<!-- image -->

<!-- page: 153 -->

一

一

一

一

<!-- image -->

scope of the information security program primarily depends on how roles of responsibilities are designed. Often, asset processes are owned by one department while they are managed or operated by another department. Therefore, it is useful to develop a wellaligned RACI (responsible, accountable, consulted, informed) matrix before the preparation of information security program. Without clearly defined responsibilities, the security manager will find it difficult to determine what to manage or how well a given security function is meeting objectives.

Information security managers coming into new situations should take the time to gain an understanding of the relevant responsibilities, scope, authority, budgets, reporting requirements, etc., from those they will be reporting to. It will be useful to specifically document these elements and obtain agreement with management.

In terms of the chain of command, it is vital to understand where the information security function fits into the overall organizational structure. In many situations, there will be inherent structural conflicts that the manager should be aware of and carefully consider. It may also be prudent to discuss any potential conflicts of interest with management and understand how they will be handled.

The information security department largely performs an internal regulatory function, and its ability to operate effectively precludes reporting to those it is supposed to regulate. While there may be exceptions, information security managers who report in the technology chain of command or to other operational managers tend to be limited in their ability to provide effective information security across the enterprise.

If a program is established and has been functioning well, it is likely that many security program functions will already be accepted practice. Nevertheless, it will be useful to determine whether responsibilities are clearly defined and well documented. In many instances, a prior manager will have assumed a variety of functions and taken on responsibilities that were not formally defined and documented. Such managers may have been effective through being persuasive and influential rather than through defined and documented processes and structures. If the prior manager is available for orientation, it would be prudent to use whatever time is available to gain insight into the existing situation. If the prior manager is not available, it may take a thorough investigation to determine what the manager's responsibilities were and how tasks were accomplished.

The ability to be effective in a particular enterprise will be heavily impacted by culture and the information security manager's understanding of it. Security is often politically charged, and success may hinge more on developing the right relationships than on any particular expertise. To a varying extent, enterprises do not operate in the manner defined by organizational charts, but by undocumented relationships and influence. Much as a search engine determines relative importance by the number of links to a particular site, the influence of individuals is affected by their relationships to other people within the enterprise.

It is also essential to gain a thorough understanding of the current state of security functions in the enterprise. This may include the assessment elements such as risk assessment and business impact analysis (BIA). The state of governance and strategy will need to be ascertained, as will the condition of policies and standards, compliance, etc. Reviews of recent audits, incidents and other pertinent reports will be useful as well. Once these assessments and reviews are completed, the balance of the elements identified in Chapter 1 can be considered, and the information security manager will have a basis for moving forward with implementation of an information security management framework.

Figure 3.1 shows a summary of the steps in developing an information security program. While many of these tasks will fall to the information security manager, some may be under the purview of other departments.

<!-- page: 154 -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The scope of an information security program is established by the development of a strategy as discussed in Chapter 1, in combination with risk management responsibilities covered in Chapter 2. The extent to which management supports the implementation of the strategy and risk management activities determines the charter.

Implementation of a security program impacts an enterprise's established way of doing things. Within an existing structure of people, processes and technology, the information security manager must strive to integrate changes to established processes and policies. Inevitably, this will result in some degree of resistance to change, which the information security manager should plan to address.

In the absence of an adopted information security strategy and where no formal charter is documented, an information security manager can fall back on industry standards, such as a customized version of ISACA's description of a mature information security program, which might read:

Information security is a joint responsibility of business, information security and IT management and is integrated with corporate business objectives. Information security requirements are clearly defined, optimized and included in a verified security plan. Security functions are integrated with applications at the design stage and end users are increasingly accountable for managing security. Information security reporting provides early warning of changing and emerging risk, using automated active monitoring approaches for critical systems. Incidents are promptly addressed with formalized incident response procedures supported by automated tools. Periodic security assessments evaluate the effectiveness of implementation of the security plan. Information on new threats and vulnerabilities is systematically collected and analyzed, and adequate mitigating controls are promptly communicated and implemented. Intrusion testing, root cause analysis of security incidents and proactive identification of risk are the basis for continuous improvements. Security processes and technologies are integrated enterprise-wide.

This approach, coupled with COBIT or ISO/IEC 27001's requirements descriptions, can serve as the basis for a strategy and help define the scope and charter of the information security program.

## 3.2.4 Common Information Security Program Challenges

Initiating, refining or expanding a security program will often result in a surprising array of unexpected impediments for the information security manager. These include:

- Organizational resistance due to changes in areas of responsibility introduced by the program
- A perception that increased security will reduce access required for job functions
- Overreliance on subjective metrics
- Failure of strategy
- Assumptions of procedural compliance without confirming oversight
- Ineffective project management, delaying security initiatives
- Previously undetected, broken or buggy security software
- Poor management or monitoring of vendor/thirdparty security activities
- Lack of program alignment with business goals and objectives

There are always cultural and organizational challenges in any job function and the path is not cleared for the information security manager simply by virtue of gaining senior management support. To implement a truly successful program, the cooperation of many others in the enterprise is important as well.

Figure 3.2 identifies some constraints inherent in road map development for three different organizations. An information security manager must be aware of the type of constraints inherent in the organization when designing control activities and strive to minimize their impact on the information security program objectives. Historically, some enterprise leaders have failed to recognize information security risk as requiring the same level of governance and oversight as other critical risks, and instead have viewed IT risk as a low-level, technology-based cost center. While universally recognized as necessary, information security has been viewed as an impediment to getting the job done. In the past, this viewpoint was accentuated by information security personnel who failed to achieve balance between risk treatment and efficient operations. Thankfully, this trend is diminishing, yet in many enterprises this historic misunderstanding may have produced a challenging environment for an information security manager. A few common manifestations of such an environment include lack of management support, poor resource levels for information security, a shortsighted approach to strategy and poor cooperation from other business units. Typically, the information security manager in this situation reports far down in the hierarchy and has the daunting task of trying to drive security up the organizational structure.

The situation is gradually changing for the better for a number of reasons, including legal and regulatory mandates that require improved security as a matter of national security and commercial necessity. Expectations of customers and business partners are an important consideration that has provided a positive push toward enhanced security. Another is the credit card industry's rigorous security requirements from the PCI DSS council for enterprises that process credit card information. Since these requirements impact a very wide range of enterprises, they are likely to significantly improve many aspects of information security globally. Matching the rate of adoption and improved security to the pace of increasingly sophisticated and profitable criminal elements remains a challenge.

Although the overall situation in terms of security is improving, the information security manager must deal with the situation as it exists. Regardless of organizational circumstances, a persuasive information security manager with a clear vision of the role of information security in the enterprise can often improve the overall security posture with an ongoing campaign to educate stakeholders in the role and relevance of information security. This includes defining and seeking agreement on information risk control objectives, determining the enterprise's risk appetite and identifying mission-critical information assets.

It is beneficial for information security activities to align with and support defined business objectives. This is most effective if it is an ongoing effort and suitably communicated to stakeholders. Developing meaningful KPIs and metrics is also useful in supporting information security objectives. Each information security manager must determine the appropriate breadth and depth of metrics for the enterprise to provide the information needed for management. Information security managers should also implement some form of consistent reporting to promote awareness of the importance of information security management for the achievement of organizational objectives.

Other issues the information security manager may need to deal with occur in situations in which the role of information security has been elevated within an enterprise. Even for mature information security programs, requirements and demands are rapidly changing, driven by technical and regulatory pressures. The challenges described in the following sections do not represent an exhaustive list, but they do illustrate methods for assessing and addressing several of the most common concerns. The information security manager should be cognizant of common challenges to effective information security management, the reasons behind those challenges and the strategies for addressing them.

<!-- page: 157 -->

<!-- image -->

## CHAPTER 3—INFORMATION SECURITY PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT CHAPTER 3—INFORMATION SECURITY PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT

## Management Support

Lack of management support is most common in smaller enterprises or in those of any size that are not in securityintensive industries. Such enterprises often have no compulsory requirement to address information security and, therefore, often view it as a marginally important issue that adds cost with little value. Those views often reflect a misunderstanding of the enterprise's dependence on information systems, the threat and risk environment, or the impact the enterprise may face or could already be unknowingly experiencing.

In such circumstances, the information security manager must use resources such as industry statistics, organizational impact and dependency analyses and reviews of common threats to the enterprise's specific information processing systems. In addition, management may require guidance on what actions are expected and information on approaches industry peers are taking to address information security. Even if initial education does not result in immediate strengthening of support, ongoing education should still be conducted to develop awareness of security needs.

It is important that the information security program strategy include provisions for managing changes and updates. Management support requires an ongoing dialogue with periodic review of objectives and strategy. Without regular updates, changes to business priorities may reduce the actual or perceived alignment of security priorities with those business needs and objectives.

## Funding

Inadequate funding for information security initiatives is one of the most frustrating and challenging issues the information security manager must address. While this issue may be a symptom of an underlying lack of management support, there are often other factors the information security manager is able to influence. Some funding-related issues that may need to be addressed by the information security manager include:

- Management not recognizing the value of security investments
- Security being viewed as a low-value cost center
- Management not understanding where existing money is going
- The organizational need for a security investment not being understood
- The need for more awareness of industry trends in security investment

If additional funding to close financial gaps is not available, the information security manager must exercise strategies that minimize the impact of the financial shortfall on the enterprise's information risk posture. Some common strategies that can be applied include:

- Leveraging the budgets of other organizational units (e.g., product development, internal audit, information systems) to implement needed security program components
- Improving the efficiency of existing information security program components
- Working with the information security steering committee to reprioritize security resource assignments, and providing senior management with an analysis of which security components will become under-resourced and the associated risk implications

The information security manager should pay close attention to funding issues and work on them on an ongoing basis. It is often too late for analyzing needs and educating management once the actual budgeting process begins, delaying needed investments by months or years.

It is also important for the information security manager to understand that financing an information security program is often difficult. If the program is working successfully, management may not see where the money is going and may wonder why so much is being spent. If the program is not successful, management may not understand the need to budget significant amounts of money for systems that are still being compromised. It is essential for the information security manager to find ways to show that security is important, functional and business-related.

## Staffing

The root cause of funding issues is often inadequate staff to meet security program requirements. Obstacles to obtaining effective staffing levels might include:

- Poor understanding of what activities new resources will do
- Questioning the need or benefit of new resource activities

<!-- page: 158 -->

## CHAPTER 3—INFORMATION SECURITY PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT

- Lack of awareness of existing staff utilization levels or activities
- Belief that existing staff are underutilized
- Desire to examine outsourcing alternatives

When presented with these issues, the information security manager should use workload management procedures to generate personnel workload analyses, utilization reports and other metrics that demonstrate the level of effort currently expended. In addition, charts that associate specific information security roles or teams with the protection they provide to enterprise information systems are helpful. High or growing levels of productivity also help demonstrate that the information security program is utilizing resources effectively and efficiently.

If the enterprise is unable to allocate additional HR to the program, the information security manager may wish to consider implementing the following strategies to minimize the impact of understaffing on information security program effectiveness:

- Collaborate with other business units to determine if they can assume more information security responsibilities; delegate appropriate tasks with oversight.
- Analyze outsourcing possibilities, especially for high-volume operational activities; be prepared to demonstrate how freed resources would be immediately redeployed to higher-value activities.
- Work with the information security steering committee to reprioritize security personnel assignments; provide senior management with an analysis of what security activities will not be addressed with current staff, and communicate risk implications.

## 3.2.5 Common Information Security Program Constraints

In addition to the challenges mentioned, there are numerous overarching constraints that should be considered while developing an information security program. They will set the boundaries for the options available and should be thoroughly understood before initiating program development.

## Physical

A variety of physical and environmental factors may influence or constrain an information security program. The obvious ones include capacity, space, environmental hazards and availability of infrastructure. The security strategy and program should make certain that provisions are made for the consideration of environmental hazards and adequate infrastructure capacity. Consideration should include physical requirements for recovery in the case of a disaster.

The strategy must include consideration of personnel and resource safety.

## Ethics

The perception that customers and the public at large have of the enterprise's ethical behavior can have a major impact on the enterprise and affect its value. These perceptions are often influenced by location and culture, and an effective program will include ethical considerations in the areas of the enterprise's operations.

## Culture

The enterprise's internal culture must be considered when developing a security program. The culture in which the enterprise operates must also be considered. A program that is at odds with cultural norms may encounter resistance and may be difficult to implement successfully.

## Organizational Structure

Organizational structure will have a significant impact on how a governance strategy can be devised, implemented and translated into an information security program. Often, various assurance functions exist in silos that have different reporting structures and authority. Cooperation among these functions is important and typically requires senior management buy-in and involvement.

## Costs

The development and implementation of a strategy consumes resources including time and money. The most cost-effective way to implement a program is an important consideration.

<!-- image -->

<!-- page: 159 -->

<!-- image -->

## CHAPTER 3—INFORMATION SECURITY PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT CHAPTER 3—INFORMATION SECURITY PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT

Enterprises often justify spending based on a project's value. With security projects, however, control of specific risk and compliance with regulations are typically the primary drivers.

Generally, from a business perspective, a cost-benefit or other financial analysis is the most accepted approach to justifying expenditures and should be considered when developing a program.

A traditional, but speculative, approach is to consider the value of avoiding specific risk by estimating the potential losses incurred by a specific event and multiplying by the probability of it occurring in a given year. This results in an annual loss expectancy (ALE). Thus, the cost of the controls required to preclude such an event can be compared to the ALE to determine the return on investment (ROI).

Risk exposure can include losses that are challenging to quantify, so it can be difficult to directly calculate ROI. For example, calculating the benefit of controls to support compliance with regulatory provisions may include intangible consequences, such as prison sentences and large fines for senior executives. The ROI on programs to prevent such penalties can be difficult to quantify, although a subjective value from the affected executives should be readily obtainable.

Technological advances, such as single sign-on and user access provisioning technologies and procedures, have resulted in savings in time and cost over traditional manual administration techniques, which may provide a reasonable basis for ROI calculations. There are many examples that compare the costs of traditional processes against the newer procedures, which can be used in developing a business case.

## Personnel

A security strategy must consider what resistance may be encountered during implementation. Resistance to significant changes, along with possible resentment against new constraints possibly viewed as making tasks more difficult or time-consuming, should be expected.

## Resources

An effective strategy must consider available budgets; the total cost of ownership (TCO) of new or additional technologies; and the manpower requirements of design, implementation, operation, maintenance and eventual decommissioning. Typically, the TCO must be developed for the full life cycle of technologies, processes and personnel.

## Capabilities

The resources available to implement a strategy should include the known capabilities of the enterprise, including expertise and skills. A strategy that relies on demonstrated capabilities is more likely to succeed than one that does not.

## Time

Time is a major constraint in developing and implementing a strategy. There may be compliance deadlines that must be met or support for certain strategic operations, such as a merger, that must be accommodated. There may be windows of opportunity for particular business activities that mandate specific timelines for implementation of certain strategies.

## Technology

Technological complexities may constrain the implementation of a security strategy consistently across the enterprise. There may be existing legacy and unsupported systems that are unable to support the security control implementation until they are decommissioned. Exemption processes may be developed to consider and manage the risk arising from these constraints.

## 3.3 Information Asset Identification and Classification

Because the key purpose of the information security program is to ensure cost-effective protection of valuable resources, commensurate with stakeholder expectations, it is important that the information security program provide for adequate and consistent identification and classification of the assets to be protected. Notably, assets include the broad array of data, personnel, devices, systems, facilities and other resources that enable the enterprise to achieve business objectives. The identification and classification activities should include a determination of those assets' relative importance to

<!-- page: 160 -->

## CHAPTER 3—INFORMATION SECURITY PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT CHAPTER 3—INFORMATION SECURITY PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT

organizational objectives and the enterprise's risk strategy.

## 3.3.1 Information Asset Identification and Valuation

An important step for the information security program is to identify and inventory information assets and determine their relative or approximate business value (i.e., criticality or sensitivity). This is necessary because the business value is a part of the risk determination (i.e., risk exists only if there is likelihood of impact and consequences [risk = likelihood × consequences]). In addition, it is not possible to determine vulnerability and the extent of exposure of unidentified assets. The business value will also be needed for classification purposes and to provide justification for the level of protection required.

The process of valuation, which consists of relating all values in a common financial form, is straightforward for some assets. Hardware can be easily valued based on replacement costs. The value of information, in some cases, is the cost of recreating or restoring it, or it may be based on the contribution to generating revenues. In other cases, the value is related to the consequential costs and possible regulatory sanctions stemming from the exposure of confidential information or the loss of trade secrets.

The impact or consequences of a breach of personally identifiable information (PII) can be regulatory sanctions. Other potential impacts can arise if the individuals suffering identity theft losses file lawsuits for damages, or if attorneys file class-action lawsuits on behalf of thousands of victims. Another consequence is possible reputational damage, often resulting in loss of share value. In this case, the damage assessment cannot be based on the intrinsic value of the information, which may be low or zero. Rather, valuation must be based on the total range of potential losses and other impacts.

Marketing materials——another type of information with no intrinsic value——can nevertheless create unintended liabilities and, therefore, risk that must be considered.

<!-- image -->

Inaccurate representations of products or services or information leading to wrong investor decisions can result in significant losses as a consequence of various legal actions. Therefore, a prudent enterprise must consider ensuring systematic review and control of information to manage the risk of potential liability created by publicly released information.

Categories of typical information assets that must be assigned a value and protected include, but are not limited to:

- Proprietary information and processes of all types, including information that can damage the enterprise
- Current financial records and future projections
- Acquisition or merger plans
- Strategic marketing plans ●
- Trade secrets
- Patent-related information
- Privacy-related information, including PII and ● protected health information (PHI)
- Customer data, including payment card information (PCI)

## 3.3.2 Information Asset Valuation Strategies

Some enterprises may avoid asset valuation due to the complexity of agreeing about relative priorities and mission importance. Many enterprises do not have an accurate list of information assets, and the effort to inventory and categorize their assets can appear to be a daunting task. Another reason is that even if assets are known, it is often difficult to place an exact value on less tangible assets, such as PII or trade secrets. However, a high degree of accuracy is not necessary.

In most cases, effective resource valuation is best based on loss scenarios. Information can be classified and put into a matrix with each loss scenario to make a complex problem more manageable and understandable. Loss scenario considerations should include an evaluation of the potential impact of a loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability, as described in Chapter 2. See figure 3.3.

<!-- page: 161 -->
