By definition, incidents are unexpected events. The ability to detect, identify and assess the situation, determine the causes and quickly arrive at solutions can mean the difference between an inconvenience and a disaster. An important consideration is recognizing the point at which an incident becomes a problem and, subsequently, when the inability to adequately address a problem calls for the declaration of a disaster. The time to make those determinations is not in the middle of a crisis. The progression of a disaster is shown in figure 4.2.

<!-- image -->

Rigorous planning and commitment of resources are necessary to adequately plan for such events. As with other aspects of security, it is critical to achieve stakeholder consensus and senior management support for an effective incident management capability. Support can be gained as a result of unacceptable impacts of prior incidents to the enterprise or from developing a persuasive business case detailing examples of similar events in other enterprises that show the consequences of inadequate incident management. Incident management and response can lead to lower overall security costs by setting baselines to address common events and providing protection with an adequate response, containment and recovery capability. This is similar to the common approach for protecting against fire by a combination of reasonable preventive controls, coupled with an effective fire detection system, evacuation plans and triggers for fire department response, complemented with insurance policies in the event that incident management and response measures fall short. While a totally fireproof structure could be built, optimal costeffectiveness uses a combination of risk management approaches developed through trial and error.

Many enterprises have a separate department responsible for BC planning and DR and the extent of information security involvement and authority varies widely. Regardless of how these departments are structured, it is essential that they work together closely and that the plans are complementary and well-integrated. The individuals in charge of various types of events must be clearly defined and there must be clear severity and declaration criteria.

<!-- page: 262 -->

Severity criteria should be consistent, concisely described and easy to understand so severity levels of similar events are uniformly determined. Escalation and incident declaration criteria must also be established so it is clear who has the authority to determine the response level, activate the teams, declare an incident or disaster and mobilize the appropriate teams to initiate containment and recovery processes. Severity criteria and their use must be widely published and communicated to all relevant parties. Personnel must be trained to recognize potential incidents and provide proper classification, and they must be trained in notification, reporting and escalation requirements. The information security manager must be aware that, regardless of how well incidents are planned for and handled, there is always the possibility that events will escalate to a disaster.

## 4.2 Incident Management and Incident Response Plans

Effective incident management ensures that incidents are identified, detected, recorded and managed to limit impacts. Recording incidents is required so incident response activities can be tracked, information can be provided to aid planning activities and no aspect of an incident is inadvertently overlooked. Recording is required to properly document information, potentially including forensics data that can be used to pursue disciplinary or legal options. Incidents must be classified to ensure that they are correctly prioritized and routed to the correct resources. Incident management includes initial support processes that allow new incidents to be checked against known errors and problems so that any previously identified workarounds can be quickly identified.

Incident management provides a structure for investigating, diagnosing, resolving and then closing incidents. The process ensures that the incidents are owned, tracked and monitored throughout their life cycle. There may be occasions when major incidents require a response above and beyond what is provided through the normal incident process, and they may require activation of C/DR capabilities.

<!-- image -->

Incident response is the last step in an incident-handling process that encompasses the planning, coordination and execution of appropriate containment, eradication and recovery activities and may include the development of recommendations or lead to follow-on mitigation activities identified during the lessons learned.

The information security manager must be aware of nontechnical incidents to be planned for and addressed. These incidents can include social engineering, lost or stolen backup tapes or devices, physical theft of sensitive materials and natural disasters.

## 4.2.1 Importance of Incident Management

As enterprises increasingly rely on information processes and systems and significant disruption to those activities results in unacceptably severe impacts, the criticality of effective incident management and response has grown. Some factors that intensify the necessity of effective incident management include:

- The trend of both increased occurrences and escalating losses resulting from information security incidents (e.g., ransomware)
- The increase of vulnerabilities in software or ● systems affecting large parts of an enterprise's infrastructure and impacting operations
- Failure of security controls to prevent incidents
- Legal and regulatory mandates requiring the development of an incident management capability
- Growing sophistication and capabilities of threat ● actors
- Advanced persistent threats (APTs)
- Exploitation of poorly managed IT processes and practices
- Increasing zero-day attacks

## 4.2.2 Outcomes of Incident Management

Outcomes of good incident management and response include the following:

- The enterprise can deal effectively with unanticipated events that might threaten to disrupt the business (e.g., recovery time objective [RTO] and recovery point objective [RPO]).

<!-- page: 263 -->

<!-- image -->

- The enterprise will have sufficient detection and monitoring capabilities to ensure that incidents are detected in a timely manner.
- Well-defined severity and declaration criteria will be in place, as will defined escalation and notification processes.
- Personnel will be trained in the recognition of incidents, the application of severity criteria, and proper reporting and escalation procedures.
- The enterprise will have response capabilities that demonstrably support the business strategy by being responsive to the criticality and sensitivity of the resources protected.
- The enterprise will serve to proactively manage the risk of incidents appropriately in a cost-effective manner and will provide integration of securityrelated organizational functions to maximize effectiveness.
- The enterprise will provide monitoring and metrics to gauge performance of incident management and response capabilities, and it will periodically test its capabilities and ensure that information and plans are updated regularly, and are current and accessible when needed.

The monitoring and metrics activities will ensure that:

- Information assets are adequately protected and the risk level is within acceptable limits.
- Properly trained and equipped incident management and response teams are in place.
- Effective incident response plans (IRPs) are in place and understood by relevant stakeholders (e.g., management, IT departments, end users, incident handlers).
- Incidents are quickly identified, correctly categorized and contained, and the root cause is addressed to allow recovery within defined recovery objectives.
- Communication flows to different stakeholders and external parties are well controlled, as documented in the communication plan.
- Lessons learned are documented and shared with stakeholders to increase the level of security awareness and serve as a basis for improvement.
- Assurance is provided to internal and external stakeholders (e.g., customers, suppliers, business partners) that the enterprise has adequate control and is prepared to ensure business survivability in the long term.

## 4.2.3 Incident Management Resources

A number of internal and external resources may be used in the development of an incident management and response plan. In a typical enterprise, these resources may include, but not be limited to, the following:

- Compliance office
- Facilities management
- HR
- Industry and national community emergency response teams
- Information sharing and analysis centers
- Insurance provider
- Internal audit
- IT department
- Law enforcement
- Legal department
- Local government
- Physical security
- Privacy officer
- Public relations
- Risk management
- Sales and marketing
- Senior management
- Third-party providers
- Training partners
- Trusted advisors
- Vendors/suppliers

As with other aspects of information security, it is essential to develop a clear scope, objectives and implementation strategy. The strategy must consider the elements needed to move from the current state of incident management to the desired state, as defined by the enterprise. It should clarify what resources are required and how they must be deployed.

<!-- page: 264 -->

## 4.2.4 Policies and Standards

The incident response plan (IRP) must be supported by well-defined policies, standards and procedures. A documented set of policies, standards and procedures is important to:

- Ensure that incident management activities are aligned with the incident management team (IMT) mission.
- Set correct expectations.
- Provide guidance for operational needs.
- Maintain consistency and reliability of services.
- Clearly understand roles and responsibilities.
- Set requirements for identified alternative personnel for all important functions.

## 4.2.5 Incident Management Objectives

At its core, incident management exists to address the inevitable events that threaten the operation of any enterprise. It serves as the next-to-last safety net after controls have failed to prevent or contain an incident. The primary purpose is to respond to and contain security incidents and restore normal operations as quickly as possible in the event of an incident. Failing to do so will often result in the declaration of a disaster, and the need for recovery operations. This may include the move to an alternative site to restore operations as defined within the BC/DR plans.

The objectives of incident management are to:

- Handle incidents when they occur so the exposure can be contained or eradicated to enable recovery within recovery time objectives (RTOs) and recovery point objectives (RPOs).
- Restore systems and business processes to normal operation.
- Prevent incidents from recurring by documenting and learning from past incidents.
- Deploy proactive countermeasures to ● prevent/minimize the probability of incidents occurring in the future.
- Deploy safeguards to protect and reduce impact to assets in the event of an incident occurring.

Ideally, incident management and response capabilities must effectively address a wide range of possible unexpected events. Enterprises need to ensure not only that they have well-developed monitoring capabilities for key controls in order to provide early detection of potential problems, but also that these capabilities are accessible to the appropriate incident management personnel. Personnel should be trained in assessing the situation, conducting triage and managing effective responses that maximize operational continuity and minimize impacts. Incident managers will have provisions in place to capture all relevant information and apply previously learned lessons. They will be prepared for a disaster through well-defined criteria, experience, knowledge and authority to invoke the disaster recovery processes necessary to maintain or recover operational status.

<!-- image -->

## 4.2.6 Strategic Alignment

Similar to many other support functions, incident management must be aligned with an enterprise's strategic plan. The following components may help to accomplish this alignment:

- Constituency——To whom does the incident ● management team (IMT) provide services? It is important to know who the stakeholders are for this function and identify their expectations and information needs. For example, senior management in financial institutions may be bound by Basel III or another regulation. Thus, the IMT should meet applicable performance and reporting requirements.
- Mission—The mission defines the purpose of the team and the primary objectives and goals that are provided by the IMT. An example of a possible IMT mission statement follows: "The mission of the incident management team is to develop, maintain and deliver incident management capabilities and services to safeguard the enterprise's information assets against computer incidents. We strive to provide assurance to our stakeholders that risk and cyber- or IT-related incidents are dealt with in an efficient and effective manner and that we will prevent/minimize losses resulting from such incidents.' 66
- Services—Services provided by the IMT should be clearly defined to manage stakeholder expectations. Services offered in enterprises may differ significantly, and normally have a positive correlation with the size of the enterprise and the extent of senior management support. At a high level, these services include functions such as incident management, vulnerability management,

<!-- page: 265 -->

<!-- image -->

situational awareness, knowledge transfer and event management.27

- Organizational structure—The structure of the IMT should effectively support the enterprise's structure. For multinational companies, a geography-based structure may be the best. For enterprises with multiple subsidiaries, one IMT may be developed for each major subsidiary. The best structure would provide the business with the maximum availability of IMT services on the most cost-effective basis.
- Resources—Sufficient qualified staffing is needed for both effectiveness and efficiency. Because incident management can include a wide range of services, most of the time it is not possible to have all the resources available within one IMT. Ways to solve this issue include establishing virtual team members and complementing the team with external resources.
- Funding—The IMT usually consists of highly specialized members. The training, equipment and systems used in the course of providing their services tend to be very specialized, requiring greater capital expenditures. Sufficient funding is required to ensure the continuity of criticalincident response services.
- Management support—Senior management buy-in is essential for establishing a successful incident management capability within an enterprise. A lack of support can result in a number of issues. For example, the inability to respond to an incident due to existing silos within the enterprise, untrained team members due to underfunding, insufficient budget allocation to allow for effective and efficient response, or to attract or retain qualified personnel. Without the commitment of senior management, the incident management and response capabilities will rely on personal heroics at best or introduce a variety of legal risk (e.g., the spoliation or mishandling of evidence).

## 4.2.7 Response and Recovery Plan

Enterprises should have a formal, focused and coordinated approach to responding to incidents, including an incident response plan (IRP) that provides the road map for implementing the incident response capability. Each enterprise needs a plan that meets its unique requirements, which relate to the enterprise's mission, size, structure and functions. The plan should lay out the necessary resources and management support. The IRP should include the following elements:

- Mission
- Strategies and goals
- Senior management approval
- Organizational approach to incident response
- Key decision-making personnel and responsibilities
- Communication with the rest of the enterprise and with other enterprises
- Metrics for measuring the incident response capability and its effectiveness
- Road map for maturing the incident response capability
- How the program fits into the overall enterprise

The enterprise mission, strategies and goals for incident response should help in determining the structure of its incident response capability. The incident response program structure should also be discussed within the plan. Once an enterprise develops a plan and gains management approval, the enterprise should implement the plan and review it at least annually (or when there is any significant change that could introduce unplanned risk) to ensure the enterprise is following the road map for maturing its capability and fulfilling its goals for incident response.

The following section covers the necessity for incident response capabilities and the typical responsibilities of an information security manager. These responsibilities can vary significantly in different enterprises and, in some cases, may include some DR and BC activities.

## 4.2.8 The Role of the Information Security Manager in Incident Management

The role the information security manager has within BC, DR planning and incident response is going to be influenced by multiple factors, such as the enterprise's size, the industry, applicable regulatory requirements and the maturity of BC, DR and incident response capabilities. The information security manager typically is responsible for responding to information securityrelated incidents.

27 FIRST, "FIRST CSIRT Services Framework" Version 2.1, www.first.org/standards/frameworks/csirts/csirt\_services\_framework\_v2.1

<!-- page: 266 -->

In smaller enterprises, the information security manager may be involved in all BC, DR and incident response functions—assisting the business units in completing their business impact analyses (BIAs), working with the IT department to identify suitable backup and recovery solutions, coordinating incident response efforts as events are escalated, and delivering normal information security services needed by the enterprise.

In larger enterprises, BC, DR and incident response business functions may be separate departments, each with their own dedicated staff and budgets needed to support operations. Here, the role of the information security manager may be an internal consultant, advising as a subject matter expert in any of the related functions. The information security manager may be a general contributor—supporting and augmenting existing operations and delivering services in support of business need—or may function purely as a business peer, with security incidents being reported for the purposes of monitoring, prioritization and remediation, and with response efforts performed by the incident response department.

Regardless of the environment the information security manager is operating in, it is important to have a good conceptual and practical understanding of what is required to adequately address related responsibilities. In addition, there must be a good understanding of the BC and DR processes. This is to ensure that incident management and response plans and activities integrate well with the overall BCP and DRP in the event that an incident escalates to a disaster.

## 4.2.9 Risk Management

Effective incident management and response capabilities are necessary for successful outcomes of risk management. Any risk that materializes and is not prevented by the enterprise's internal controls constitutes an incident that must be managed and responded to with the intent that it does not escalate into a disaster.

## 4.2.10 Assurance Process Integration

The type and nature of incidents the information security manager may deal with often require the involvement of a number of other organizational functions, such as physical security, HR and legal. It is important to ensure that incident management and recovery plans actively incorporate and integrate those functions as required. An effective outcome is a set of plans that define which departments are involved in various incident management and response activities and specify that those linkages have been tested under realistic conditions.

<!-- image -->

## 4.2.11 Value Delivery

Incident management capabilities must be closely integrated with business functions and provide the last line of defense to support cost-effective risk management. Incident management involves more than the technology controls to prevent or respond to incidents; it includes a set of processes that can provide an optimal balance between prevention, containment and restoration.

To deliver value, incident management should:

- Integrate with business processes and structures as seamlessly as possible.
- Improve the capability of businesses to manage risk and provide assurance to stakeholders.
- Integrate with the business continuity plan (BCP).
- Become part of an enterprise's overall strategy and effort to protect and secure critical business functions and assets.
- Provide the backstop and optimize risk management ● efforts

## 4.2.12 Resource Management

Resource management encompasses time, people, budget and other factors to achieve objectives efficiently under given resource constraints. Incident management and response activities consume resources that must be managed to achieve optimal effectiveness. This is accomplished by ensuring appropriate oversight, monitoring of resources and regular reporting. When it is not possible to achieve all objectives, effective resource management ensures that the most important priorities are addressed first. In terms of incident response, effective triage capabilities ensure that limited resources are applied most effectively to contain and limit damage. This is based on quickly identifying compromised assets that cannot be quickly addressed, the assets that are unaffected and can wait, and the ones that can most efficiently be restored with the available resources.

<!-- page: 267 -->

<!-- image -->

## 4.2.13 Defining Incident Management Procedures

There is no single, fixed, one-size-fits-all set of incident management procedures for every enterprise. However, there are a number of good practices that most enterprises adopt and customize to meet their own specific needs. Commonly adopted approaches are available from CMU SEI and the SANS Institute, among others.

## 4.2.14 Detailed Plan of Action for Incident Management

There are a number of approaches to developing the incident management plan and IRP.

CMU/SEI's Defining Incident Management Processes describes the following approach (figure 4.3):28

1. Prepare (prepare/improve/sustain)—This process defines all program preparation work that has to be completed prior to having any capability to respond to incidents. It contains subprocesses to evaluate incident-handling capability and postmortem review of incidents for improvements. Subprocesses include:
2. Coordinate planning and design:
3. Identify incident management requirements.
4. Establish vision and mission.
5. Obtain funding and sponsorship.
6. Develop implementation plan.
7. Coordinate implementation:
8. Develop policies, processes and plans.
9. Establish incident-handling criteria.
10. Implement defined resources.
11. Evaluate incident management capability.
12. Conduct postmortem review.
13. Determine incident management process changes.
14. Implement incident management process changes.
2. Protect (reputation/brand/infrastructure/data) From the business perspective, the goal is to protect the enterprise's reputation and brand. From a

technology perspective, the goal is a process that aims to protect and secure critical data and computing infraśtructure and its constituency when responding to incidents. It also proposes improvement on a predetermined schedule while keeping the appropriate security context in consideration. Subprocesses include:

- Implement changes to computing infrastructure to mitigate an ongoing or potential incident.
- Implement infrastructure protection improvements from postmortem reviews or other process improvement mechanisms.
- ■ Evaluate computing infrastructure by performing proactive security assessment and evaluation.
- Provide input to detect process on incidents/potential incidents.
3. Detect (events/incidents/anomalies)The detect process identifies unusual, suspicious or malicious activity that might impact critical business functions or infrastructure. Subprocesses include:
- Proactive detection—The detect process is conducted regularly prior to an incident. The IMT monitors various types of information from online/periodic vulnerability scanning, network monitoring, antivirus and firewall alerts, security information and event management (SIEM) products, file integrity management products, data loss prevention products, thirdparty monitoring service alerts, commercial vulnerability alert services, risk analysis threat intelligence reports and security audit/assessments.
- Reactive detection—The detect process is conducted when there are reports from system users or other enterprises. Users may notice unusual or suspicious activity and report it to the IMT. It is also possible that another enterprise's IMT will provide advisories when its system has received malicious activity from an enterprise.
- For the IMT to receive the report promptly, there should be multiple communication channels from end users to the IMT. This can be in the form of phone calls, faxes, email messages, web-form reporting, team collaboration suites, or automated intrusion detection systems (IDSs).

28 Alberts, C; A. Dorofee; G. Killcrece; R. Ruefle; M. Zajicek; Defining Incident Management Processes for CSIRTs: A Work in Progress, Carnegie Mellon University, USA, 2004

<!-- page: 268 -->

4. Triage—Triage is a process of sorting, categorizing, correlating, prioritizing and assigning incoming reports/events into (typically three) categories: the problems that cannot be readily resolved, those that can wait and those that can be efficiently addressed with the resources available. It is an essential element of any incident management capability to ensure maximum effectiveness of limited resources. When there are multiple incident reports coming into the IMT, triage allows events to be prioritized appropriately, thus maximizing response effectiveness. It can also serve as a single point of entry for any IMT communication and information.
2. Properly organized, triage can provide a snapshot of the current status of all incident activity reported, a central location for incident status reporting and an initial assessment of incoming reports for further handling. Triage prioritization can be done at two levels:
3. Tactical—Based on a set of criteria
4. Strategic—Based on the activity's impact on the ability to achieve business goals and objectives
5. Subprocesses include:
6. Categorization—This is the use of predetermined criteria to classify all incoming reports/events. There are many ways to categorize events, such as:
7. Denial of service (DoS)
8. Malicious code
9. Unauthorized access 0
10. 0 Inappropriate usage
11. 0 Login successes and failures
12. Elevation of account privileges 0
13. 0 Privileged account access
14. 0 Data extraction
15. 0 Extended account use
16. 0 Remote access patterns
17. 0 Changes in logging/audit settings
18. Phishing attacks, viruses, worms, etc. 0
19. Correlation—This subprocess correlates a report/event with other relevant information. A higher correlation of a report/event provides more information that is useful for the IMT to decide on the

29 Ibid appropriate response. For example, a specific event may be the cause of an incident whereas another may be a consequence and dealing with it would not resolve the issue.

<!-- image -->

- Prioritization—In an ideal world, every 0 undesirable event is followed up as soon as possible. However, resources are limited, and it may not always be possible. To ensure minimal impact to critical business functions or information assets, incidents are usually prioritized based on their potential impact rather than a specific set of criteria. Remediation efforts obviously start with the highest priority and then move down to the lowest priority.

Assignment——When an incident or potential incident has been identified, it is assigned to the IMT to initiate the response effort. Assignment may be based on:

- Workload of IMT members
- 0 IMT members who have handled similar incidents
- 0 Category or priority of the event
- 0 Relevant business unit
5. Respond—The response process includes steps taken to address, resolve or mitigate an incident. CMU SEI defines three types of response activities:29
- Technical response—It is appropriate for technical IMT members, such as incident handlers and IT representatives, to analyze and resolve an incident. Technical response forms include the following:
- Collecting data for further analysis
- Analyzing incident-supporting information such as log files
- Researching corresponding technical mitigation strategies and recovery options
- Consulting telephone or email technical assistance
- Securing onsite assistance
- Analyzing logs
- Developing and deploying patches and workarounds

<!-- page: 269 -->

<!-- image -->

- Management response—The management response includes activities that require supervisory or management intervention, notification, interaction, escalation or approval as part of the response effort. This response activity is normally executed by business managers, senior management and members of the affected business units.
- Legal response—The legal response is associated with activity that relates to investigation, prosecution, liability, copyright and privacy issues, laws, regulations and nondisclosure agreements. Because this response may require in-depth knowledge on legal matters, it is usually referred to the corporate legal team.

<!-- image -->

## 4.2.15 Current State of Incident Response Capability

Most enterprises have some sort of ad hoc or formal incident response capability. The information security manager must identify what is already in place as a basis for understanding the current state. There are many ways to do this, including:

- Survey of senior management, business managers and IT representatives—Uses input from senior management, business line managers and technology representatives, employee surveys and focus groups to gather information to help determine the past performance and perception of the IMT and its process capabilities.
- Self-assessment—Self-assessment is conducted by the IMT against a set of criteria to develop an understanding of current capabilities. This is the easiest method because it does not require participation from many stakeholders. The disadvantage of this method is that it may provide only a limited view of current capabilities and other aspects that stakeholders may consider important.
- External assessment or audit—This is the most comprehensive option, and it combines interviews, surveys, simulation and other assessment techniques in the assessment. This option is normally used for an enterprise that already has an adequate incident management capability but is further improving it or reengineering the processes.

These techniques will help to determine if the current state is effective and, if not, will help with determining the desired state of the incident response capability.

## Threats

Threats are any event that may cause harm to an enterprise's assets, operations or personnel. There are a number of threats that must be considered, including:

- Environmental—Environmental threats include natural disasters. While natural disasters vary among

locations, some natural disasters may occur for prolonged periods of time and others may occur annually. Some potentially catastrophic threats are rare enough and impractical to address effectively, so they are either generally disregarded (e.g., comet strike) or might be addressed with some type of business interruption insurance.

<!-- page: 271 -->

<!-- image -->

- Technical—Technical threats include fire; electrical failure; heating, ventilating and air conditioning (HVAC) failure; information system and software issues; telecommunications failure; and gas/water leakage. Technical threats are normally found in every enterprise and are quite common. With sufficient planning, most technical threats can be managed adequately. The exceptions may be advanced persistent threats and zero-day attacks.
- Human driven—Threats that arise from humaninitiated actions may include damage by disgruntled employees, accidents in the workplace, taking shortcuts to save time, and political instability, which may degrade or severely impact business functions. Many of these threats may be easy to identify while some, such as corporate sabotage/espionage or embezzlement, will be far more difficult.

## Vulnerabilities

A weakness in a system, technology, process, person or control that can be exploited and result in compromise is a vulnerability. A vulnerability that can be exploited by threats results in risk. One aspect of risk management is managing vulnerabilities to maintain risk within acceptable limits as determined by the enterprise's risk appetite and tolerance criteria. Vulnerability management is part of the incident management capability; it is the proactive identification, monitoring and repair of any weaknesses.

## 4.2.16 Developing an Incident Response Plan

The IRP is the operational component of incident management. The plan details the actions, personnel and activities that take place in case adverse events result in the loss of data, information systems or processes. The plan should include the formation, management and maintenance of the incident response team.

## Elements of an Incident Response Plan

A common approach to developing an IRP is to base it on a six-phase model of incident response that covers preparation, identification, containment, eradication, restoration and follow-up. Those stages are defined as follows:

1. PreparationThis phase prepares an enterprise to develop an IRP prior to an incident. Sufficient preparation facilitates smooth execution. Activities in this phase include:
2. Establishing an approach to handle incidents
3. Establishing policy and warning banners in information systems to deter intruders and allow information collection
4. Establishing a communication plan for stakeholders
5. Developing criteria on when to report an incident to authorities
6. Developing a process to activate the IMT
7. Establishing a secure location to execute the IRP
8. Ensuring equipment needed is available
9. Establishing a capability to create a baseline for information security risk metrics
10. Establishing a capability to automate rapid collection, analysis and escalation of information security risk status
2. Identification—This phase aims to verify if an incident has happened and to find out more details about it. Reports on possible incidents may come from information systems, end users or other enterprises. Not all reports are valid incidents; they may be false alarms or may not qualify as an incident. Activities in this phase include:
12. 厦 Assigning ownership of an incident or potential incident to an incident handler
13. Verifying that reports or events qualify as an incident
14. Establishing chain of custody when handling potential evidence
15. Determining the severity of an incident and escalating it as necessary
3. Containment—After an incident has been identified and confirmed, the IMT is activated and information from the incident handler is shared. The team will conduct a detailed assessment and contact the system owner or business manager of the affected information systems/assets to coordinate further action. The action taken in this phase is to limit the exposure. Activities in this phase include:
17. Activating the IMT/IRT to contain the incident
18. Notifying appropriate stakeholders affected by the incident
19. Obtaining agreement on actions taken that may affect availability of a service or risk of the containment process

<!-- page: 272 -->

- Getting the IT representative and relevant virtual team members involved to implement containment procedures
- Obtaining and preserving evidence
- Documenting actions and making backups from this phase onward
- Controlling and managing the PR team's communications to the public
4. Eradication—When containment measures have been deployed, it is time to determine the root cause of the incident and eradicate it. Eradication can be done in a number of ways: restoring backups to achieve a clean state of the system, removing the root cause, improving defenses and performing a vulnerability analysis to identify any additionally impacted systems with the same root cause. Activities in this phase include:
- Determining the signs and cause of incidents
- Locating the most recent version of backups or alternative solutions
- Removing the root cause. In the event of worm or virus infection, it can be removed by deploying appropriate patches and updating antivirus software.
- Improving defenses by implementing protection techniques
- Performing a vulnerability analysis to discover related vulnerabilities identified during root cause analysis
5. Recovery—This phase ensures that affected systems or services are restored to a condition specified in the service delivery objectives (SDO) or BCP. The time constraint up to this phase is documented in the RTO. Activities in this phase include:
- Restoring operations as defined in the SDO
- Validating that actions taken on restored systems were successful
- Getting involvement of system owners to test the system
- Facilitating system owners to declare normal operation
6. Lessons learned—At the end of the incident response process, a report should always be developed to share what has happened, what actions were taken, and the results after the plan was executed. Part of the report should contain lessons learned that provide the IMT and other stakeholders

<!-- image -->

valuable learning points on what could have been done better. These lessons should be developed into a plan to enhance the incident management capability and the documentation of the IRP. Activities in this phase include:

- Creating the incident report
- Analyzing issues encountered during incident response efforts
- Proposing improvement based on issues encountered
- Presenting the report to relevant stakeholders

## Gap Analysis—Basis for an Incident Response Plan

A gap analysis provides information on the gap between current incident response capabilities and the desired level determined by senior management. Comparing the two levels allows improvements in capabilities, skills and technology to be identified, including:

- Processes that need to be improved to be more efficient and effective
- Resources needed to achieve the objectives for the incident response capability

The resulting gap analysis report can be used for planning purposes to determine the steps needed to close the gaps between the current state and the desired state. It can also be useful in determining the most effective strategy to achieve the objectives and prioritize efforts. The priorities should be based on the areas of greatest potential impact and on the best cost benefit.

## Logistics

The plan must include provisions for all logistical support necessary for continuing normal business activities during the recovery effort. This includes detailed, up-to-date hard-copy procedures that can be followed easily by staff and contract personnel who are unfamiliar with the standard and recovery operations. This ensures that the plan can be implemented, even if members of the regular staff are unavailable. Also, a supply of special forms, such as check stock, invoice forms and order forms, should be secured at an offsite location.

If the data entry function is dependent on certain hardware devices or software programs, these programs and equipment, including specialized electronic data interchange (EDI) equipment and programs, must also be provided at the recovery site.

## 4.2.17 Incident Management and Response Teams

The plan must identify teams and define their assigned responsibilities ahead of an incident occurring. To implement the strategies that have been developed for business recovery, key decision-making, technical and end-user team leaders need to be designated and trained. Depending on the size of the business operation, the team may consist of a single person. The involvement of these teams depends on the level of the disruption of service and the types of assets lost, compromised, damaged or endangered. A matrix should be developed that indicates the correlations among the functions of the different teams. This will facilitate estimating the magnitude of the effort and activating the appropriate combination of teams. Examples of the kinds of teams usually needed include:

- Emergency action team—Designated first responders whose function is to deal with fires or other emergency response scenarios.
- Damage assessment team—Qualified individuals who assess the extent of damage to assets and make an initial determination regarding what is a complete loss versus what is restorable or salvageable.
- Emergency management team—Responsible for coordinating the activities of all other recovery teams and handling key decision-making.
- Relocation team—Responsible for coordinating the process of moving from the affected location to an alternative site or to the restored original location.
- Security team—When no designated/formal capability is defined by the enterprise, the security team will often become the de facto CSIRT. It is responsible for monitoring the security of systems and communication links, containing any ongoing security threats, resolving any security issues that impede the expeditious system recovery and ensuring the proper installation and functioning of every security software package.

A number of key decisions must be agreed on during the planning, implementation and evaluation phases of the response and recovery plan. These include:

- Goals/requirements/products/services for each phase
- Key goal indicators (KGIs)/key performance indicators (KPIs)
- RTO/RPO
- Reporting criteria
- Critical success factors and critical path aspects of implementation
- Alternative facilities in which tasks and operations can be performed
- Critical information resources to deploy (e.g., data and systems)
- Decision authority and persons responsible for completion
- Available resources—including financial, personnel and technical—to aid in deployment
- Scheduling of activities with established priorities

## 4.2.18 Organizing, Training and Equipping the Response Staff

Training the response teams is not only essential but also critical. The information security manager should develop reasonable, real-world event scenarios and test the response and recovery plans to ensure that team participants are familiar with their tasks and responsibilities. Through this process, the teams will identify the resources they require for response and recovery. An added value of training is detecting and modifying ambiguous procedures to achieve clarity and determining recovery resources that may not be adequate or effective.

IMT members should undergo the following training program:

- Induction to the IMTThe induction should provide the essential information required to be an effective IMT member.
- Mentoring team members regarding roles, ● responsibilities and procedures—Existing IMT members can provide valuable knowledge to aid new members after induction. To facilitate effective mentoring, the buddy system can be used, pairing new members with experienced members.
- On-the-job training—This may serve to provide an understanding of company policies, standards, procedures, available tools and applications, acceptable codes of conduct, etc.

<!-- page: 274 -->

- Formal training—Team members may require formal training to attain an adequate level of competence necessary to support the overall incident management capability.

## 4.2.19 Incident Notification Process

Having an effective and timely security incident notification process is a critical component of any security program. The information security manager should understand how obtaining timely and relevant information can help the enterprise respond quickly and efficiently and will ultimately limit the potential loss and damage that may occur as the result of an incident. Notification mechanisms that enable an automated detection system or monitor to send email or phone messages should be used whenever possible. The following functions are most likely to need information concerning incidents when they occur:

- Application development
- Business process owners
- Cybersecurity
- HR (when an incident appears to involve insiders)
- IT department
- Legal/general counsel
- Network operations
- Physical and information security
- Privacy department (when an incident appears to impact privacy)
- PR/corporate communications
- Risk management
- Senior management
- Threat intelligence team

Notification activities are effective only if knowledgeable personnel understand their responsibilities and perform them in an efficient and timely manner. The information security manager therefore needs to define the responsibilities and communicate them to key personnel. It can also be effective to work with HR to determine how responsibilities can be documented in employees'job descriptions.
