## 4.8.4 Skills

To build an IRT with capable incident handlers, enterprises need people with both soft and technical skill sets——abilities that enable them to respond to incidents, perform analysis tasks, and communicate effectively with the constituency and external contacts. They must also be competent problem solvers, easily adapt to change, and effective in their daily activities.

The set of basic skills that IRT members need can be separated into two broad groups: personal and technical skills.

Personal skills are the major parts of the incident handier's daily activity. They include:

- Communication—The ability to communicate ● effectively is a critical component of the skills needed by IRTs. They need to be effective communicators to ensure that they obtain and supply the information necessary to be helpful. They need to be good listeners, understanding what is said (or not said), to enable them to gain details about an incident that is being reported. They also remain in control of these communications to most effectively determine what is happening, what facts are important and what assistance is necessary.
- Members of an IRT need to communicate with:
- Team members
- IT staff
- Application owners
- Users of the systems
- Technical experts
- Management and other administrative staff
- HR
- Law enforcement
- Media/PR staff
- Vendors
- Communication can take many forms, including:
- Email responses concerning incidents
- Documentation of event or incident reports, vulnerabilities and other technical information
- Notifications and guidelines that are provided to the constituency
- Internal development policies and procedures
- Other external communications to staff, management or other relevant parties

<!-- page: 307 -->

<!-- image -->

- Leadership skills—Members of an IRT are often faced with directing and getting support of other members of the enterprise, so leadership is an important attribute.
- Presentation skills—An IRT's skills are needed for technical presentations, management or sponsor briefings, a panel discussion at a conference, or some other form of public speaking engagement. The specialist member's skills might extend to providing expert testimony in legal or other proceedings on behalf of the team or users.
- Ability to follow policies and procedures—Team members need the ability to follow and support the established policies and procedures for incident response management.
- Team skills—IRT members must have the ability to work in a team environment as productive and cordial team players; to be aware of responsibilities; to contribute to the goals of the team; and to work together to share information, workload and experiences. Members must be flexible and willing to adapt to change. There may be a need for one or more team members to act in a leadership role to support the smaller groups or technical teams.
- Integrity—Team members often deal with information that is sensitive and, occasionally, they may have access to information that is newsworthy. Members must be trustworthy, discreet and able to handle information in confidence.
- Self-understanding—Team members must be able to recognize their limitations and actively seek support from their team members, other experts or management.
- Coping with stress—The IRT is likely to face stressful situations. The members need to be able to recognize when they are becoming stressed, be willing to make their fellow team members aware of the situation and take the necessary steps to control and maintain their composure.
- Problem solving—Without good problem-solving skills, team members could become overwhelmed with the volumes of data related to incidents and other tasks that need to be handled. Problem-solving skills also include an ability to think outside the box or look at issues from multiple perspectives to identify relevant information or data. This includes knowing who else to contact or approach for additional information, creative ideas or added technical insight.
- Time management—Team members might be confronted with a multitude of tasks, ranging from analyzing, coordinating and responding to incidents, to performing duties such as prioritizing their workload, attending and preparing for meetings, completing time sheets, collecting statistics, conducting research, giving briefings and presentations, traveling to conferences, providing onsite technical support, and prioritizing tasks. Team members must be able to balance efforts between completing the tasks and recognizing when to seek help or guidance.

Technical skills are the basic skills required by IRT members and are of two types:

- Technical foundation skills—These require a basic ● understanding of the underlying technologies used by the enterprise.
- Incident-handling skills—These require an understanding of the techniques, decision points and supporting tools (software or applications) required in daily activities.

## 4.8.5 Awareness and Education

While high-profile breaches and security incidents have increased the security awareness of most individuals, end users are the first line of defense in preventing security breaches. Therefore, it is essential for the information security manager to ensure that an ongoing awareness campaign highlights the importance of being mindful in order to reduce susceptibility to activities that may lead to a security breach (e.g., phishing attacks, malicious websites).

Periodically, a skills assessment is useful to determine whether the required expertise is available in the enterprise for the IRT. In some cases, relevant training or education may serve to provide the necessary skills. If an enterprise is unable to find internal experts or to hire/train staff to provide the necessary incident response specialist skills, it may be able to develop relationships with experts in the field to provide the necessary skills. When a situation arises in which in-house knowledge is insufficient, these technical specialists can be called on to fill the gap in expertise.

<!-- page: 308 -->

## 4.8.6 Audits

Internal and external audits are performed to verify compliance with policies, standards and procedures defined by an enterprise. Internal audits are conducted by specialists within the enterprise and are usually intended to support compliance requirements or improve risk and incident management. External audits involve a third party, who performs the tasks. While most external audits are exercised as part of mandatory requirements, they are often imposed as part of business collaboration.

Both types of audits can be useful in reviewing incident management and response plans and capabilities. Periodic audits of the processes and procedures specified in the plans can provide validation that security will not be compromised in the event of an incident, and policy compliance and legal requirements are addressed appropriately. Audits can provide an objective view of the overall completeness and functionality of the incident management and response plans and provide assurance that major gaps in the processes do not exist.

## 4.8.7 Outsourced Security Providers

Outsourcing incident management capability may be a cost-effective option, especially for smaller enterprises (see Section 3.13.2 Third-Party Service Providers). These enterprises simply may not have the internal resources to adequately provide the necessary IMT/IRT skills.

Enterprises that outsource their IT operations may benefit from close integration if incident management is outsourced to the same vendor. These enterprises still require an IRP overseen by an IRT, even if components of incident management are outsourced. It will be essential to clearly understand the outsourcer's capabilities, response times, etc., and develop proper SLAs containing appropriate indemnity clauses.

The information security manager should consider the following when security functions are fully or partially outsourced:

- Matching the enterprise's incident reference numbers with the vendors for each applicable incident: This ensures a common understanding of incident details between enterprises. This also helps to identify the actual organizational recovery time. For example, the vendor may report that service was

<!-- image -->

restored at 4:00 p.m.; however, the outsourcing enterprise may note that the incident ended at 6:00 p.m. This means that it took the enterprise an additional two hours to recover internally from the incident. This can be determined by matching the enterprise's incident reference numbers with the vendor's.

- Integration of the enterprise's change management functions with the vendor's (to the extent possible): Depending on the nature of the service provided, the enterprise's change management functions may be linked via leaders on the change advisory board or have a platform where the security group can view the vendor's changes and follow-up with key points of contact from the vendor. Also, this contributes to awareness of system changes by both enterprises.
- Requirement from the vendor for periodic review of incidents that occurs on a regular basis (e.g., monthly, annually): Operational leadership from both the enterprise and the vendor attend these meetings, and all incidents/events are reviewed. Follow-up items are generally taken from these meetings to help prevent incidents from recurring.

## 4.9 Incident Investigation and Evaluation

Not every event is an incident, and the information security manager must be aware of the subtle difference between the two. An event is something that happens at a specific place or time: an account logon, a door opening, an automated process ending. These are all events, lacking any context, that occur with little to no concern. Contextual data adjacent or related to the event need to be investigated to determine if the event was in fact normal or abnormal.

For example, a user account logging in during business hours is an event that, according to an established baseline (see Section 2.2.1 Security Control Baselines), occurs normally throughout the business day. Any deviation to that, such as a user account attempting to log in after business hours, is an event that may warrant further investigation as it is outside of established norms. Additional contextual information may yield this as being either a legitimate event (i.e., the user is currently traveling abroad, with the login coinciding with the user's local business day) or it could be a malicious event (i.e., credentials were acquired by an unauthorized third-party and are being used to access enterprise

As the event is not part of enterprise standard operations and may cause an interruption or reduce quality of service in addition to exposing the enterprise to unacceptable risks, it should be declared an incident.

Once sufficient, proper context around an event has been investigated and evaluated, then appropriate action can be taken. This may result in implementation and execution of the enterprise response and recovery plans in varying degrees depending upon the severity and impact of the incident to the enterprise.

## 4.9.1 Executing Response and Recovery Plans

Given that a major incident usually causes considerable confusion and a host of unexpected conditions, it is essential that the incident management and response plans have been tested under realistic conditions. It is possible that untested plans will not work as expected. It is also safe to expect that the more severe the incident, the greater the potential chaos, confusion and problems facing the incident management and response teams. Incidents can range from an attack bringing down IT systems to an earthquake bringing down the building. To provide reasonable assurance that the enterprise is preserved under foreseeable circumstances, all reasonably possible events must be anticipated and prepared for and the planning must be thorough, realistic and tested.

## Ensuring Execution as Required

To ensure the response and recovery plans are executed as required, the plans need a facilitator to direct the tasks within the plans, oversee their execution, liaise with senior management and make decisions as necessary. The information security manager may or may not be the appropriate person to act as the recovery plan coordinator but must be certain the role is assigned to someone who can perform this critical function.

Developing appropriate response and recovery strategies and alternatives is an essential component in the overall process of executing the response and recovery plans. It will provide reasonable assurance that the enterprise can recover its key business functions in the event of a disruption and respond appropriately to a securityrelated incident.

<!-- page: 310 -->

Testing the plans is essential to ensuring that plans can be executed as required. It will also help employees become familiar with the process so when an incident occurs they can respond accordingly.

The information security manager should appoint an independent observer to record progress and document any exceptions that occur during testing and during an actual event. Through a post-event review, the information security manager and key recovery personnel can then review the observations and make adjustments to the plan accordingly.

## 4.10 Incident Containment Methods

As each incident is unique, methods to contain the incident must be tailored. Understanding the benefits and drawbacks associated with initiating containment is vital. Senior management must be fully aware and understand the implications, as they can have a significant impact on immediate response efforts and may result in unplanned outcomes.

Containment includes all the activities, tasks and steps taken in the attempt of limiting or reducing the impact of an incident. Containment is a short-term, tactical action that is meant to purely to stop the bleeding, not necessarily to identify or correct the root cause that allowed the incident to occur.

Common containment activities performed during a security incident may include, but are not limited to, the following:

- Notification and escalation to relevant stakeholders
- Memory captures and analysis
- Enterprise-wide password changes of all accounts
- Updating firewall rule sets to block/deny/drop traffic
- Updating IDS signatures
- Log collection, review and analysis
- Forensically image impacted systems
- Malware reverse engineering
- Removing the device from the network

<!-- image -->

For example, if the incident involves a malware-infected system actively being controlled by an adversary, the enterprise may choose to disconnect the system from the network, update firewall rules to block identified IP addresses and domains associated with the adversary or scan for indicators of compromise to identify other compromised systems. The purpose is to identify all potentially impacted systems in order to remove the adversary from the environment.

Weighing the benefits and risk as to when to initiate containment efforts is not a decision that should be made without senior management's full understanding and approval. Ultimately senior managementwith recommendations from the legal counsel, the information security manager and the IMT—will need to make a decision at what point and how prepared the enterprise is to contain the incident. This is because once containment efforts are initiated, the adversary will be aware their presence is noticed, and they may retaliate.

## 4.11 Incident Response Communications

As an incident has the potential for impacting various aspects of an enterprise, clear lines of authorized and authoritative communication channels need to be defined in advance. This is to ensure that chances of misunderstanding and limiting misinformation are reduced as much as possible. Because things can change as an incident unfolds, keep in mind that what was truthful when initially reported may become factually inaccurate upon further investigation and will need to be addressed appropriately.

Given the number of personnel associated with responding to an incident, establishing an authoritative source for communicating is mandatory. Often speculation may be taken for fact or facts downplayed due to misunderstanding or lacking appropriate insight and context. There will be different communication channels and methods that need to be defined prior to an incident being declared. These need to be documented and conveyed to each member to ensure that during an incident everyone knows who and where the authoritative information relating to the incidents is coming from.

There are a number of communication channels that should be established during an incident, as communications will need to occur between the IMT manager and senior management over decisions on whether to communicate with enterprise staff, external third parties and affected business partners. Each communication channel needs to be clearly defined, understood and conveyed to all affected members to ensure the proper messages are communicated to their respective audiences.

<!-- page: 311 -->

<!-- image -->

From a technical perspective, the IMT members will need a method to facilitate communications out-of-band or to communicate by other than normal communication methods. For example, in responding to a suspected network intrusion, users should not communicate over suspected compromised infrastructure that may alert intruders that they have been identified. This results in the IMT members switching to an approved browserbased email platform (e.g., Google Business) instead of the normal enterprise business email (e.g., Microsoft 365).

## 4.11.1 Notification Requirements

Notification requirements are key parts of the IRP and incident management. The IRP should include a directory of key decision-making personnel, IRT members, information systems owners, end users and others required to initiate and carry out response efforts. This directory should include multiple communication methods (telephone, cellular phone, texting, email, etc.) in the event of any communications channel failure.

The directory should include, at a minimum, the following individuals:

- Representatives of equipment and software vendors
- Contacts within companies that have been designated to provide supplies and equipment or services
- Contacts at recovery facilities, including hot site ● representatives or predefined network communications rerouting services
- Contacts at offsite media storage facilities and the contacts within the company who are authorized to retrieve media from the offsite facility
- Insurance company agents
- Contact information for regulatory bodies
- Contacts at HR and contract personnel services
- Law enforcement contacts

Note that the decision to bring in law enforcement during such an incident rests solely with senior management. It is generally not the role of an information security manager to inform external organizations. There are companies that handle automated emergency response communications. However, as with any other outsourced service, careful consideration should be given to the required processes that must be in place to ensure the effectiveness of this solution.

## 4.11.2 Communication Networks

The plan must contain details of the enterprise's telecommunication networks needed to restore business operations. Because of the criticality of these networks, the procedures to ensure continuous telecommunication capabilities should be given a high priority. Telecommunication networks are susceptible to the same natural disasters as data centers but are also vulnerable to disruptive events unique to telecommunications. These include central switching office disasters, cable cuts, communication software glitches and errors, security breaches from hacking (phone hackers are known as phreakers), and a host of other human errors. The local exchange carrier is typically not responsible for providing backup services. Although many carriers normally back up main components within their systems, the enterprise should make provisions for backing up its own telecommunication facilities.

Telecommunications capabilities to consider include telephone voice circuits, wide area networks (WANs) (connections to distributed data centers), LANs and third-party providers. Options can include satellite and microwave links and, depending on criticality and location, wireless links or even single sideband radiotelephone communications. Critical capacity requirements should be identified for the various thresholds of outage, such as two hours, eight hours or 24 hours, for each telecommunications capability. Uninterruptable power supplies (UPSs) should be sufficient to provide backup for both telecommunications equipment and computer equipment.

## 4.12 Incident Eradication and Recovery

While containment is a short-term approach to limit an incident and keep it from spreading, eradication includes the activities, tasks and steps taken to correct the root cause that led to the incident occurring. This should be properly planned out and executed once containment efforts have been deemed successful.

<!-- page: 312 -->

## 4.12.1 Eradication Activities

Common eradication activities performed during a security incident include, but are not limited to, the following:

- Root cause analysis
- Cleanup and removal of any artifacts left behind from the incident
- Application of any outstanding patches
- DNS null routing (sinkhole) of malicious IP addresses and fully qualified domain names
- Additional changes to firewalls and IDSs as needed
- Scanning for additional indicators of compromise (IoCs)
- Removing malicious software
- Wipe/rebuilding impacted systems
- Restoring from backups

## 4.12.2 Recovery

Recovery efforts follow only after the successful containment and eradication phases of the incident response process life cycle. After the incident has been fully addressed and root cause issues remediated, the focus shifts to ensuring that the business can successfully return to operations, which means restoring impacted systems to normal. During this phase, the information security manager should remain vigilant, as rushing an impacted system back into production may reintroduce the same vulnerabilities and causes that initiated the original incident.

During the recovery phase, the activities should be planned and implemented to prevent similar events from occurring. Common recovery activities performed after a security incident has been successfully eradicated include, but are not limited to, the following:

- Testing and validating the security baseline.
- Monitoring network for known indicators of attack (IoAs) and IoCs.
- Actively searching for identified adversary artifacts across the enterprise.
- Moving impacted systems back into production once recovered and verified to meet the security baseline.

<!-- image -->

Note: Avoid the rush to recovery. Once a system has been compromised by an adversary, the fidelity in that system is zero. It may appear easier to attempt to remove identified adversary artifacts (e.g., backdoors, tool kits, etc.) from the system in an effort to quickly restore services to the business. However, once a system has been compromised, there is no assurance of what may have gone undetected or missed.

Once recovery efforts are started, most enterprises are satisfied with simply returning to business as usual (BAU) operations. Keep in mind, these are the same BAU operations that allowed the incident to occur initially. The need to properly address and remediate the root cause of the incident is important to ensure that business risk is managed properly. While the immediate incident has been resolved, the work is just beginning.

## 4.13 Post-Incident Review Practices

Understanding the purpose and structure of post-incident reviews and follow-up procedures enables the information security manager to continuously improve the security program. A consistent methodology should be adopted within the information security enterprise so that when a problem is found, an action plan is developed to reduce/mitigate it. Once the action plan is created, steps should be taken to implement the solution. By following these basic principles, the information security program is able to adapt to changes in the enterprise and the threats it faces. In addition, this reduces the amount of time personnel need to react to security incidents, so they are able to spend more time on proactive activities.

The follow-up process in incident response is potentially the most valuable part of the effort. Lessons learned during incident handling can improve both the security practice and the incident response process itself. Additionally, the information security manager needs to calculate the cost of the incident once all response efforts are completed by adding the cost of any loss or damage plus the cost of labor and any special software or hardware needed to handle the incident. The cost provides a useful metric, especially in justifying the existence of the response team to senior management, and may be used as evidence in a court case.

When concluding and closing out an incident, common post-incident activities need to be planned and carried out. Once the business has successfully recovered, activities may include, but are not limited to, the following:

<!-- page: 313 -->

<!-- image -->

- Documenting the incident
- Stakeholder review and feedback
- Finalizing the report for senior management
- Identifying changes required
- Identifying any process issues
- Updating procedures as needed
- Developing remediation plans to mitigate incident root cause
- Seeking resource and funding approval

The information security manager should manage postincident reviews to learn from each incident and the resulting response and recovery effort; this information can then be used to improve the enterprise's response and recovery procedures. The information security manager may perform these reviews with the help of third-party specialists if detailed forensic skills are needed.

## 4.13.1 Identifying Causes and Corrective Actions

Security incidents can be the result of externally initiated attacks, internally initiated attacks or failures in security controls that have been implemented. For a systematic review of security incidents, the information security manager should appoint an incident review team. This team should review any evidence and develop recommendations to enhance the information security program by identifying root causes of a specific incident and necessary measures to prevent the same/similar events from recurring. The root causes of many system compromises, for example, are weak or nonexistent vulnerability assessment and patch management efforts.

The analysis should be done to determine answers to questions such as:

- Who is involved?
- What has happened?
- Where did the attack originate?
- When (what time frame)?
- Why did it happen?
- How was the system vulnerable or how did the attack occur?
- What was the reason for the attack (i.e., the perpetrator's motivation)?

## 4.13.2 Documenting Events

During and subsequent to any actual or potential security incident, the information security manager should have processes in place to develop a clear record of events. Preserving this information will enable investigation of events and it can be provided to a forensics team or authorities if necessary. To ensure this record-keeping occurs, one or more individuals should be specifically charged with incident documentation and the preservation of evidence. Documentation of any event that has possible security implications can provide clarity as to whether an incident is an accident, a mistake or a deliberate attack.

A serious incident is typically chaotic. Good documentation will prove invaluable in post-incident investigation and forensics and may also be helpful in incident resolution.

## 4.13.3 Establishing Legal Procedures to Assist in Post-incident Activities

Having solid, legally defensible procedures in place prior to an incident being declared is key to successful recovery and response.32 As cybercrime has surged in recent years, regulators, legislatures and plaintiffs' attorneys have placed cyber preparedness and incident response under a microscope. This has led to potentially significant risk and exposure arising from compliance with a myriad of new laws and regulatory reforms. Given this landscape, it is imperative that enterprises involve legal counsel in the preparation for and participation in incident response.

Preparing a comprehensive IRP is an important first step to ensure an efficient and effective response to a security incident and the inevitable swell of legal and regulatory landmines. A good IRP is one that is customized to the enterprise and has been developed, vetted and tested by legal counsel and key internal stakeholders. While it may be easy to pull a standard IRP form from the internet, this check-the-box approach is not helpful when an incident actually occurs. An IRP should:

32 In development of this section specifically, the U.S.-based fitm Vorys, Sater, Seymour and Pease LLP—recognized experts specializing in IT, privacy and data security—was consulted to identify some key concerns and considerations from the legal aspect, with consideration relating to incident response.

<!-- page: 314 -->

- Identify a core team of responders who will manage the response.
- Provide a procedure for documentation of the events leading up to and following the discovery of a compromise (including third parties who have access to organizational information).
- Establish a clear and immediate communication plan that includes communications to internal contacts, third parties (including law enforcement and regulators), advisors (including legal counsel and insurance carriers), customers and the media.
- Set forth key decision points that need to be made.
- Include forms for notifications that can be quickly modified to send to regulators and customers in sufficient time to comply with notification deadlines.

In a highly regulated environment, an IRP should position the enterprise for the legal and technical hurdles it may encounter when responding to an incident. When a security incident occurs, legal counsel should be consulted immediately, as this will help ensure that an investigation is covered by the attorney-client privilege. Legal counsel is also vital in analyzing and fulfilling any notification requirements within the legally mandated number of hours following discovery. Every state has different notice requirements applicable to both individuals and state agencies, and there may be additional notification requirements to third parties, such as insurance carriers or business partners. Complying with these various notification requirements is a complicated process fraught with significant risk of mistakes and legal and regulatory exposure.

<!-- image -->

investment and resources and are critical for key stakeholders, while also encouraging team building among the participants.

The business case for proactive incident response preparedness is a compelling one. According to IBM Security's 2021 report, the average data breach in the United States costs an enterprise $4.24 million, a 10 percent increase from 2020. Remote working increased the average total cost of a data breach. However, enterprises that prepared and tested their IRPs prior to an incident averaged a response cost difference of 54.9 percent less than those with no plan or testing.33

Having a good legal framework is important to provide options to the enterprise, including pursuing civil or criminal legal action against the perpetrators. The information security manager should develop data preservation procedures with the advice and assistance of legal counsel, the enterprise's managers and knowledgeable law enforcement officials to ensure that the procedures provide sufficient guidance to IT and security staff. With the assistance of these specialized resources, the information security manager can develop procedures to handle security events in a manner that preserves evidence, ensures legally sufficient chain of custody, and is appropriate to meet business objectives.

Once an enterprise has developed its IRP, it should be tested with a team including legal counsel. For many enterprises, annual testing of the IRP is required. Tabletop trainings evaluate the enterprise's ability to effectively execute the IRP by simulating a real-world data security incident. Benefits of tabletop tests include reviewing the plan in a real-world scenario, preparing members of executive management for their responsibilities in an incident and identifying and closing any gaps and bottlenecks that are discovered. Tabletop exercises are a modest commitment in terms of time, There are a few basic actions that the information systems staff must understand, including doing nothing that could change, modify or contaminate potential or actual evidence. Trained forensics personnel can inspect computer systems that have been attacked, but if the enterprise's personnel contaminate the information, the data may not be admissible in a court of law and the forensics staff may be unable to use the data in investigating an incident. Computer forensics and gathering and handling information and physical objects relevant to a security incident in a systematic manner so they can be used as evidence in a court of law should be performed by specially trained staff, third-party specialists, security IRT or law enforcement officials. The initial response by the system administrator should include:

- Determining privileged versus non-privileged investigation by legal counsel.
- Retrieving information needed to confirm an incident.

## 4.13.5 Legal Aspects of Forensic Evidence

For evidence to be admissible in legal proceedings, it must have been acquired in a forensically sound manner and its chain of custody maintained. The information security manager in charge of an incident must have established and documented procedures for acquisition of evidence by properly trained independent personnel.

The required documentation to maintain legally admissible evidence must include:

- Chain of custody forms that provide:
- Name and contact information of custodians
- When, why and by whom an evidence item was acquired or moved
- Detailed identification of the evidence (serial numbers, model information, etc.)
- Where it is stored (physically or logically)
- When/if it was returned
- Checklists for acquiring technicians (including details of legally acceptable forensic practices)
- Detailed activity log templates for acquiring technicians
- Signed nondisclosure/confidentiality forms for all ● technicians involved in recovering evidence
- An up-to-date case log that outlines:
- Dates when requests were received
- Dates investigations were assigned to 器 investigators
- Name and contact information of investigators and requestors
- M Identifying case number
- Basic notes about the case and its requirements and completed procedures
- Date when completed

<!-- page: 316 -->

- Investigation report templates that include:
- Name and contact information of investigators
- Date of investigation and an identifying case number
- ■ Details of any interviews or communications with management or staff regarding the investigation
- Details of devices or data that were acquired (serial numbers, models, physical or logical locations)
- Details of software or hardware tools used for acquisition or analysis (must be recognized forensically sound tools)
- Details of findings including samples or copies of relevant data and references to their storage location
- ⅢI Final signatures of investigator in charge

Procedures for initiating a forensics investigation need to be agreed to, documented, followed carefully and understood by everyone in the enterprise. The information security manager should work with management and HR (and other stakeholders) to establish a process that ensures that all investigations are fair, unbiased and well documented.

It is important to be aware that legal requirements vary in different jurisdictions. As a result, informed legal advice for appropriate processes that meet judicial standards will be required.

Depending on the way an enterprise's security information and event management (SIEM) tool is set up, it is possible for the same incident to be reported multiple times through numerous sources. ## APPENDIX A: CISM Exam General Information

ISACA is a professional membership association composed of individuals interested in IS audit, assurance, control, security and governance. The CISM Certification Working Group is responsible for establishing policies for the CISM certification program and for developing the exam.

Note: Because information regarding the CISM examination may change, please refer to www.isaca.org/credentialing/CISM for the most current information.

## Requirements for Certification

The CISM designation is awarded to those individuals who have met the following requirements: 1) achieve a passing score on the CISM exam, 2) adhere to the Code of Professional Ethics, 3) adhere to the continuing education policy and 4) demonstrate the required minimum work experience supporting the governance of the IT-related contribution to an enterprise.

## Successful Completion of the CISM Exam

The exam is open to all individuals who wish to take it. Successful exam candidates are not certified until they apply for certification (and demonstrate that they have met all requirements) and receive approval from ISACA.

## Experience in Information Security

CISM candidates must meet the stated experience requirements to become certified. Please refer to the www.isaca.org/credentialing/cism/get-cism-certifiedfor experience requirements and a list of experience waivers.

Experience must have been gained within the 10-year period preceding the application date for certification or within five years from the date of initially passing the exam. A completed application for certification must be submitted within five years from the passing date of the CISM exam. All experience must be independently verified with employers.

## Description of the Exam

The CISM Certification Working Group oversees the development of the exam and ensures the currency of its content. Questions for the CISM exam are developed through a multitiered process designed to enhance the ultimate quality of the exam.

The purpose of the exam is to evaluate a candidate's knowledge and experience in data privacy. The exam consists of 150 multiple-choice questions, administered during a three-hour session.

## Registration for the CISM Exam

The CISM exam is administered on a continuous basis at qualifying test sites Please refer to the ISACA Exam Candidate Information Guide at www.isaca.org/credentialing/cism for specific exam registration information including registration, scheduling and languages, and other important key information for exam day. Exam registrations can be made online at www.isaca.org/credentialing/cism.

## CISM Program Accreditation Renewed UnderISO/IEC 17024:2012

The American National Standards Institute (ANSI) has voted to continue the accreditation for the CISA, CISM, CGEIT, CRISC and CISM certifications, under ISO/IEC 17024:2012, General Requirements for Bodies Operating Certification Systems of Persons. ANSI, a private, nonprofit organization, accredits other organizations to serve as third-party product, system and personnel certifiers.

ISO/IEC 17024 specifies the requirements to be followed by organizations certifying individual against specific requirements. ANSI describes ISO/IEC 17024 as "expected to play a prominent role in facilitating global standardization of the certification community, increasing mobility among countries, enhancing public safety, and protecting consumers."

## APPENDIX A: CISM EXAM GENERAL INFORMATION APPENDIX A: CISM EXAM GENERAL INFORMATION

ANSI's accreditation:

- Promotes the unique qualifications and expertise ISACA's certifications provide.
- Protects the integrity of the certifications and provides legal defensibility.
- Enhances consumer and public confidence in the certifications and the people who hold them.
- Facilitates mobility across borders or industries.

Accreditation by ANSI signifies that ISACA's procedures meet ANSI's essential requirements for openness, balance, consensus and due process. With this accreditation, ISACA anticipates that significant opportunities for CISAs, CISMs, CGEITs and CRISCs will continue to open in the United States and around the world.

## Scheduling the Exam

The CISM exam can be scheduled directly from your My ISACA Certification Dashboard. Please see the Exam Candidate Information Guide for complete instructions. Exams can be scheduled for any available time slot. Exams may be rescheduled a minimum of 48 hours prior to the originally scheduled appointment. If you are within 48 hours of your original appointment, you must take your exam or forfeit the exam registration fee.

## Sitting for the Exam

Prior to the day of the exam make sure you:

- Locate the test center and confirm the start time.
- Plan to arrive 15 minutes prior to exam start time.
- Plan to store personal belongings.
- Review the exam day rules.

You must present an acceptable form of identification (ID) in order to enter the testing center. Please see the Exam Candidate Information Guide for acceptable forms of ID.

You are prohibited from bringing the following into the test center:

- Reference materials, paper, notepads, or language dictionaries
- Calculators
- Any type of communication, surveillance or recording devices such as:
- Mobile phones
- Tablets
- Smartwatches or glasses
- Mobile devices
- Baggage of any kind including handbags, purses or è briefcases
- Weapons
- Tobacco products
- Food or beverages
- Visitors

<!-- image -->

If exam candidates are viewed with any such communication, surveillance or recording devices during the exam administration, their exam will be voided, and they will be asked to immediately leave the exam site.

Personal items brought to the testing center must be stored in a locker or other designated area until the exam is completed and submitted.

Avoid activities that would invalidate your test score:

- Creating a disturbance.
- Giving or receiving help; using notes, papers, or other aids.
- Attempting to take the exam for someone else. ●
- Possession of communication, surveillance or recording device, including but not limited to cellphones, tablets, smart glasses, smartwatches, mobile devices, etc., during the exam administration.
- Attempting to share test questions or answers or ● other information contained in the exam (as such are the confidential information of ISACA); including sharing test questions subsequent to the exam.
- Leaving the testing area without authorization. ● (These individuals will not be allowed to return to the testing room.)
- Accessing items stored in the personal belongings area before the completion of the exam.

## Budgeting Your Time

The exam is administered over a three-hour period. This allows for a little over 1.5 minutes per question.

<!-- page: 325 -->

<!-- image -->

Therefore, it is advisable that candidates pace themselves to complete the entire exam.

## Grading the Exam

Candidate scores are reported as a scaled score. A scaled score is a conversion of a candidate's raw score on an exam to a common scale. ISACA uses and reports scores on a common scale from 200 to 800.

A candidate must receive a score of 450 or higher to pass the exam. A score of 450 represents a minimum consistent standard of knowledge as established by ISACA's CISM Certification Working Group. A candidate receiving a passing score may then apply for certification if all other requirements are met.

Passing the exam does not grant the CISM designation. To become a CISM, each candidate must complete all requirements, including submitting an application and receiving approval for certification.

The CISM examination contains some questions that are included for research and analysis purposes only. These questions are not separately identified, and the candidate's final score will be based only on the common scored questions. There are various versions of each exam but only the common questions are scored for your results.

A candidate receiving a score less than 450 is not successful and can retake the exam by registering and paying the appropriate exam fee. To assist with future study, the result letter each candidate receives will include a score analysis by content area.

You will receive a preliminary score on screen immediately following the completion of your exam. Your official score will be emailed to you and available online within 10 working days. Questionlevel results cannot be provided.

In order to become CISM-certified, candidates must pass the CISM exam and must complete and submit an application for certification (and must receive confirmation from ISACA that the application is approved). The application is available on the ISACA website at www.isaca.org/credentialing/cism. Once the application is approved, the applicant will be sent confirmation of the approval. The candidate is not CISM-certified, and cannot use the CISM designation, until the candidate's application is approved. A

processing fee must accompany CISM applications for certification.

Candidates receiving a failing score on the exam may request a rescoring of their exam within 30 days following the release of the exam results. All requests must include the candidate's name, exam identification number and mailing address. A fee of US $75 must accompany this request.

## A A

Acceptable interruption windowperiod of time that a system can be compromising the achievement of business objectives. Acceptable interruption window—The maximum period of time that a system can be unavailable before compromising the achievement of the enterprise's business objectives.

Acceptable use policy—A policy t agreement between users and the e for all parties, the ranges of use tha gaining access to a network or the Acceptable use policy—A policy that establishes an agreement between users and the enterprise that defines, for all parties, the ranges of use that are approved before gaining access to a network or the Internet

Access control—The processes, ru mechanisms that control access to i resources and physical access to pr Access controlThe processes, rules and deployment mechanisms that control access to information systems, resources and physical access to premises

Access path—The logical route th access computerized information. Access path—The logical route that an end user takes to access computerized information.

Scope Notes: Typically includes a r operating system, telecommunicati application software and the access Scope Notes: Typically includes a route through the operating system, telecommunications software, selected application software and the access control system.

Access rights—The permission or users, programs or workstations to or view data and files within a syste rules established by data owners an security policy Access rights—The permission or privileges granted to users, programs or workstations to create, change, delete or view data and files within a system, as defined by rules established by data owners and the information security policy

Accountability—The ability to ma event back to the responsible party Accountability—The ability to map a given activity or event back to the responsible party

Administrative control—The rule practices dealing with operational e efficiency and adherence to regulat policies. Administrative controlThe rules, procedures and practices dealing with operational effectiveness, efficiency and adherence to regulations and management policies.

Advanced Encryption Standard algorithm that supports keys from size Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)—A public algorithm that supports keys from 128 bits to 256 bits in size

Advanced persistent threat (APT possesses sophisticated levels of ex significant resources, which allow opportunities to achieve their objec multiple attack vectors, e.g., cyber, deception. These objectives typical establishing and extending footholo Advanced persistent threat (APT)An adversary that possesses sophisticated levels of expertise and significant resources, which allow them to create opportunities to achieve their objectives by using multiple attack vectors, e.g., cyber, physical, and deception. These objectives typically include establishing and extending footholds within the information technology infrastructure of the targeted organizations for purposes of exfiltrating information; undermining or impeding critical aspects of a mission themselves to carry out these objectives in the future. An advanced persistent threat (APT):

- Pursues its objectives repeatedly over an extended period of time
- Adapts to defenders' efforts to resist it
- Is determined to maintain the level of interaction needed to execute its objectives

Source: CMMC-NIST SP800-39

Alert situation—The point in an emergency procedure when the elapsed time passes a threshold and the interruption is not resolved. The enterprise entering into an alert situation initiates a series of escalation steps.

Algorithm—A finite set of well-defined, unambiguous rules for the solution of a problem in a finite number of steps, it is a sequence of operational actions that lead to a desired goal and is the basic building block of a program

Alternate facilities——Locations and infrastructures from which emergency or backup processes are executed, when the main premises are unavailable or destroyed Scope Notes: Includes other buildings, offices or data processing centers

Alternate process—Automatic or manual process designed and established to continue critical business processes from point-of-failure to return-to-normal

Annual loss expectancy (ALE)—The total expected loss divided by the number of years in te forecast period yielding the average annual loss

Anomaly detection—Detection on the basis of whether the system activity matches that defined as abnormal

Antimalware—A widely used technology to prevent, detect and remove many categories of malware, including computer viruses, worms, Trojans, keyloggers, malicious browser plug-ins, adware and spyware

Antiphishing—Software that identifies phishing content and attempts to block the content or warn the user about the suspicious nature of the content

Antivirus software—An application software deployed at multiple points in an IT architecture. It is designed to detect and potentially eliminate virus code before damage is done and repair or quarantine files that have already been infected.

<!-- page: 330 -->

Application controls——The policies, procedures and activities designed to provide reasonable assurance that objectives relevant to a given automated solution (application) are achieved.

Application programming interface (API)—A set of routines, protocols and tools referred to as building blocks used in business application software development

Application service provider (ASP)—Also known as managed service provider (MSP), it deploys, hosts and manages access to a packaged application to multiple parties from a centrally managed facility.

Scope Notes: The applications are delivered over networks on a subscription basis.

Architecture—Description of the fundamental underlying design of the components of the business system, or of one element of the business system (e.g., technology), the relationships among them, and the manner in which they support enterprise objectives

Asset—Something of either tangible or intangible value that is worth protecting, including people, information, infrastructure, finances and reputation

Asset inventory—A register that is used to record all relevant assets

Asset value—The value of an asset to both the business and to competitors

Asymmetric key (public key)—A cipher technique in which different cryptographic keys are used to encrypt and decrypt a message

Scope Notes: See public key encryption.

Attack vector—A path or route used by the adversary to gain access to the target (asset)

Scope Notes: There are two types of attack vectors: ingress and egress (also known as data exfiltration).

Audit trailData in the form of a logical path linking a sequence of events, used to trace the transactions that have affected the contents of a record

Source : ISO

Authentication—1. The act of verifying identity, i.e., user, system

Scope Notes: Can also refer to the verification of the correctness of a piece of data.

2. The act of verifying the identity of a user, the user's eligibility to access computerized information Scope Notes: Authentication is designed to protect against fraudulent logon activity. It can also refer to the verification of the correctness of a piece of data.

<!-- image -->

Authorization—The process of determining if the end user is permitted to have access to an information asset or the information system containing the asset.

Availability—Ensuring timely and reliable access to and use of information

## B

Backup center—An alternate facility to continue IT/IS operations when the primary data processing (DP) center is unavailable.

Baseline security—The minimum security controls required for safeguarding an IT system based on its identified needs for confidentiality, integrity and/or availability protection

Benchmarking—A systematic approach to comparing

enterprise performance against peers and competitors in an effort to learn the best ways of conducting business.

Scope Notes: Examples include benchmarking of quality, logistic efficiency and various other metrics.

Bit—A contraction of the term binary digit, and the most basic and smallest unit of computing information. A bit may be in one of two states, logic 1 or logic 0. It can be thought of as a switch that is either on or off. Bits are usually combined into computer words of various sizes, named bytes.

Bit copy—Provides an exact image of the original and is a requirement for legally justifiable forensics

Bit-stream image—Bit-stream backups, also referred to as mirror image backups, involve the backup of all areas of a computer hard disk drive or other type of storage media.

Scope Notes: Such backups exactly replicate all sectors on a given storage device including all files and ambient data storage areas.

Blue team—A group that proactively conducts systematic examinations of information systems or products to determine the adequacy of security measures, identify security deficiencies, responds to technical security incidents and confirms the adequacy of such measures after implementation. Blue teams are typically internal security personnel that may or may not be part of an enterprise security operations center.
